alchemy-ancient-and-modern-being-a-brief: Alchemy Ancient and Modern, 1911. The alchemical survey. This book preserves that history. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. Those who study the era will use it in their work.
andreyev-king-hunger-1911:
King Hunger, Leonid Andreyev's allegorical play, appeared in English in Poet Lore in the winter of 1911. Eugene M. Kayden made the translation. King Hunger, a gaunt personified power, rouses the starving poor of a great city to rise against the rich who feast above them.

Bells, judges, and workers people the stark, symbolic stages of the play. The rising swells toward a climax that Andreyev shapes as vision rather than report. He called such works dramas of ideas, meant to stage the forces that move crowds. Of all his plays, this one presses revolution most directly. The Poet Lore printing gave American readers an early taste of his radical theater.
arxiv-2512-00011:
Pablo Villacorta-Aylagas and co-authors present MRSeqStudio, a web platform for designing MRI sequences. Magnetic resonance imaging depends on pulse sequences, the timed patterns that produce each kind of scan. Building and testing them usually needs specialist software and hardware access.

Their free, open-source service pairs a sequence designer in the browser with the KomaMRI physics simulator behind it. The mix of accessibility, interactivity, and flexibility suits both teaching and research. Students can learn sequence design hands-on, without a scanner. Education and research are the twin audiences, since the same environment serves classroom learning and sequence development.
arxiv-2512-00311:
Intelligent tutoring systems work best when they know what a student understands right now. Jungyang Park and co-authors trace mathematical proficiency through problem-solving processes in 2025, rather than through answers alone. Traditional knowledge tracing models rely only on whether responses were correct.

Correctness hides the rich information inside a student's steps, false starts, and strategies. Using the process itself should improve predictions of future performance and make the model's judgments explainable to teachers. Better tracing supports tutoring that responds to how a student thinks, not just to a string of right and wrong marks. Problem-solving traces can be captured by tutoring software without extra testing time. That makes the approach cheap to add to systems already in classrooms.
arxiv-2512-00411:
Superconducting leads joined through a normal metal form Josephson junctions, workhorses of quantum devices. Bobkov and co-authors develop a theory of planar quasi-ballistic Josephson junctions in 2025. Multiple leads couple through a large, nearly ballistic normal metal crystal.

Their approach rests on quasiclassical Eilenberger equations. It emphasizes reflections of electrons from crystal surfaces or single impurities, a mechanism distinct from both purely ballistic and diffusive limits. The theory matches the multiterminal devices now being built, helping experimentalists predict supercurrents in cleaner, larger junctions. Quasi-ballistic means electrons cross the metal almost without scattering, yet reflections still matter. The framework is built to match the planar devices experimentalists now fabricate. For teams who build such links, the gain is a firm base for tests. They can check a new chip face to face with what the math says it should do.
arxiv-2512-00511:
Compressing speech for automatic recognition is different from compressing it for human ears. Ellison Murray, Morriel Kasher, and Predrag Spasojevic present a low-complexity speech codec using parametric dithering in 2025. Dithering, usually a perceptual trick, is justified here by proofs and by tests for recognition input.

The authors pin down what best recognition performance means under lossy input compression. Their parametric dithering technique then shapes the compression noise deliberately. A cheap codec that keeps recognition accuracy high would help voice assistants and transcription services run on low-bandwidth links and small devices. Recognition systems care about word errors, not how pleasant the audio sounds. Low complexity keeps the codec usable inside the recognition pipeline itself. For folks who build voice tools, the gain is a cheap front end. Speech can be shrunk hard, and the words still come through for the tool to read well.
arxiv-2512-00811:
Tony Puthenpurakal wrote a 2025 algebra paper on invariant rings. A finite group can act on a vector space, reshuffling its points by symmetry. The invariant ring collects the polynomial functions that the group leaves unchanged, a central object in algebra.

The paper studies fixed points and the grade of a Hilbert polynomial tied to that ring. The Hilbert polynomial counts dimensions of the ring's pieces and grows in a regular way for large sizes. Results like these link symmetry, counting, and depth in one package. They give algebraists sharper tools for rings that arise from group actions.
arxiv-2512-01411:
Fabrice Baudoin, Teije Kuijper, and Jing Wang study Brownian motion on a quaternionic flag shape. That shape is a space of nested planes over quaternions. Brownian motion there is a random walk with no jumps. The team gives a clean way to build it.

They build it from a symplectic Brownian motion as a matrix flow. They then link its radial part to motion on a quaternionic sphere. That link yields a closed form for a key joint law. Such forms help in random matrix theory and in physics models with quaternionic traits.
arxiv-2512-01511:
Sabalbal and co-authors sharpen planet hunting in the SHINE survey. High-contrast imaging seeks faint planets next to bright stars. A new method, the Regime Switching Model, mixes many image tricks at once. It aims to split true planet light from star speckles.

The team gauges how much the method lifts detection limits in the F150 data. Better limits mean smaller, dimmer planets can be found. Each new find adds to the census of young giant planets. That census tests how such planets form and move in their first ages. RSM gains grow where speckles are worst, near the star, which is just where young planets are most prized and hardest to see.
arxiv-2512-02011:
Robots with multi-fingered hands struggle to learn delicate tasks in simulation, because contact forces and touch signals are so hard to imitate faithfully. Elvis Hsieh and co-authors present DexScrew in 2025, a framework that carries skills learned in imperfect simulations onto real hardware.

They demonstrate the transfer on two demanding jobs: fastening a nut onto a bolt and driving a screw with a multi-fingered hand. Both tasks depend on rich contact and tactile feedback, exactly what simulators model worst. Showing that learning can survive those flaws widens the range of manipulation skills robots can practice safely in virtual worlds first.
arxiv-2512-02211:
A group in algebra can sometimes be covered entirely by the centralizers of its elements, the subgroups of members that commute with a given one. Mark Lewis and Ryan McCulloch prove in 2025 two clean statements about such covers of finite groups.

They show that the centralizers that are maximal under inclusion already form a cover, and so do those that are minimal. Both extremes suffice, a tidy symmetry in the structure of finite groups. Covering problems sound abstract, but they measure how a group's commuting patterns fit together, a basic fingerprint used across group theory.
arxiv-2512-02611:
Semeon A. Bogaty and Alexey A. Tuzhilin extend a classic way to compare shapes and spaces. The Gromov-Hausdorff distance measures how far two metric spaces are from matching exactly. Shape comparison tools across geometry and data science rest on this idea.

Their continuous version also accounts for topological differences, not just distances. Two spaces can sit close in distance yet differ in how they connect. A distance that sees both gaps gives a fuller test of sameness. The paper lays foundations for this refined measure, which may serve geometry, imaging, and shape analysis. A sharper yard stick for shape helps fields as far apart as drug scans and parts checks for planes.
arxiv-2512-02911:
Hsuanling Lee and four co-authors present FluxLab, a toolkit for printing objects that change shape and sense their own bending. Shape changing devices promise interfaces and tools that adapt in the hand. Sensing the deformation from inside the printed part is the hard part.

Their printable nesting structure wraps a shape memory alloy channel for sensing and actuation. Lattice padding gives support and tunable elasticity, while helix surface wires preserve form and anchor guided motion. Designers of tangible interfaces gain a route to custom, responsive objects without hand built electronics. Print, bend, and sense in one part cuts the wires and boards that make soft rigs stiff, dear, and hard to fix in the field.
arxiv-2512-03311:
Agents that know almost nothing about their network can still coordinate. Sandy Irani and Michael Luby introduce a broadcast model called the singing model in this 2025 work. Agents do not know the network's size or shape, not even their own neighbors.

Agents can sing several notes, heard by neighbors nearby. The model extends the beeping model, where agents emit only one tone. The authors use it to sing a maximal independent set, a group with no two members linked. Simple rules like these aid sensor networks. Singing uses pitch variety, which gives agents a richer signal than a single beep.
arxiv-2512-03411:
Dark energy may change over time, recent data suggest. Tonatiuh Matos presents a conformal holographic model for it in this 2025 work. Results from the DESI collaboration favor evolving dark energy over a fixed cosmological constant.

The data also show tension in the inferred matter density between DESI and Planck. Neutrino mass estimates press against their lower bounds too. A holographic model tied to conformal ideas offers another account of the expansion. Testing it against data may clarify the cosmic energy budget. Holographic ideas tie dark energy to entropy bounds, a link this model explores.
arxiv-2512-03511:
Magnetic groups change how some algebraic objects are sorted. Higinio Serrano and Bernardo Uribe work out a Brauer group for that case in this 2025 work. For a magnetic finite group, they look at classes of graded algebras over the complex numbers.

These algebras are central and simple, and they transform under the group in a set way. The classes form the magnetic graded Brauer group. The authors find its full structure as an abelian group. Such sorting tools serve topology and physics, where Brauer groups label states of matter. The result gives other scholars a firm base for later work.
arxiv-2512-03611:
Seeing the Sun's poles directly was long impossible from Earth. D. Calchetti and a large team report the first such observations in this 2025 work. Views from the ecliptic plane, where Earth orbits, hide the solar poles.

In spring 2025, Solar Orbiter observed the poles from out of the ecliptic with its remote-sensing instruments. The team presents the first out-of-ecliptic look at the polar magnetic field. Polar fields drive the Sun's activity cycle and solar wind. Direct views could improve space weather forecasts. Spring 2025 gave the first window, as Solar Orbiter's tilt grew enough to see over the Sun's equator toward its poles.
arxiv-2512-03811:
A calorimeter measures particle energy by watching how much light a material gives off when particles pass through. Sergey Barsuk, Mykhailo Yeresko, and colleagues tested a small prototype of the GRAiNITA detector concept at a CERN test beam in June 2024. Their 2025 instrumentation preprint reports the first results from two days of pion beam data.

The analysis estimates how much detector non-uniformity blurs the energy measurement, a contribution captured by a constant term in the resolution. Even with a small prototype, that term came out well below one percent. The team also confirmed that the statistical contribution from counting photo-electrons shrinks with energy in the expected way. Together the numbers match the design hopes for GRAiNITA. They now feed into plans for optimising a full-scale version of the detector.
arxiv-2512-03911:
Brain-inspired computer chips promise robot control that is fast and frugal with energy. Kenneth Stewart and colleagues demonstrate that promise in a 2025 robotics preprint, running a learned controller for the Astrobee free-flyer on Intel's Loihi 2 neuromorphic hardware. Their pipeline converts ordinary neural networks into spiking ones that such chips can execute.

The original policy was trained by reinforcement learning entirely in simulation, using simple rectified units. The team transformed it into a spiking sigma-delta network compatible with the Loihi 2 architecture, then closed the loop inside a detailed physics simulator. They compare execution on the neuromorphic chip against a graphics processor. The converted controller still flies the simulated robot, showing that simulation-trained policies can survive the move to spiking hardware. The authors frame the work as a path toward real-time, energy-efficient autonomy for space and ground robots alike.
arxiv-2512-04011:
Gravitational waves born in the early universe carry a spectrum that later cosmic conditions can bend. Giuseppe Fanizza, Eliseo Pavone, and Luigi Tedesco study one influence in a 2025 cosmology preprint: shear viscosity in the cosmic fluid after inflation.

The authors show viscosity adds a damping term to the wave equation, reshaping both the transfer function and the energy spectrum. Constant viscosity relative to the expansion rate tilts the spectrum redder, while time-varying viscosity makes the spectral index run with frequency. Their framework applies to standard and exotic histories alike. As a case study, they compute the effect of the electron-photon-baryon plasma before recombination. Wave freeze-out from that phase leaves a slight blue tilt. Future detectors could read such tilts as fossils of the cosmic fluid.
arxiv-2601-06811:
Luigi Romano wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on friction where a wheel or ball rolls on a surface. The paper works with a model called FrBD, short for Friction with Bristle Dynamics. Past work with the model dealt with one plane of slip at a time.

Romano now extends the model to two planes at once. The new form can deal with slip along the roll and slip to the side at the same time. It can also deal with spin. It tracks how the contact patch moves and turns. The patch has a set size and shape. For work on tires and wheels, the model gives a fuller view of grip.
arxiv-2601-07411:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Zihao Fu and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers SCALPEL. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Large language models have achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, yet their deployment in many applications such as healthcare.

Legal systems, and autonomous decision-making remains limited by our incomplete understanding of their internal mechanisms. As these models become increasingly integrated into high-stakes systems, understanding how they encode and execute specific capabilities has become fundamental to interpretability research. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07711:
Pietro Ferrazzi and colleagues test whether fancier retrieval really helps question answering, in a 2026 preprint. Retrieval-augmented generation pairs a generator with search over a knowledge base. Basic versions suffer from noisy retrieval, poor query matching, and misuse on out-of-scope questions. Generator cost and variability add further problems. Agentic RAG promises to fix these issues with more steps and decisions.

The authors run an experimental comparison of RAG approaches. Their title asks the blunt question: is agentic RAG worth it? Extra agent steps cost time and money, so gains must be proven, not assumed. A careful comparison helps teams choose simpler systems when they perform just as well. The paper speaks to engineers building search-backed assistants. It treats added complexity as a cost that must earn its place.
arxiv-2601-08011:
Xin Jin, Yichuan Zhong, and Yapeng Tian blend a new object and a new style into images in one pass. Text-conditioned diffusion editors handle single object replacement well. They struggle when an object and a style must change together. Their system, TP-Blend, receives two separate prompts: one for the blend object, one for the target style. Both are injected into a single denoising trajectory. The 2026 preprint describes the training-free framework.

Twin-prompt attention pairing keeps the two prompts from interfering. Training-free means users can apply it to existing models without new data. Precise blending serves designers who need a specific object rendered in a specific look. Keeping object and style controls separate matches how people describe edits. The paper serves computer vision scholars in image editing. It adds fine control without added training cost.
arxiv-2601-08411: Particle filtering under low or degenerate observation noise is the subject of a 2026 arXiv paper. The filtering problem tracks a hidden state from noisy measurements over discrete time. Here the observation equation is a linear function of the state, and the additive noise is low or degenerate. The authors place minimal assumptions on the hidden state process itself. Degenerate noise breaks standard filters that expect noise in every direction. New methods could sharpen tracking in navigation and sensing systems with near-exact measurements.
arxiv-2601-08711:
Shifa Sulaiman, Francesco Schetter, Mehul Menon, and Fanny Ficuciello combine model-based and data-based control for a prosthetic hand wrist. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that advanced control algorithms help prosthetic hands replicate intricate human hand motions. The target device is the tendon-driven soft continuum wrist of PRISMA HAND II.

The controller joins an artificial neural network approach with a sliding mode controller. Model-based design gives structure, while the network adapts to behavior the model misses. A wrist that moves naturally and holds position under load can make a prosthesis far more usable. Hybrid control offers a practical route when soft hardware is hard to model exactly.
arxiv-2601-09011:
Steven Frank writes on a famed rule by Fisher on how selection shifts gene counts. The rule says the shift from selection is the gene shift times a set of slope weights. Those weights are the mean effect of each gene on fitness. The rule has sparked long fights in bio work on what it does and does not claim.

Frank ties the rule to slope tools used in cause work. That tie may clear what the weights mean, and when they can be read as cause marks. Old fights oft rest on a mix of math form and cause sense. A reader in bio theory gets a bridge. It links a classic rule to tools that cause work uses each day.
arxiv-2601-09111:
Yang Li and three co-authors free nav agents from a closed world bind. A nav agent must go to a goal based on words, such as go to the red door past the desk. Past tests train and test in the same homes with the same word style. Real homes are new, and real words vary wild. Closed tools fail hard in that open world.

Their agent thinks in two gears. A fast gear acts on clear steps. A slow gear plans when the scene or words are new. The gears swap as need shifts. A reader who builds guide bots gets a plan for the open world, where each home and each ask can be a first.
arxiv-2601-09211:
Chunghyun Park, Seunghyeon Lee, and Minsu Cho find where on a thing a named act can be done, in full 3D. Give a shot with depth and a text ask, such as grasp the handle. Past tools mark the zone on the seen face just. The back face, hid from the shot, gets no mark, yet a robot may need it.

Their tool is called Affostruction. It first grows the full shape of the thing from the part shot. It then marks act zones on the whole shape, hid parts too. A reader in robot sight gets marks that fit a real grasp, not just a flat view. The grown shape is the key step.
arxiv-2601-09411:
Anuj Jakhar, Ravi Kalwaniya, Anwesh Ray, and Bidisha Roy study the shapes of a family of number fields. Their 2026 arXiv paper concerns sextic pure number fields, fields built by adjoining a sixth root. The shape of a number field is the form of its ring of integers, seen as a lattice up to rotation, reflection, and scaling.

Shapes give a compact fingerprint of a field's arithmetic geometry. The authors work out how these shapes are distributed across the family. Distribution results show whether shapes cluster on special forms or spread evenly. Such counts connect lattice geometry with the statistics of number fields, a theme of modern arithmetic statistics.
arxiv-2601-09611:
Irina Ya. Aref'eva, Ali Hajilou, Kristina Rannu, and Pavel Slepov study how heavy quarks lose energy in hot quark matter. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses a holographic model of the quark-gluon plasma. The tool is the spatial Wilson loop, whose tension sets an effective potential.

The plasma here has two kinds of anisotropy: an external magnetic field and a spatial one. Both twist how quarks drag through the medium. Holography turns the hard strong-force problem into a geometry problem in one more dimension. Results feed the reading of heavy-ion collision data, where quark energy loss is a key signal.
arxiv-2601-09811:
Maria Vasilyeva and five co-authors fit modern learning tools to classic models of disease and ecology. Their 2026 arXiv paper compares neural ODEs, Kolmogorov-Arnold network ODEs, and SINDy on coupled systems. The base models are the SIR epidemic model and the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey system.

The authors then merge the two into a coupled Lotka-Volterra-SIS model. Neural ODEs learn the dynamics as a continuous flow; SINDy seeks a sparse equation instead. Comparing the three on the same systems shows what each recovers well. The work guides modelers who must learn epidemics that interact with ecosystems.
arxiv-2601-09911:
Younghun Kim, Spiro Gicev, Martin Sevior, and Muhammad Usman write about quantum LDPC codes. These codes are a way to store quantum states with low cost. They guard the stored states against errors. A key need is a full set of gates that can act on the stored states.

Recent work points to shift moves as a core piece of that full gate set. The paper deals with time based circuits that carry out such shifts. The goal is to do so in a fault safe way. That means small errors in the circuit should not grow and spoil the stored state. The work speaks to those who build quantum memory.
arxiv-2601-10011:
Zerui Yang and co authors build a tool that turns plain words into code queries. The task is named NL2SQL. A user asks a fact in plain words. The tool must write a query that pulls the right rows. Past tools learn from right cases only.

That leaves a rich source untapped. Past wrong tries and their fixes show where tools fail. The team built Memo-SQL to use those pairs. It splits a hard ask into parts. It also fixes its own tries based on past fixes. The plan needs no fresh training. It learns from saved tries at test time.
arxiv-2601-10611:
The Molmo2 release gives the open community weights and data for vision-language models that handle video. Such models watch images and clips and answer in words. Today's strongest ones are closed products. Open rivals often train on synthetic data made by those closed models, or hide their training data and recipe.

That gap leaves open-source teams with weak ground to build on. Molmo2 targets video understanding and grounding, the skill of pointing words at the right part of a scene. By sharing both weights and data, the release lets others check, retrain, and improve the models. It aims to reset what open video-language work can start from.
arxiv-2601-10811:
Emmanuel J. Greenfield and James E. Owen study what disk photoevaporation does to giant planets locked in resonance. A young star's light boils gas off its planet-forming disk. That slow loss changes the forces on planets over millions of years. Planet pairs in mean motion resonance, circling in a fixed rhythm, are a sharp test case.

The team runs two-dimensional fluid simulations with the FARGO3D code, adding mass loss from photoevaporation. They scan disk mass, viscosity, planet mass, and resonance type. The runs show which resonant pairs survive the disk's decay and which break apart. The results feed models of how mature planetary systems got their final shapes.
arxiv-2601-10911:
Xiaocai Zhang and co-authors train ship navigation that is both autonomous and sustainable. Maritime transport faces pressure on emissions and on safety. Traditional navigation leans on human experience. It often lacks autonomy and emission awareness, and human error can put crews and coasts at risk. The authors aim to do better with learning.

They propose realistic curriculum reinforcement learning for vessel navigation. A curriculum starts the agent on easy routes and adds harder ones over time. Realistic settings keep the lessons close to true seas and traffic. The goal is routes that cut greenhouse gas output while staying safe. The work speaks to shipping firms that must go green without new risks.
arxiv-2601-11311:
Zhihan Yang and eight coauthors revive random forests with language models. Their 2026 preprint is named ForestLLM, on few-shot tabular learning. Tables drive high-stakes choices in finance, health, and science. Learning from tables with few labeled rows is still hard.

Classic tree methods lean on purity scores to split data. With few labels, those scores turn shaky and prone to overfit. Random forests, a strong classic tool, falter in that regime. ForestLLM brings large language model knowledge to the trees. The aim is splits guided by meaning, not just counts. That help could steady tree learning when labels are scarce.
arxiv-2601-11411:
Igor Kuzmenko, Y. Band, Yshai Avishai, and Marek Trippenbach find memory in a refractive index. Their 2026 preprint studies a uniform, isotropic medium. The complex refractive index can show hysteresis there. Hysteresis means the response depends on the path taken.

The team computes the permittivity of the medium in full. They model it as a Duffing oscillator for the math. The medium has a quadratic electro-optic effect built in. A Duffing oscillator is a spring with a cubic twist. That twist gives the strong nonlinearity the study needs. From the model they trace how the index lags and loops. Such loops matter for switches and memory in photonics.
arxiv-2601-11511:
Danilo Polo Ojito and Emil Prodan study a diagonal tied to the toric code. Their 2026 preprint works in the 2-infinity UHF algebra. Kitaev's toric code is a famed model of topological order. Its star and face operators are the building blocks here.

Those operators generate an abelian sub-C-star-algebra. The team shows it is a C-star-diagonal in that algebra. It matches the canonical diagonal of the matrix algebra M. UHF algebras are limits of ever larger matrix algebras. A diagonal that matches the canonical one is a strong fact. Such results link quantum codes to operator algebra theory. They may guide how topological memories are classified.
arxiv-2601-11611:
Marina Vicini, Martin Rudorfer, Zhuangzhuang Dai, and Luis Manso read homes to spot activities. Their 2026 preprint adds temporal context to streaming sensor data. The global population is ageing year by year. Living independently and safely at home is the goal for many.

Cheap sensors can watch daily life without wearables or cameras. Passive infrared sensors and door sensors are the tools named. They feed streams that mark motion and room use. Activity recognition turns those streams into daily routines. Temporal context helps tell like patterns apart in time. Better reads support preventative healthcare for the elderly. The study sits in an Innovate UK smart home project.
arxiv-2601-11811:
Yuki Ueno, Hiroaki Natsukawa, and Koji Koyamada test how boxes shape the use of a graph layout. The layout, called group-in-a-box, packs node groups into boxes on screen. It shows group size plus links in and between groups at once.

A view may mix nodes, edges, and boxes in many ways. Yet little firm advice exists on which mix helps users explore best. Their study checks if the boxes change how users search and how well they do. The results can guide the design of tools for grouped network data.
arxiv-2601-11911:
Alfe Suny, MD Sakib Ul Islam, and Md. Imran Hossain test if small image models can be trusted on small data sets. Big image networks win on large sets. On small sets they can overfit, learning noise in place of true traits.

They test a compact CNN on five real data sets from Bangladesh. The sets cover city growth, vehicles, road damage, and farm crops. A small model that holds up would suit low cost field use. The study checks where compact models stay sound and where they fail.  The sets are small, so the tests stress true skill, not scale.
arxiv-2601-12011:
Yize Zhao and Christos Thrampoulidis explain why re-weighting loss helps early in training, yet not at the end. In big neural nets trained to the end, re-weighting seems to change little. Yet tests show clear gains early in training.

They bring in a small-scale model to show the effect in a clean way. In that model, the early phase can be tracked with care. The split helps users know when re-weighting is worth its cost. It also guides early stop rules in real training runs.  The small model makes each phase of training clear to read.
arxiv-2601-12111:
Wyatt McCurdy, Xin Zhang, Yuqi Song, and Min Gao build a face forgery spotter meant to work across domains. AI tools now make fake faces that look real with ease. Past spotters do well when train and test data match, yet fade when domains shift.

Their network, named RCDN in the work, centres its features in a new way. Centred features may hold up better on new cameras and codecs. A robust spotter helps news and courts check image truth. The work tests that cross-domain strength.  Cross domain strength is the main claim in the work.
arxiv-2601-12211:
Khiem Hong Phan and Quang Hoang-Minh Pham compute neutral scalar pair output via W boson fusion at muon colliders. They work at multi-TeV energies in the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model, which adds a second Higgs field. First, they compute full one-loop electroweak corrections in the Standard Model.

That loop step is done for this process for the first time, they state. Then they rate pair output through vector boson fusion in the wider model. Rates tell collider teams if such scalars can be seen. The work sets targets for a future muon collider.
arxiv-2601-12311:
Xiaofeng Luo, Jiayi He, Jiawen Kang, and a broad team guard location privacy for vehicles that work in both real and virtual worlds. 6G vehicular metaverses let cars act across physical and virtual space via linked nets. Cars place AI aides on edge servers for driving help and in-car services.

Those aides need location data, which is private. Their method joins a language model with a generative diffusion model to guard that data. Strong guards let metaverse driving grow with less risk. The work is in vehicular network privacy.  Guards must keep car help fast as well as private.
arxiv-2601-12511:
A. R. Altamura and a large ALICE team report beam test studies of a detector prototype. The detector is meant for ALICE 3, a new apparatus planned for later runs of the Large Hadron Collider. Its job is to identify charged particles at high energy. The design is a ring imaging Cherenkov detector in a proximity focusing layout.

It uses aerogel as its radiator, the medium that makes Cherenkov light. Silicon photomultipliers serve as its photon sensors. Beam tests put the prototype in real particle beams to check its response. Such tests reveal flaws that lab bench work cannot. They also confirm whether ring images stay sharp enough to tell particle types apart. The results feed the final design of the ALICE 3 system.
arxiv-2601-12711:
Kevin Wang and ten co authors ask when to tune model weights and when to rewrite prompts instead. Large language models can be adapted in two broad ways. Numerical updates change model parameters, while symbolic updates change prompts or logical constraints. Fine tuning excels at injecting new factual knowledge into a model.

Symbolic updates offer flexible control of style and alignment without retraining. The team introduce a neurosymbolic LoRA framework that combines both strategies. It switches or blends the two dynamically, case by case. Knowing which lever to pull for each task could save compute and improve results. The work gives practitioners a principled way to choose.
arxiv-2601-12811:
Julien Malka, Stefano Zacchiroli, and Theo Zimmermann warn that Docker does not by itself make work reproducible. Teams in software work need to rerun code and get the same result. That need touches joint work, supply chain safety, and science itself. Docker packs a full software setup into an image, a saved copy of a file system that can be shared.

A saved copy feels like proof, but it is not proof. Images can change, lean on live services, or hide steps no one wrote down. The team spell out where the promise of containers breaks. Their point is not to drop Docker, but to stop treating it as a guarantee. Stronger habits must back it up.
arxiv-2601-13011:
Shoya Yoshida, Katsuhiro Takahashi, and Katsunori Wakabayashi study the charge flow traits of a crystal known as the K4 crystal. They build a tight binding model, a grid model where charge hops from site to site. Their aim is to map the bands and the states that live on the surface.

In the bulk bands they find Weyl nodes, which are sharp touch points of two bands. Some nodes carry charge plus or minus two. Others carry charge plus or minus one. The nodes sit at points of high symmetry in the zone that holds all wave states. The authors also treat Fermi arcs and surface states, which link the nodes at the surface.
arxiv-2601-13111:
Hassan Soliman, Vivek Gupta, Dan Roth, and Iryna Gurevych tackle a choke point in text to SQL work. In such work a plain text query must turn into a database query. Real tasks often need to join many tables at once. Picking the right set of tables thus sets the score of the whole chain.

The team studies an open book case. Queries must be met from huge mixed pools of tables drawn from many sources. No clean tag marks which source a query needs. Their method, CORE-T, aims to pull the right tables as one linked set, not one by one. For data teams, sharp table picks cut wrong joins and bad answers.
arxiv-2601-13411:
Hector O. Silva, Giovanni Tambalo, Kostas Glampedakis, and Kent Yagi ring black holes in a theory past Einstein's and ask if the ring tones stay matched. A merged hole rings with tones called quasinormal modes. In Einstein's theory, two tone sets that should match do match, a trait called isospectrality.

The team works in the most plain past Einstein model where first rule sums can be done. It adds cubic curve terms to the theory. The holes do not spin. They ask how tones are stirred and if the match breaks in the wave form. A break would be a clean sign of new gravity in loud hole rings.
arxiv-2601-13511:
Nguyen Quang Huy and co-authors find hid convexity in quadratic systems and use it for quadratic programs. A quadratic map sends a point to a set of degree two sums. Its image need not be convex. The team gives terms where the image plus the plus orthant is convex in spite of that.

That hid trait then firms up the trust region task with straight side binds. Trust region tasks are a core opt form, to step in a ball where a model is trusted. Their new terms are set next to the old terms from a 2014 paper. For opt staff, more cases with a sworn convex form mean more tasks that can be solved to a global best.
arxiv-2601-13711:
Lotta Kiefer and co-authors build a large test set for authorship checks in German in 2026. Authorship verification asks if two texts share one author. The task has been studied much for English texts. For other languages, large benchmarks and firm tests are still scarce.

Their benchmark, GerAV, holds over 600,000 labeled text pairs in German. They also fine-tune large language models on this task. Big, clean test sets let the field judge methods in a fair way. German tools for fraud checks and forensics stand to gain from this base.
arxiv-2601-13811:
Michael Kaicher and co-authors build a fast mean-field theory for a broad class of quantum spins in 2026. Their target is general spin-1/2 Hamiltonians, with any geometry and interactions. Mean-field theory replaces complex links with an average field, for speed. Their version uses parity-violating fermionic Gaussian states.

They derive explicit equations of motion for this PV-FMFT method. The equations cover both real-time and imaginary-time evolution. Fast spin simulation aids the study of magnets and quantum materials. A method that keeps parity violation in view opens cases older tools miss. The work gives spin model teams a fast tool to test more cases in less time.
arxiv-2601-14211:
Johannes Niederhauser and Aart Middeldorp present a logic result in this 2026 paper. Their topic is unification, the task of making two formal terms match by filling in their free parts. They work on one class of terms called deterministic higher-order patterns. Yokoyama and others first set out this class of typed lambda terms. Matching within the class is known to give one clear answer.

The authors give a method that is both sound and complete for this task. Sound means each answer it gives is right. Complete means it finds an answer when one exists. They also show their method sits inside full higher-order unification. In that wider task, the hard flex-flex pairs can still be solved in the most general way.
arxiv-2601-14311:
Richard Hohensinner and five co-authors survey data tracking for large language models in this 2026 paper. These models are deployed at scale, yet the life cycle of their training data stays opaque. No one can easily say where the data came from or how it changed. The survey pulls together ten years of research.

The work is sorted into three main axes. They are data provenance, transparency, and traceability. Three supporting pillars sit under them: bias and uncertainty, data privacy, and tools and techniques that put the ideas to work. Readers get one map of a scattered field, plus the open gaps the authors see.
arxiv-2601-14411:
Larry Guth, Hong Wang, and Joshua Zahl present a proof of a famous math problem in this 2026 paper. The Kakeya set conjecture concerns Besicovitch sets. A Besicovitch set is a compact set that contains a unit line segment pointing in every direction. Such sets can be strangely small, and the conjecture pins down how small they can be.

The authors give a streamlined and simplified proof for three-dimensional space. Their title stresses the streamlining: the argument is shorter and cleaner than past routes. Readers get a landmark result in harmonic analysis in a form meant to be easier to follow and teach.
arxiv-2601-14511:
Griffin Higgins, Roozbeh Razavi-Far, Hossein Shokouhinejad, and Ali A. Ghorbani build a malware detector in this 2026 paper. Malware keeps growing more sophisticated, threatening, and evasive. Detection systems must keep pace, and they must be transparent as well as strong. Users need to know why a file was flagged.

The team proposes the Assembly Flow Graph, or AFG. It represents the assembly flow of a binary executable as graph data, in comprehensive form. Graph neural networks then read that graph to detect malware. The design gives granular explainability at the assembly flow level. Readers get a detector whose verdicts come with a traceable path through the code.
arxiv-2601-14611:
Jiangen He and Jiqun Liu study how chatbots show their sources in this 2026 paper. Conversational AI systems increasingly serve as primary interfaces for information seeking. Yet how they present sources to support information evaluation remains under-explored. The authors investigate how source transparency design shapes information seeking, trust, and critical engagement.

They ran a controlled between-subjects experiment with 372 participants. It compared four source presentation interfaces: Collapsible, Hover Card, Footer, and Aligned Sidebar. The designs vary in visibility and accessibility. The test was run with care. Each group saw one form, so no one could game the task. Readers get measured evidence on which source displays help users judge what a chatbot tells them.
arxiv-2601-14711:
Mingxuan Song and seven co-authors work on online advertising budgets in this 2026 paper, set for the ACM Web Conference. Optimizing an advertiser's cumulative value of winning impressions under budget constraints is a complex challenge. It sits under the paradigm of AI-Generated Bidding. Advertisers often have personalized objectives but limited historical interaction data.

That scarcity creates few-shot scenarios, where traditional reinforcement learning methods struggle. The team's method, DARA, allocates budgets in few-shot settings via in-context decision making with RL-finetuned LLMs. In-context means the model decides from examples placed in its prompt. The gain is trust. A new shop with thin past data can still bid with a firm plan. Readers get a bidding method for advertisers who cannot feed a learner months of past data.
arxiv-2601-14811:
Zhi-yuan Ao and four co-authors measure an atomic constant in this 2026 paper. They work with beryllium-9 ions held in a linear Paul trap. A Paul trap holds charged particles with oscillating electric fields. The team measures the ground-state hyperfine constant of the beryllium ion. Hyperfine structure comes from the interplay of the electron and the nucleus.

They use magnetically insensitive hyperfine transitions, from the F equals 2, mF equals 0 state to the F equals 1, mF equals 0 state. Microwave-driven state transfer performs the measurement. Insensitive transitions shrug off magnetic field noise, so the value comes out clean. Readers get a precision constant for a workhorse ion in quantum technology.
arxiv-2601-15011:
Jiayu Li, Feng-Ren Fan, and Wang Yao study smooth shifts between phases of matter with topological order. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with continuous topological phase transitions. At such a shift, a gap in the energy spectrum closes.

Near that closing, rough symmetries can appear. They show up in the low-energy space. The authors call them quasisymmetries. They set out the idea of quasisymmetry enrichment. For shifts from a normal insulator to a Chern insulator, these charges split one class of transitions into finer, more distinct kinds. That split adds a new label to each shift.
arxiv-2601-15111:
Anmol Goel, Alan Ritter, and Iryna Gurevych audit whether language models truly forget. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with machine unlearning, methods that claim to erase chosen data from a model. The methods look like they work, yet a problem hides inside.

The authors show that facts about the erased data can still be read off. The traces sit in the model's internal states and can be decoded in a straight-line way. They build an audit frame based on information theory. It uses partial information decomposition to measure what remains after unlearning.
arxiv-2601-15311:
Mustafa Arslan gives long-running language model agents a memory that acts less like a pile of notes. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with a core limit of these models. Self-attention costs grow with the square of the context length, and quality fades in the middle of long inputs.

Most fixes use flat retrieval over a vector store. That treats memory as an unstructured bag of embeddings. Arslan presents Aeon, a neuro-symbolic memory manager for long-horizon agents. It aims for high performance by giving the stored past a structure the agent can reason over.
arxiv-2601-15411:
D. Russell Luke, Johannes-Carl Schnebel, and co-authors study random dynamical systems that work at several scales at once. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with stochastic differential inclusions with multiscale effects. The systems are built to solve generalized variational inequalities.

That class of problems is broad. It covers constrained convex optimization, saddle-point problems, and equilibrium problems in economics and engineering. To respect constraints, the authors use a penalty approach. The penalty makes the evolution system depend on time explicitly. They analyze the long-run behavior of the coupled systems as time goes on.
arxiv-2601-15911:
Miguel A. Piñar builds a spectral method for problems on the unit ball in a 2026 arXiv paper. His main aim is to show how Sobolev orthogonal polynomials serve inside such methods. Spectral methods solve equations by expanding solutions in special functions. Boundary-value problems are the target here. The example treats a stationary Schrödinger equation on the unit ball. A variational perspective frames the solution.

Fully diagonalized is the title's promise. Diagonal systems split into independent pieces that are cheap to solve. Orthogonal polynomials with Sobolev inner products respect boundary behavior well. That makes them natural bases for ball-shaped domains. Problems in physics and engineering often live on balls or spheres. A clean, fast solver for them has broad use.
arxiv-2601-16111:
Prashant Singh, David Kessler and Eli Barkai study where a quantum walk ends up. Their 2026 preprint tracks a walk watched as it moves in time. The walk can hit one of two marks. The odds of each mark are called split odds. In a chance walk of old type, those odds shift in a smooth way.

For the quantum walk, the odds jump in a sharp, non smooth way. The jump is set by how oft the marks are checked. That sharp shift looks like a phase change in matter. The find shows how watch acts shape quantum paths. It parts in kind from the old chance walk case.
arxiv-2601-16211:
Geo Ahn and five coauthors find why action models fail on new verb and object pairs. Their 2026 preprint deals with video sense of acts in parts. Models must spot the verb and the object, then join them. Joins must work for pairs not seen in training. The team finds a key flaw: models lean on the object to guess the verb.

That lean is a short cut that breaks on new pairs. A drawer that will not open shows the flaw in real terms. Past tests missed this flaw as a main cause of fails. Name the flaw and teams can build drills to break it. The work aims for act sense that truly joins parts.
arxiv-2601-16311:
Katelynn Huneycutt, Samantha Sandberg-Clark and Liz Vivas study non autonomous parabolic break in maps. Their 2026 preprint links that break to sets of matched curve maps. The maps stem from steps of Möbius maps, a class of plane maps. Set breaks shift the maps from a fixed form. Some breaks shift by chance at each step in the chain.

The team sorts which curve sets grow from which break types. Each set tells of how the maps act in the long run. Break tales in maps pair with curve sets in a neat way. That pair helps read wild map acts with maths. The work sits in pure plane map theory.
arxiv-2601-16511:
Piotr Faliszewski and four coauthors study who can be added to swing a budget vote. Their 2026 preprint deals with shared budget votes by groups. In such votes, funds go to the plans with most back. A chief may add or drop names to force a set win. That chief act is called candidate control in vote maths.

The team weighs how hard that control is to sum. Hard sums mean the vote is safe from chief tricks in real use. Easy sums mean guards must block such adds by rule. Shared funds touch real towns and groups each year. The work maps safe and weak vote forms.
arxiv-2601-16711:
Shanshan Liu and a team of eight co-authors tackle a hard task in drug and health data. Tools must spot named health terms in text. New terms show up all the time, with no hand-made lists. Their 2026 preprint builds a test frame for this gap. It also builds a way to tag terms with no human hand.

Their test frame ranks terms in a tree of groups. Fresh scores gauge how well tools catch new terms. A big language model then tags text on its own. Those tags can train tools with less cost. Sound term tags feed search, care, and drug watch tasks.
arxiv-2601-16911:
Joshua Vedral and Dmitri Kuzmin add a shock guard to high-order flow codes. Flow codes track waves in gas, water, and plasma. Sharp fronts in flow can make codes ring and fail. Their 2026 preprint builds a guard that acts just at fronts. The guard sits in cell-vertex form for fin element codes.

Both joined and split element forms take the guard. A spread-based WENO scheme sets how much calm to add. The guard uses fine quad points to place that calm. Sharp fronts then pass with no wild rings. Such codes serve flight, weather, and star work.
arxiv-2601-17111:
Xuan-Phi Nguyen, Shrey Pandit, Austin Xu, Caiming Xiong, and Shafiq Joty fix load skew in expert-mix models. Such models split work among expert parts by a router. Train rules push loads to spread even. Yet trained models still route in a skewed way. Some experts hog work while the rest sit idle. Their 2026 preprint treats that skew as a trait to use, not fight.

Their plan pairs each ask with the least-loaded apt expert. Skew then shows where deep skill pools in the net. Hot experts hold the dense facts of a field. Lean loads cut lag and waste in big bots. The plan turns a flaw in a guide.
arxiv-2601-17211:
Anzhe Cheng, Italo Ivo Lima Dias Pinto, and Paul Bogdan study how the build of the brain changes with age. They use brain scans made with magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI for short. Their work adapts a tool called structural complexity analysis so it can handle three-dimensional signals like these scans.

The method shrinks the scan step by step to larger and larger scales. At each step it counts how much detail is lost from one scale to the next. That loss shows how the brain is put together across scales. The authors use those patterns to track changes linked to age. The work gives brain research a fresh way to read age from scan structure.
arxiv-2601-17311:
Bang Liu, Linglong Kong, and Jian Pei model when teams of AI agents help and when they fail. More agents can raise reliability. But under a fixed budget, gains can level off. They can even collapse. The authors build a small, testable theory of that turn. It rests on three limits in today's agent stacks.

The limits are finite context windows, lossy talk between agents, and shared flaws among like agents. From them, the theory predicts help, saturation, or collapse zones. Teams can fit the model to their own stack. That helps them spend budget where agents add value. It warns when more agents just add shared error.
arxiv-2601-17611:
Davide Berghi and Philip J. B. Jackson present ToS, a Team of Specialists for sound event work. The task is 3D sound event localization and detection with distance. In video, the system must name each active sound per frame. It must also place that sound in space. Meaning, space, and time must be read at once.

Single models strain at that joint task. A team of specialists splits the load by strength. Stereo input gives the spatial cues the team needs. Such systems serve smart cameras and hearing aids. They also help robots find who or what made a sound. The ensemble design mirrors how human teams split hard jobs.
arxiv-2601-17811:
Xiang Li, Wei He, and Per Ola Kristensson ask how researchers should judge what people feel inside virtual worlds. Their 2026 preprint surveys the study of immersive experience. The field has grown for decades, yet it stays split into parts. Studies use overlapping terms, mixed tools, and little shared sense of what counts as being immersed. That split makes results hard to compare.

The authors take stock of the constructs and measures in use. They look for where terms clash and where tools agree. A shared base would let studies build on each other with more trust. It would also help designers test headsets and virtual spaces on common ground. The paper is a call to tidy a crowded field.
arxiv-2601-18011:
Niaz Mohammad Ramaki and Florian Schintke add a blockchain trail to live data pipelines. Their 2026 preprint deals with stream processing, where data is handled as it arrives. Auditing and replaying such pipelines is hard. Output depends on run order, window triggers, and network jitter, so the same input can yield different results. The team builds a provenance design backed by a blockchain and tests it on weather data with Kafka Streams.

Provenance records where each output came from and how it was made. A chain-backed record is hard to alter after the fact. The weather case study shows the design at work on a real stream. Trustworthy trails matter wherever streams drive money, safety, or science.
arxiv-2601-18111:
Jean Kossaifi and co-authors strip weather AI down to what really makes it skillful. Their 2026 preprint deals with data-driven probabilistic forecasting at medium range. The field has boomed, but it has also splintered into complex, bespoke designs and training tricks. That splintering hides the true drivers of forecast skill. The authors show that top-level probabilistic skill needs neither intricate architecture rules nor special training heuristics.

A simpler recipe that matches the best models is good news. It lowers the cost of entry for new teams. It also tells the field where to stop adding parts. Weather forecasts guide farms, grids, and disaster plans, so clarity about what works has wide value.
arxiv-2601-18311:
Leo Hirata and co-authors measure light from highly charged ions to serve X-ray astronomy. Their 2026 preprint uses a compact electron beam ion trap at a synchrotron site. Modern X-ray satellites carry grating spectrometers and microcalorimeters that read the sky in fine detail. Reading those spectra needs accurate atomic data. Current models lean heavily on theory, whose errors can mislead the reading of real sources.

Photoexcitation spectroscopy in the trap gives lab values to check the theory. A compact trap at a synchrotron makes such checks far more practical. Better atomic data sharpen every claim made from satellite spectra. The work links lab atomic physics with the study of hot cosmic gas.
arxiv-2601-19811:
TrungKhang Tran and colleagues revisit a family of algorithms for streaming estimation. Modern statistics often faces data that arrive continuously in high volume. Batch algorithms need repeated passes over the full dataset, which streaming makes impractical. Incremental stochastic methods update estimates as data arrive, including a stochastic version of the EM algorithm.

The authors study incremental stochastic majorization-minimization algorithms. These replace a hard objective with an easier upper bound at each step. Their application is mixture of experts models, which route inputs among specialised sub-models. Sound theory for streaming updates matters as data pipelines grow. The work sharpens the guarantees behind methods practitioners already use. The fix is old and well known: run the same task more than once.
arxiv-2601-20011:
A search with the CMS detector looks for heavy new particles that decay into pairs of Higgs bosons. Such resonances, predicted by several extensions of the Standard Model, would appear as bumps in the mass spectrum. The search covers masses from one to several teraelectronvolts. The final state studied pairs bottom quark jets with tau leptons.

The data come from proton-proton collisions recorded by CMS at the CERN LHC during its 2016 to 2018 run. No claim of a discovery is made in the summary; the search sets the scale of what is excluded. Each null result narrows where new physics can hide. Higgs pair channels are among the most sensitive probes of extended Higgs sectors. The work feeds the broader programme of resonance hunting.
arxiv-2601-20211:
Moritz Hütten maps port activity at high resolution using open vessel-tracking data from Tokyo Bay. Ships broadcast their position through the Automatic Identification System, and land receivers collect those signals. Such knowledge of vessel movements informs economic readings, shipping decisions, and maritime safety.

Hütten shows that this open data can reveal port activities with precision close to official statistics. That matters because official figures often arrive late and at coarse detail. A cheap, timely view of a major port could help operators and analysts spot shifts in trade and traffic as they happen.
arxiv-2601-20311:
Zihan Zhou and five colleagues present DiagLink, a diagnostic assistance system meant to serve both doctors and patients. A global shortage of medical experts, spread unevenly, blocks fair access to accurate diagnosis. Earlier smart systems showed promise but struggled with two-user interaction and with keeping medical knowledge current.

DiagLink joins expert knowledge with large language models and knowledge graphs. The design lets both sides of a consultation draw on the same structured knowledge. A system that serves clinician and patient together could shorten the path from symptom to sound advice, above all where specialists are scarce.
arxiv-2601-20511:
Zelong Sun and four colleagues introduce portrait collection generation. In this task, a set of portraits is created by editing one reference portrait with natural language instructions. Social media users increasingly want varied, high-quality portrait sets without a photo shoot. The edits must keep the collection coherent, so the same person reads as themselves across every image.

The authors name the task Say Cheese and frame its requirements. Edits given in plain words, such as changing style or setting, should apply cleanly across the set. The task sets a benchmark for editing tools that must balance change with identity.
arxiv-2601-20811:
Charles Audet and five co-authors build a solver for hard optimization problems with constraints. Their 2026 paper presents MADS-PIP. The base method, MADS, is mesh adaptive direct search, a tool for nonsmooth blackbox problems. A blackbox problem gives answers only through trials, with no formula to inspect. Constraints can demand equality or set bounds that must hold.

The new framework folds a penalty-interior point strategy into MADS. The constraints are split into two subsets. One subset is handled with a logarithmic barrier on the total violation. The other is handled with an exterior quadratic penalty. Blending the two styles aims for speed and reliability at once. The solver serves engineers who must optimize systems they can only test, not solve on paper.
arxiv-2601-20911:
Haochen Zhang and five co-authors tackle image generation that must remember a whole conversation. Their 2026 paper studies multi-round conversational image generation. A model must follow user instructions across many rounds. The chat history mixes text and images that pile up over time. Recent multimodal models can generate and edit images in this setting. Yet most benchmarks and training recipes are effectively Markov.

Markov here means the next output leans mainly on the most recent image. That allows shortcut solutions that ignore long-range history. The authors call their setting non-Markov to stress the full memory demand. A good model must respect choices made many turns ago. The work pushes image tools toward true collaboration. It matters for design tasks where users refine one picture over a long session.
arxiv-2601-21111:
The Euclid Collaboration measures the glow that all galaxies together leave on the sky. Their 2026 paper studies fluctuations in the extragalactic background light. In the optical and near-infrared, this background encodes the cumulative emission of unresolved galaxies. Part comes from integrated galaxy light. Another part is diffuse intra-halo light, shed by stars between galaxies. A third part may come from the epoch of reionisation, the dawn of the modern universe.

These parts are hard to disentangle with auto-spectra alone. An auto-spectrum measures each signal only against itself. Cross-checks between wavelengths and maps can separate the blend. The paper prepares that separation for Euclid data. Knowing the background's makeup sharpens every measurement taken against it. It also writes a history of light the eye cannot resolve.
arxiv-2601-21411:
Chengchao Yuan and Ruo-Yu Liu chase the source of very-high-energy gamma rays from a quiet galaxy. The galaxy NGC 4278 hosts a weak active nucleus, yet a large observatory in China caught TeV rays from it. The team models its light across X-ray, GeV, and TeV bands.

They test two candidate sources: jets from the nucleus and winds it drives. Each is modeled in both quiet and active states of the galaxy. The fit helps judge whether weak nuclei can feed the background glow of neutrinos seen across the sky. Even faint galaxies could matter if there are enough of them.
arxiv-2601-21511:
Niki van Stein, Anna V. Kononova, Lars Kotthoff, and Thomas Bäck add structural feedback to the automatic design of algorithms. Language models can now write optimization algorithms from plain prompts. The strongest design loops judge each attempt by its score alone and ignore the code itself.

The authors feed back explanations of the code's structure, drawn from explainable AI tools. That tells the search why an attempt works, not just how well. Their system builds on an existing evolutionary design loop. Richer feedback should steer the search toward sound designs faster and help humans learn from what the machine invents.
arxiv-2601-21611:
Baopu Qiu, Hao Chen, and eight co-authors sharpen relevance ranking for e-commerce search. Matching results to user intent drives the shopping experience. Language models now help where older rankers failed, above all on rare and ambiguous queries.

The authors distill reasoning from several viewpoints into a fast model. The teacher thinks broadly, weighing many angles of what a query wants. The student learns to act fast at serving time. That split suits online shops, where ranking must be both smart and instant across millions of searches a day.
arxiv-2601-21811:
G. Cigler and M. Kandić work in functional analysis, the abstract study of spaces of functions and the operators that act on them. Their setting is an Archimedean vector lattice, an ordered vector space with a well-behaved notion of size. They study subalgebras of regular operators on such a space.

The algebras they consider must contain all rank-one operators built from the atoms of the space, its smallest indivisible elements. Within that setting, the authors investigate positive automorphisms, the structure-preserving maps that also respect the order. Their 2026 preprint adds to the pure theory of operator algebras on lattices. Results from that field underpin parts of economics, probability, and quantum theory.
arxiv-2601-22211:
Lingkai Kong and co-authors give reinforcement learning a policy shaped for combinatorial choices. When actions are combinations, the feasible set grows exponentially and obeys complex constraints. Directly parameterizing a policy over such a set is impractical, so existing methods lean on task-specific value functions or rigid deterministic policies.

Their 2026 preprint proposes a latent spherical flow policy. The policy lives in a latent space with spherical geometry, where sampling combinations stays tractable, and flows map those samples to feasible actions. Combinatorial action spaces appear in logistics, network control, and chip design. A general policy for them could bring reinforcement learning to problems now handled by handcrafted solvers.
arxiv-2601-22611:
Manika Bag, Sheetal Dharmatti, Subrata Majumdar, and Debanjana Mitra study whether a coupled flow can be steered near a steady state with one local control. Their 2026 preprint treats the one-dimensional Cahn-Hilliard-Burgers' equation, which joins phase spread with fluid push. The control acts only inside the domain, and only on the concentration part.

They first linearize the system around the steady state. Local controllability means small targets near that state can be reached. Such results guide mix and coating control. The work is careful PDE theory. It shows how little control can suffice.
arxiv-2601-22711:
Matteo Gambella, Fabrizio Pittorino, Giuliano Casale, and Manuel Roveri built SQUAD, a team-vote system on early-exit networks. Early-exit nets give a quick answer mid-way when they feel sure. Their 2026 preprint notes that a lone model's sense of sure is often off, thanks to its own quirks.

SQUAD pools a quorum of early exits, adapting the bar as it goes. A team call is steadier than a lone hunch. The gain is speed where safe, care where not. The work serves live systems that must answer fast. It borrows wisdom from voting theory.
arxiv-2601-22911:
Rob Cornish and Andi Q. Wang recast a cornerstone sampling algorithm in the language of category theory. The algorithm, Metropolis–Hastings, builds a Markov chain whose long-run pattern matches a target distribution. It underlies much of Bayesian statistics and machine learning.

The authors ask whether the method can be stated and analyzed with categorical probability, a newer formal framework. They test the idea on a recent involutive version of the algorithm. A clean abstract form could reveal which parts of the method are essential, and guide new variants. Using a recent involutive variant as the case study keeps the categorical treatment concrete rather than purely abstract.
arxiv-2601-23211:
Paulius Rauba, Simonas Cepenas, and Mihaela van der Schaar argue that multi-agent AI systems are principal-agent problems. In these systems, a supervisor agent assigns subtasks to specialists and merges their answers. Information is asymmetric: agents see task details and reasoning traces the supervisor cannot fully check.

That asymmetry is exactly what principal-agent theory, from economics, was built to study. Framing AI teams this way imports tools for incentives, monitoring, and trust. It could guide safer designs as agent teams take on real work. Information asymmetry is the core property imported from principal-agent theory, where one side knows more than the other.
arxiv-2603-01711:
Louis-Pierre Arguin and Nathan Creighton bound rare large values of the Riemann zeta function on its critical line. Their 2026 work builds on a prior study of the same function just off that line. Large deviations ask how often the function strays far from its typical size.

They prove an unconditional lower bound for real large deviations of a set logarithmic order. Unconditional means the proof needs no unproven hypotheses, a high bar in this field. The bound matches the order of the best known upper bound across a stated range. It also yields a fresh proof of the sharpest known lower bounds for fractional moments of zeta. Moments summarize average powers of the function, so the two results reinforce each other and the random-matrix view of zeta.
arxiv-2603-01811:
Filippus Roux argues that nature resists placing large masses in two places at once in this 2026 work. Quantum theory allows superpositions, where an object sits in a blend of two states at once. For heavy masses, such a blend could entangle with the geometry of spacetime itself.

Roux models the split mass as a Schrodinger cat state, the famed blend of two distinct states. Total energy of that state dips as a function of the gap between the two mass positions. That dip acts like a force that pushes back against forming the split in the first place. A broader form of the effect is then discussed in connection with the measurement problem. If the effect holds, gravity itself may help explain why big objects never show quantum splits.
arxiv-2603-02111:
Thang Pham, Andrea Pinamonti, Dung Tran, and Boqing Xue study line patterns in special finite groups in this 2026 paper. The groups are finite Heisenberg groups, built from a finite number field. Their operator averages a function along flat lines inside the group. Such averages are called Kakeya maximal operators in this field.

For directions alone, the problem drops to a known field case, and the team finds exact growth rates. A richer version also records a line's central slope. For the smallest group, they prove a sharp bound for that richer version. From it they derive exact mixed rates and floor sizes for Kakeya sets. The proof uses wave methods only, not the polynomial trick common in this area.
arxiv-2603-02511:
Chrisantus Eze, Ryan Julian, and Christopher Crick retrieve objects from dense clutter with a robot in this 2026 paper. Large end-to-end models can manipulate objects but learn slowly and resist inspection. The authors argue for specialized, decoupled systems instead. Their framework, Unveiler, splits spatial reasoning from action execution.

A lightweight transformer encoder scans the clutter and picks the most critical obstacle. That choice passes to a rotation-invariant decoder that carries out the removal. Training starts by imitating a heuristic, then reinforcement fine-tuning discovers better strategies. Success reached high levels even when targets were fully hidden in simulation. The reasoning module moved to real scenes with no retraining. A physical robot validated the full system after only geometric calibration.
arxiv-2603-02911:
Moha Naeimi, Ingo Barke, and Sylvia Speller show how two colors of light can write and erase charge patterns in tiny crystals. Their 2026 paper studies rubrene microcrystals that grow in two sector shapes with strikingly different glow and behavior. The team probes the crystals' inner electronic structure with a time-of-flight photoemission method.

Under ultraviolet light, the diamond-shaped sectors pile up charge while the triangular sectors stay nearly neutral, a split traced to direction-dependent conductivity. A second, weaker light then generates carriers that cancel the stored charge on demand. A model combining surface capacitance with drift and diffusion matches the observed energy shifts closely. austen-sense-and-sensibility-1811:
Jane Austen published Sense and Sensibility in 1811, her first novel in print. The story tracks the Dashwood sisters after their father's death strips their income. Elinor stands for sense, and Marianne for open, strong feeling in love and grief.

Both sisters fall in love, and both face loss, gossip, and hard reversals. Marianne's romance with Willoughby ends in public shame and deep illness at Cleveland. Elinor hides her own pain while she nurses her sister back to health. Austen weighs heart and reason without mocking either side of the scale. The prose is crisp, ironic, and quietly fond of its flawed young women.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-11:
Volume eleven of Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud holds the first part of Tract Baba Metzia, the Middle Gate. Baba Metzia is the Talmud's richest field of everyday civil law. Its cases come from markets, workshops, and shared courtyards across the rabbinic world.

The tractate opens with two men clutching one cloak, each swearing it is his: the court must split the claim. From there it runs through found goods, deposits left with a keeper, wages owed to laborers, and loans and interest. Rodkinson's notes flag the hardest turns in the debate. Business readers meet an ancient law of trade that still feels alive.
bakunin-oeuvres-vol5-1911:
Volume 5 of Guillaume's Bakunin edition appeared in 1911, gathering the writings of the revolutionary's last great campaigns. By 1870 Bakunin was old and ill, but the Franco-Prussian War and the Paris Commune drew him back into action. He even joined a failed rising at Lyon, hoping to spark a wider revolt.

The texts include his appeals for a commune in Lyon and his letters and drafts from the Commune's brief life in Paris. He argued that war and empire had to be answered by revolution from below, not by new governments. The volume shows the old rebel's energy undimmed at the end of his active life. Guillaume's edition moves toward its close with Bakunin still, in his editor's phrase, in full cry.
bancroft-history-us-vol-11:
Bancroft turns to the making of the Constitution in the first volume of his 1882 sequel on its formation. Delegates gather at Philadelphia in 1787 to rebuild a failing union. Their debates, kept half secret, invent a republic meant to last.

The old historian treats the Convention as the capstone of his life's work. State rivalries, bold plans, and wise compromises fill his account. He sees the founding as deliberate, almost sacred work. Readers meet Washington, Madison, and Hamilton in the act of design. Bancroft's fervor gives the dry work of framing laws the glow of national epic.
bergson-creative-evolution-mitchell-1911:
Henri Bergson published Creative Evolution in 1907, a French work of philosophy about life and change. The English text here is Arthur Mitchell's translation of 1911. Bergson sets the elan vital, a vital impulse driving life forward, against cold mechanism. Evolution, he argues, creates new forms in ways no machine model can capture.

He criticizes both Darwinian mechanism and fixed final goals. Intellect, he says, slices living flow into static parts, while intuition grasps it whole. The book was a sensation and won Bergson worldwide fame. It shaped process thought and much art of its era. Many call it the most influential philosophy of life of its century.
bergson-laughter-brereton-1911:
Henri Bergson published Laughter in 1900, a short French essay on why we laugh. The English text here is the 1911 translation by Cloudesley Brereton and Fred Rothwell. Bergson argues that laughter targets rigidity in people. We laugh when a living person acts like a stiff machine or a thing.

Comedy, he says, works as a social correction that shames inelastic habits. The comic figure is often vain, absent-minded, or stuck in a groove. Bergson studies farce, caricature, and wordplay for support. The theory is elegant and still widely taught. Later theories of humor often start by answering Bergson.
bergson-matter-memory-paul-1911:
Henri Bergson published Matter and Memory in 1896, a French study of mind and body. The English text here is the 1911 translation by Nancy Margaret Paul and W. Scott Palmer. Bergson asks how memory joins the material world. He argues that memory is not stored in the brain like goods in a box.

He distinguishes habit memory, held in the body, from pure memory of the past. Perception, for him, selects images for action rather than copying the world. The book attacks materialism while respecting science. It founded much modern philosophy of mind. Thinkers on time, self, and brain science still engage its claims.
blackwood-centaur-1911:
Algernon Blackwood turned from ghost tales to a tale of faith in The Centaur, his novel of 1911. A man who feels trapped by town life sails and walks in search of a truer world. In the hills he meets hints that old myths still live.

The tale claims that earth holds a deep shared soul. The last centaurs stand for a pure bond with wild life. Blackwood pours his love of woods and hills into the prose. It is the peak of his tales of awe in wild places. Some fans find its creed dense. Yet its love for green hills and clean air rings true, and its quest has real ache in it.
bleek-lloyd-specimens-of-bushman-folklor:
Wilhelm Bleek and Lucy Lloyd preserved the |Xam people's stories in Specimens of Bushman Folklore, published in 1911. In Cape Town, |Xam men dictated myths, legends, and beliefs to the two scholars over years of patient work. The original |Xam text stands beside the English translation, line for careful line.

The trickster Mantis, the moon, rain, and the early people of the world move through these tales. The speakers' own people and language have since nearly vanished, which makes the record irreplaceable. The volume stands as the founding text of Khoisan ethnography, a whole world saved in notebooks.
boas-mind-primitive-man-1911:
Franz Boas taught at Columbia and is often called the father of American anthropology. His 1911 book The Mind of Primitive Man attacks the claim that some races are born with stronger minds than others. It draws on years of field work and museum study.

Boas shows that race, language, and culture move on separate tracks and must not be confused. A people's tools, tales, and habits, he argues, grow from their history, not from their blood. The book laid the ground for cultural relativism, the view that each culture must be judged on its own terms.
bonaventure-tria-opuscula-1911:
Bonaventure, the Franciscan master who led his order and taught at Paris, wrote three short works that hold his whole thought in seed. The Quaracchi edition of 1911 prints them together in Latin: the Breviloquium, the Itinerarium Mentis in Deum, and the De Reductione Artium ad Theologiam. No complete English version in the public domain exists.

The Breviloquium sums up the whole of theology in seven tight parts. The Itinerarium leads the soul up six steps, through the world and the mind, to rest in God. The third piece shows how every art and science leads back to theology. Together they are the handbook of Franciscan thought at its height.
boule-la-chapelle-aux-saints-1911:
Marcellin Boule, a French sage of fossil man, wrote this memoir in French on the La Chapelle-aux-Saints find in 1911. Quarry men in France had found a near whole Neanderthal frame in a cave in 1908. Boule got the bones for his full study in Paris.

His rebuild of the man stooped, bent at the knees, with a brutish, ape like gait. That image of the Neanderthal as a dull brute held sway for some forty years in books and museums. Later work showed the frame was bent by age and joint pain, not by race.
brentano-aristoteles-weltanschauung-1911:
Franz Brentano published his study of Aristotle and his worldview in German in 1911. Brentano, the Austrian philosopher who revived the close study of the mind, had lectured on Aristotle for decades. He found his own leading ideas, above all the mind's direction toward objects, foreshadowed in the Greek master's texts.

The book follows Aristotle's development through the stages Brentano saw in his career, from early promise to mature system. It treats the soul, knowledge, and the divine mind as Aristotle's texts present them. Brentano reads the ancient philosopher as a living thinker rather than a museum piece. The study carried his reading of Aristotle to a new generation, including students who would reshape twentieth-century philosophy.
brown-acquaintances-old-and-new-among-re: Acquaintances, Old and New, among Reformers, Brown's 1911 work. The reformer friends. This book preserves that memoir. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
cannizzaro-sketch-chemical-philosophy-19:
Stanislao Cannizzaro's Sketch of a Course of Chemical Philosophy began as his 1858 Italian Sunto. The Alembic Club reprinted the English version in 1911 as Reprint number 18. Cannizzaro revived Avogadro's hypothesis, the idea that equal gas volumes hold equal numbers of molecules. Chemists had let that idea sleep for decades.
