With it, he showed how to fix atomic weights on one firm scale. His paper reached the Karlsruhe congress of 1860 and spread among its members. The atomic weight chaos that had plagued chemistry soon ended. The short sketch changed how every chemist reckoned. It reads as a letter that reset a science.
chatelaine-de-vergi-mason-1911:
The Châtelaine de Vergi is an anonymous French tale from medieval Burgundy. It is short enough to read at one sitting, and it ends in grief. Eugene Mason translated it into English in 1911 with other tales of its period.

A knight loves the châtelaine in secret, and the secret itself keeps them safe. A jealous duchess drags the confidence out of the duke, her husband. One whispered word follows another until the trust is broken in public. The lovers die of the betrayal, and few medieval tales punish a loose tongue so harshly.
chrystal-perpetual-motion-1911:
George Chrystal, a Scots scholar of maths and physics, wrote this survey of perpetual motion for the Encyclopaedia Britannica in 1911. By then the laws of heat and work had long since closed the case. Chrystal set out the full tale for the lay reader.

He walks from the old wheel schemes to the strict proof that no such machine can work. He notes the French Academy's ban of 1775, when it shut its doors to all such claims. The piece is the learned world's last word on the long dream. It can be read in full in a short, clear sitting.
cia-0000009811:
Information on a prisoner of war camp in Ha Dong town, Ha Tay province, is set out in a November 1971 item. Ha Dong was a town on Hanoi's southwestern edge, close enough to the capital to sit under its direct control. Urban-edge camps differed from jungle sites in routine and risk.

A camp near the capital could hold men in transit between interrogation and long-term prisons. Reports from such towns came through different channels than jungle sightings. Officials weighed them alongside the known Hanoi system. This item adds a suburban point to that system, described from sources available in late 1971.
cia-0000009911:
Three American prisoners of war were used by the Viet Cong for propaganda meetings, a November 1966 report states, with an audience the title cuts off. Propaganda meetings paraded captives before villagers, cameras, or foreign guests. The men had no real choice in the performance.

Such reports told officials two things: the three were alive on a date, and their captors were exploiting them. Both facts entered the men's files. Families learned of the meetings with pain, yet the proof of life mattered too. This file captures that bitter double value in one small reported event.
cia-0000012311:
An Acting Director of Central Intelligence receives this undated Helms memo, its year estimated as 1962. Acting chiefs inherit live cases midstream, and the Penkovsky operation was the livest file in the building that year. The memo adds one more page to a record that thickened month by month as events accelerated toward the autumn crisis.

The paper trail's growth is itself evidence of the stakes. Each memo to the top marked another turn in a case moving toward October. For readers, the letter preserves the summit's attention in the climactic phase, recorded before anyone knew the ending.
cia-0000012411:
Meeting number thirty gets a bare title and a year, 1961: a milestone recorded in the plainest possible form. Thirty sittings with one Soviet colonel in a single year. The number alone conveys an intelligence haul without parallel. Each meeting meant hours of answers and hundreds of pages. Each also meant fresh risk, accepted by the source on his return to Moscow.

The record's bareness speaks as loudly as any summary could. Clerks by then were numbering history as routine paperwork. For readers, the page is the operation's scale stated in a single figure, with everything else left to imagine.
cia-0000013211:
Prison camps for allied prisoners in Cambodia, and where they answered in the chain of command, are mapped in a CIA paper from January 1971. The camps sat under the Central Office for South Vietnam, the headquarters that ran the southern war from across the border. The files diagram the structure: orders flowing down to jungle camps, reports flowing back up the same channels.

The paper shows the dungeons run like an army outfit, not a scatter of huts. Understanding who commanded the camps mattered for every rescue plan and protest. For readers, it is the prison system drawn as an organization chart.
cia-0000013611:
Could Venezuela's young democracy last? A CIA paper from January 1964 weighs the prospects for political stability there. The country had just managed a rare feat. Power had passed between elected presidents peacefully for the first time in its history. The left's gunmen still tested the state, though. They fought its troops in the hills and the cities, while oil money funded the government's promises.

The paper forecasts the vote's future with care. It asks whether ballots could survive bullets in a land new to both. For readers, it shows a working democracy graded by skeptics who had watched many others fall.
cia-0000013911: South Vietnamese soldiers and two American prisoners were seen in Laos, in a CIA note dated November 4, 1967. The prisoners belonged to the ARVN, South Vietnam's army, and to U.S. forces. Laos lay outside Vietnam, yet its trails carried much of the war. A sighting there showed prisoners could be held beyond Vietnam's borders.
cia-0000014611: A London Reuters item is preserved in a CIA file dated January 1, 1949, mis-dated against its own subject. The item quotes the wife of convicted atom spy Morton Sobell speaking in London. Sobell's spy trial came later, so the file's date sits oddly beside its text. The clip shows how press words on spy cases entered the agency's files.
cia-0000014711: Impact of the Rosenberg case is the broad subject of a CIA paper dated November 4, 1952. The paper weighed what the case had done to opinion and politics. Few spy trials have echoed so long or so far. A paper taking the case's full measure shows officials knew they were living through a landmark, not a routine trial.
cia-0000015311: A letter to Leon Davidson from J. S. Harman fills a CIA file dated April 1, 1958. Harman thanks Davidson for his letters of April 2, another small date slip. Davidson's stream of questions never quite stopped. Each reply from the agency was short, civil, and firm, and this file holds one more of them.
cia-0000015411: On April 4, 1958, CIA officers met with Mr. Chapin to plan a reply to Leon Davidson, a dogged writer on flying saucers. Notes from May add a later phone call with Major Tacker of the Air Force. Chapin agreed to draft the answer along lines used in an earlier reply. Davidson kept asking what the government knew, and the file shows how carefully each answer was weighed.
cia-0000022811: American casualties and grave sites in Kratie Province, Cambodia, are recorded in a CIA item dated in 1974. Kratie, on the Mekong, saw heavy fighting as the war spread west. Grave sites marked where men might one day be recovered and named. Mapping them was grim duty, done so that no resting place was lost to the record.
cia-0000037111: A CIA record dated February 4, 1943 lists disbursements for travel and other expenses, naming Shaw, McDonough, Sherwood, Tyler, and Wood. The page is wartime bookkeeping from the OSS years, when American secret work was still new. Each entry ties a payment to a person in the plain style of an accounts ledger. Pages like this show the office routine that supported work done far from home.
cia-0000049111: Members of the MNR issued a communique in 1985, preserved in a CIA item kept with the Truth Commission records. The MNR was a social democratic party in the opposition front, speaking for the political wing of the struggle. Communiques were how such movements put their line on record, for friends and enemies alike.
cia-0000049211: The verbatim text of a discussion on the Jesuit murders fills a CIA item from 1991, kept with the Truth Commission records. Verbatim records keep what summaries smooth away: hedges, orders of speaking, and the exact words used. In a case built on who said what, such a transcript was evidence in itself.
cia-0000049311: Declassified CIA document 0000049311, dated October 6, 1980, is titled El Salvador: Growing Rightist Ascendancy and carries a Truth Commission note. Like its companion paper of the same date, it treats the growing power of the right in El Salvador. The file offers the agency's wording on that shift, preserved as a short declassified item rather than a narrative history.
cia-0000049411: Guerrillas continuing a war of attrition in El Salvador are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049411, dated July 1, 1985. Marked for the Truth Commission, the item describes the conflict as attrition. Readers get a short declassified record whose title carries that judgment, one of the agency's mid-war characterizations of how the fighting was being waged.
cia-0000095211: A cable from Leopoldville about the intended course of action is declassified CIA document 0000095211, dated August 3, 1960. The heading does not say whose action or toward what end. The short file is a declassified cable record from the Congo station, preserved with a title that announces a plan while revealing almost nothing about it.
cia-0000112811: Herbert Moy, Active Collaborator is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112811, dated October 5, 1944. The title gives a name and a label: Herbert Moy, called an active collaborator. Collaborator is a charge, stated flatly in the heading itself. The brief record is a name and charge file from the autumn of 1944 in the files as released.
cia-0000117911: Dated June 3, 1967, declassified CIA document 0000117911 gives Prince Sihanouk's condition for restoring ties between the United States and Cambodia. Its heading calls that idea restoration, its key word in the title itself. He is named in the heading, and his condition is the whole stated topic of the file. The brief record is a short item on one man's terms for a return.
cia-0000119211:
From about January 1985, this CIA document concerns reports that American prisoners of war were executed during the 1970s. Claims like these were the darkest the agency had to weigh in its missing-persons work. The paper preserves the allegation together with the agency's handling of it.

Judging such reports meant sorting rumor, faulty memory, and possible fact. A claim of executions, if true, changed both history and policy, and if false, it could torment families for nothing. The document shows that weighing process at work. It stands as part of the record of how the government treated the hardest questions left by the war.
cia-0000119711:
An October 1953 CIA paper forecasts probable developments in Iran through 1954. It was written two months after the coup that drove out Prime Minister Mossadegh and restored the Shah's power. Washington now had to judge what the new order would bring.

The paper looks ahead at Iran's politics and at the stability of a government America had helped install. Forecasts made just after a coup carry a special interest, since they show what the winners expected and feared. For readers, this estimate is a check on those hopes: a statement of where Iran seemed bound, made when the Shah's long second reign was only beginning.
cia-0000124311: A July 1951 CIA document reports on American prisoners held at North Korean camps. The camps along the Yalu River held large numbers of men in harsh conditions. What happened inside them became one of the war's lasting disputes, and the paper records the agency's picture. Camp reporting built slowly from escapees, repatriated sick men, and letters, and papers like this one mark stages in assembling a picture long kept deliberately dark.
cia-0000132311:
Kuwaiti oil fires and the major threat they posed fill Situation Report 621 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series. The report is dated February 6, 1991. Hundreds of wells were burning at once. Smoke from the fires choked much of the region and darkened the daytime sky.

The report assesses what the fires threatened most. Health, weather, water supplies, and shipping all stood at risk. So did the hard work of putting the wells out once fighting stopped. The burning fields became one of the war's most lasting images around the world. Readers get the agency's judgment, made while the fires still raged, of how serious the damage could become.
cia-0000132511: February 4, 1961 brought yet another CIA briefing titled simply Cuba. The pile of same-day papers shows the priority the island held for Kennedy's new team, which wanted constant updates while the Bay of Pigs operation was being planned. Cuba led the agenda that winter. Released long afterward, this declassified copy is preserved from the CIA Reading Room via the Internet Archive.
cia-0000132611: Cuba alone fills part three of a CIA item dated July 1, 1960. The section is headed the West. In that section Cuba stood as the standing headline through 1960, needing no further label. A single word carried the whole Cuba file for that day. The short item preserves the entry exactly as the series labeled it.
cia-0000135711: A document in Spanish dated 1 February 1961, from the declassified papers of Brigade 2506, the Cuban exile force assembled by the CIA. February opened the brigade's last stretch of training. The catalog record names no topic for this item. Preserved in the original Spanish, it is part of the dense February run of brigade paperwork that the agency later released, and its contents must be read in the text itself.
cia-0000135911: A CIA cable dated 5 May 1954 deals with the true story, in the cable's own words, in files since declassified. The paper sits inside the CIA drive against President Arbenz, run under the code name PBSUCCESS and crowned by the June 1954 coup. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136611: An estimated date of 4 November 1960 heads this Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade files, with the estimate flagged in the catalog title. The brigade was training that fall for the invasion of Cuba. Because the date is estimated, the agency's reviewers assigned it rather than copying it from the page. No subject is recorded for the item. It is preserved in Spanish in the declassified release, among the brigade's November paperwork.
cia-0000137011: Meet with the ambassador, SKILLET proposes in this July 1954 cable. It asks the Guatemala City station to discuss a conference with JMBLUG. The ambassador hopes the station will do this. He wants the station to press him at a 23 July conference. A fragment notes he failed to mention something in a referenced message. The sample here is too short and garbled for more. The conference's subject cannot be recovered. The cable still shows the new ambassador being drawn in fast.
cia-0000137111: An estimated-date 1961 Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers; the catalog gives only the year and marks it as estimated. The Brigade was the CIA-trained Cuban exile force that landed at the Bay of Pigs in April 1961. The record names no subject or month for this item. It is preserved in the original Spanish in the declassified release, a loosely dated piece of the brigade's final-year archive.
cia-0000137411: Spanish paperwork from Brigade 2506 fills document 0000137411, dated to 1961 with the date itself marked as an estimate. The brigade was the exile unit the CIA built for the Bay of Pigs, and much of its internal writing stayed in the men's own language. No subject line comes with this record, so its precise business is left to the page itself. It stands as one small piece of a failed invasion's archive, now open to any reader.
cia-03150411: March 9, 1957: the bulletin delivered the day's intelligence. Senior officials read the analysts' summary of global developments. The Cold War's daily dose. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Kept for readers.
cia-03186011: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1961/03/16, a CIA publication. The March briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-06345911: EC AGRICULTURAL POLICY: IMPACT OF GERMAN UNIFICATION, EAST EUROPEAN REFORMS, a CIA assessment. The farm policy. This file preserves that declassified paper. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
codex-junius-11: One of the great treasures of Old English literature: a 10th-century manuscript containing biblical poems in Anglo-Saxon verse. Genesis, Exodus, and Daniel are retold in the alliterative, heroic style of Beowulf, with Satan brooding over his fall and the Israelites crossing the Red Sea. This edition makes the founding epic poetry of the English language available to modern readers.
conrad-under-western-eyes-1911:
Joseph Conrad, born in Poland under Russian rule, returned to the world of revolutionaries in Under Western Eyes, published in 1911. An English teacher of languages in Geneva tells the story. It is often called Conrad's darkest political novel.

A St. Petersburg student named Razumov shelters an assassin who has just killed a minister. Fearing ruin, Razumov betrays him, then is sent to Geneva as a spy on the exile circle. There he falls in love with the dead man's sister while living his lie. The novel dissects guilt, autocracy, and the blindness of the watching West.
constitution-canada-2011: Canada's Constitution, patriated in 1982, frames its federation. The Charter guards rights. The Tower library holds the full text. It cut London's cord. Queen stayed. Rights reigned. Provinces shared. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-gabon-2011: Gabon's 1991 Constitution, amended through 2011, frames its republic. It kept long rule. The Tower library holds the full text. It pumped oil wealth. Votes held. Power stayed. Law framed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-morocco-2011: Morocco's 2011 Constitution, passed by referendum, reformed its kingdom. The King kept power. The Tower library holds the full text. It calmed spring unrest. Crowds marched. King yielded some. Throne stayed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-oman-2011: Oman's Basic Law, amended 2011, frames its sultanate. The Sultan rules supreme. The Tower library holds the full text. It kept frankincense rule. Sultan reigned. Calm held. Desert obeyed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-paraguay-2011: Paraguay's 1992 Constitution, amended through 2011, frames its republic. It buried dictatorship. The Tower library holds the full text. It ended Stroessner. Tyrant fell. Voters came. Rivers ran. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-spain-2011: Spain's 1978 Constitution, amended through 2011, frames its kingdom. It buried Franco. The Tower library holds the full text. It ended dictatorship. Caudillo died. King steered. Democracy bloomed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
conte-ponthieu-mason-1911:
The Count of Ponthieu is an anonymous French tale from the age of the Crusades. It calls itself a story of beyond the sea. Eugene Mason translated it into English in 1911, in a volume of old French tales of love and war.

Its heroine, the count's daughter, is seized while traveling and carried off overseas. A Saracen emir falls in love with her and treats her with honor. Around her gather questions of ransom, faith, and conversion. The tale shows how medieval Christians imagined the Muslim world they fought, feared, and sometimes admired.
cotgrave-french-english-1611:
Randle Cotgrave published his Dictionarie of the French and English Tongues in 1611, the first great French-English dictionary. Cotgrave served as secretary to a great lord and spent years gathering French words from books and speech. His England was learning the tongue of Montaigne and needed a bridge between the languages.

The dictionary gives French words with generous English equivalents, proverbs, and turns of phrase, often with a flash of humor. It records the spoken French of its day beside the literary language, which makes it a treasure house of early modern speech. Four hundred years on, it remains a foundation of French study in England. Scholars of Shakespeare's age use it to catch meanings that modern French has lost, and students of both tongues still delight in its riches.
cumont-oriental-religions-showerman-1911:
Franz Cumont's The Oriental Religions in Roman Paganism appears in Grant Showerman's translation of 1911. Cumont studies the cults that flowed into Rome from the East. Isis from Egypt, Mithras from Persia, Cybele from Asia Minor, and Syrian gods transformed Roman religion. Their rites promised purity and life after death.

Cumont argues these faiths prepared the way for Christianity's triumph. His synthesis was a masterwork that reshaped the study of Roman religion. Later scholars corrected details, yet his map still guides the field. The lectures read clearly for general audiences. They remain the classic short account of Rome's eastern cults. Showerman's version served English readers well.
de-lapide-philosophorvm-tractatvs-dvodec: Twelve Latin treatises on the philosophers' stone appeared in 1611. The dozen tracts draw from nature's fount. The early modern alchemy. The archive keeps the paper open to all. This book preserves that collection. Kept for readers.
descartes-philosophical-works-haldane-ro:
Elizabeth S Haldane and G R T Ross published Volume 1 of The Philosophical Works of Descartes in 1911. Their translation became the standard English Descartes for most of the twentieth century. René Descartes, the French founder of modern philosophy, wrote the works gathered here across his career.

Volume 1 holds the Rules for the Direction of the Mind, the Discourse on Method, and the Meditations on First Philosophy. Selections from the Principles of Philosophy, The Search after Truth, and The Passions of the Soul follow. Readers meet the cogito, the doubt of the senses, and the split of mind and body in Descartes's own order. No single volume gives a fuller start on him.
dreiser-jennie-gerhardt-1911:
Theodore Dreiser published Jennie Gerhardt in 1911, eleven years after his first novel was buried by its own publisher. His editors cut the manuscript heavily, fearing its treatment of an unmarried mother. Dreiser based Jennie partly on his own sisters' hard lives in Indiana poverty.

Jennie, a poor laundress in Columbus, is seduced by an aging senator who dies before he can marry her. She then devotes herself to a rich man's son, Lester Kane, living with him outside marriage and sacrificing her happiness to protect his. Dreiser refuses to judge her; his slow, heavy prose builds pity instead. Jennie Gerhardt is his most tender and morally complex novel, and the one many readers love best.
essays-idleness-sansom-1911:
G. B. Sansom Englished Yoshida Kenko's Essays in Idleness in 1911, the first English rendering of the Tsurezuregusa. Kenko, a fourteenth-century courtier turned recluse, set down short pieces as thoughts came to him. Beauty, death, manners, and the folly of ambition drift through his meditations without fixed order.

Kenko loves old things, quiet rooms, and the turning seasons, and distrusts fuss of every kind. His book became one of Japan's most loved classics, a model of the zuihitsu, the follow-the-brush essay. Sansom's translation introduced that gentle art to English readers for the first time.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-11: The eleventh volume holds some of Montaigne's ripest essays. He writes of experience, judgment, and the limits of reason. The old Gascon's voice is mellow, sure, and full of good humor. A rich harvest of a lifetime's thought.
eucken-truth-religion-1911:
What truth does religion hold, and where does that truth rest? Rudolf Eucken, the 1908 Nobel laureate from Jena, took up both questions in Der Wahrheitsgehalt der Religion in 1901. W. Tudor Jones translated the work, and the text here follows the second edition of 1913.

Eucken argues that religion speaks to the deepest layer of human life, the life of the spirit. He tests rival views of faith and sets out the ground on which belief can stand. His case ties religion to moral effort and inner renewal. The book forms a key part of his philosophy of religion.
europmc-pmc10210811: A medical paper on the limitation and control of streptococcus and other respiratory infections. The throat germs' control. This article preserves that public health research. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc10767911:
Milacic and co-authors updated Reactome in 2024, a free knowledge base of biological pathways. Reactome charts cell processes as ordered chains of molecular steps. Each entry is curated by hand in one shared data model. The bank serves both as an archive and as a tool to mine gene data.

Work pushes toward notes on the full human protein set, Milacic reports. Disease-causing gene variants and small-molecule drugs gain pathway context as well. Cell- and tissue-specific paths are a further growth front. Links with kin resources, such as the Gene Ontology, need care to keep the web sound. The team weighs how to keep that shared network in good health.
europmc-pmc10776411:
Lin and Peddada present a new stats method for gut and soil microbe studies in this 2024 paper. A microbiome is the full mix of tiny living things in a sample. Labs often ask which microbes grow or shrink between groups of samples. Older tools handle two groups well, but many studies have three or more groups, such as stages of a disease.

Their method, ANCOM-BC2, compares many groups at once. It can adjust for other factors that differ between samples, and it can use repeat samples from the same source. Pair-by-pair checks waste power and raise false alarms, the authors note. They show the method on soil samples sorted by dryness and on gut samples from bowel disease patients before and after surgery.
europmc-pmc11122111:
GBD 2021 Diseases and Injuries Collaborators report health loss for 371 diseases and injuries across 204 countries in this 2024 study. Detailed counts of sickness and early death by cause are crucial for spotting shifting patterns over time. For three decades the Global Burden of Disease study has filled that need. This round adds, for the first time, health loss from the COVID-19 pandemic.

The team estimated years lived with disability, years of life lost, a combined burden measure, and healthy life expectancy. Counts are split by age, sex, and place, including 811 subnational locations, for 1990 to 2021. A global network of collaborators supplied, reviewed, and analysed the data. Methods were refined with each update, the authors note. They frame the estimates as a base for evidence-based action and for tracking health targets.
europmc-pmc11456611:
Li and colleagues review the signalling pathways behind colorectal cancer and its targeted therapies in this 2024 paper. Colorectal cancer is still among the top causes of cancer death worldwide. Networks that govern cell proliferation, survival, differentiation, and death run its development. Their dysregulation turns normal colon lining malignant.

The review dissects the foundational mechanisms and the molecular hallmarks of the disease. Genomic, epigenomic, and microbial features are covered: changes to DNA, changes to its chemical tags, and the gut microbes present. Targeted and immune therapies are then assessed for their clinical impact. Deepening knowledge of oncogenic signalling has revealed key nodes that drugs can exploit, the authors say. Remaining challenges include resistance and patient selection. The paper aims to state the general principles of neoplastic evolution in this cancer.
europmc-pmc12369211:
Izquierdo and a large expert panel set exercise guidance for older adults in 2021. Aging weakens every body function over time. How people live shapes how fast that decline runs. Staying active is the strongest known brake.

The panel writes for the ICFSR, an international research body. Regular exercise guards muscle, fitness, and daily independence. It also lowers risk of heart disease, stroke, and diabetes. Gains extend to mobility, mood, and quality of life. Izquierdo merges global evidence into shared advice. The guidance aims to keep older adults active and independent longer.
europmc-pmc1239911:
Wolfe, Kohane, and Butte tested a common shortcut in gene research in 2005. Genes that switch on together often share a job. So an unknown gene may be judged by the company it keeps. That shortcut is called guilt by association.

How far the shortcut truly holds was untested at scale. The team built scores linking each gene to known job groups. They checked five networks across three mammal species. Expression data came from a large and varied collection. Wolfe shows where the shortcut works and where prior knowledge misses it.
europmc-pmc1280411:
Brown, Lockwood, and Sonawane reviewed environmental risks for degenerative brain diseases in 2005. America is aging, and these diseases grow more common. Causes of most remain unknown. The review gathers population evidence on environmental suspects.

Diseases covered include Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and ALS. Related parkinsonian syndromes also enter the survey. Suspect exposures range from metals and pesticides to solvents and fields. Evidence for each link was judged not conclusive overall. Still, indications of causal links appear across studies. Brown calls the need for more research obvious. Electromagnetic fields are among the exposures surveyed. Metals and solvents get their own checks in the text.
europmc-pmc1382011:
Kilpatrick and co-authors explained West Nile epidemics through mosquito feeding shifts in 2006. The virus arrived in North America in 1999. It is now the dominant mosquito-borne disease there. Spillover from birds to humans sets epidemic intensity.

The main urban mosquito shifted feeding from birds to humans seven times. The shift came in late summer and early fall. It coincided with dispersal of its preferred host, the American robin. Human infections rose at the same time. A western mosquito showed the same amplifying shift in Colorado and California. Feeding behavior, not just virus presence, drives epidemics. Robins leave the Northeast as fall comes on.
europmc-pmc1435411:
Spending on nature protection runs into billions, yet few ask if the money works. Ferraro and Pattanayak made that charge in 2006. They argue the field of conservation policy leans on gut feel and stories from the field. Other fields, such as poverty aid and disease control, test programs with care.

The pair call for the same rigor used to test ideas about ecosystems. A sound test asks if a program beats doing nothing at all. Ferraro notes that a major global review found data-rich biology chapters, but thin proof on policy results. Without such tests, scarce funds may flow to plans that feel right but fail.
europmc-pmc1479811:
Each blood cell type runs its own set of genes. Palmer and co-authors charted those sets in 2006 for the main white cell types in human blood. They purified B cells, two T cell kinds, and other white cells from donors. Then they compared their gene activity on chips.

Like cells from unlike donors grouped together by their patterns. Each type had a signature set of genes: 427 for B cells, 411 for granulocytes, and smaller sets for others. Surface protein genes stood out among the markers. Palmer suggests the signatures can guide work on the many genes whose jobs remain unknown.
europmc-pmc1764711:
Gene-swapping enzymes for mammals mostly meant one tool, Cre. Raymond and Soriano added two more in 2007 by synthesizing mouse-optimized versions, FLPo and PhiC31o. Site-specific recombinases cut and rejoin DNA at set addresses, letting researchers delete or flip genes.

Earlier FLP and PhiC31 versions worked poorly in mammalian cells. Recoding their genes with mouse-preferred codons lifted their efficiency to match Cre. Having three efficient enzymes opens more complex genome engineering, like sequential edits using different address systems. Raymond reports the new enzymes function in living cells at high efficiency.  Tests in cells confirmed both new enzymes recombine their target sites with high efficiency.
europmc-pmc1779511:
Bonneau and colleagues presented in 2006 a computer method named the Inferelator. The method learns gene control networks from large biology data sets. A control network shows which genes switch other genes on or off, and which outside signals matter.

The core problem is that data are scarce next to the many possible controls. The Inferelator picks a short, simple set of likely controls for each gene, favoring models that stay lean. It can also handle cases where two control proteins act together, or where light and other signals change a control. Tested on the salt-loving microbe Halobacterium, the learned network predicted gene activity under new test conditions the model had not seen. That success showed the approach could rebuild global control maps from scratch.
europmc-pmc1800311:
Boutron, Ravaud and colleagues cataloged in 2007 how trialists hide treatment assignment in studies of non-drug care. Blinding, where patients or clinicians do not know who got which treatment, guards against bias. It is hard to achieve for surgery, devices, rehab, or talk therapy, so teams invent nonstandard tricks.

The authors searched major databases for randomized trials published in 2004 in high-impact journals. They found 145 reports, with the blinding method described in 123 of them. Sham procedures that mimic surgery were a main route for participants and providers. Device trials used sham prostheses, identical but switched-off machines, or machines blocked by a barrier. Another common tactic blinded patients to the study hypothesis itself rather than to the treatment they received.
europmc-pmc1849911:
Gojova, Barakat and co-authors tested in 2007 whether tiny metal oxide particles stir inflammation in human blood vessel cells. Ultrafine particles can cross from the lung into the blood, which may explain their link to heart disease. The cells lining vessels, the endothelium, drive much of that disease process.

They exposed human aortic endothelial cells for up to eight hours to particles of iron oxide, yttrium oxide, and zinc oxide across a wide dose range. They then measured three inflammation markers, including interleukin-8 and a monocyte-attracting protein. Particle delivery to the cell surface and uptake inside the cells tracked directly with the inflammatory response. Composition mattered: the three oxides did not provoke equal reactions at equal doses. The work supports direct vessel contact as a route from inhaled particles to cardiovascular harm.
europmc-pmc1854911:
Matsuo and co-authors traced in 2007 why one fruit fly species loves a fruit its cousins avoid. Drosophila sechellia feeds on Morinda citrifolia, the Tahitian noni, whose ripe fruit gives off hexanoic and octanoic acids. Sister species are repelled by those acids, while sechellia is drawn to them.

Crossing sechellia with deletion strains of a sister species pinned part of the difference on a gene named Obp57e. It codes an odorant-binding protein, a carrier that ferries smell molecules. Knocking out Obp57e and its neighbor Obp57d in the sister species changed responses to both acids. Putting the sechellia or cousin versions of the two genes into the knockout flies shifted egg-laying site choice to match the donor species. The genes thus help set host-plant preference through taste.
europmc-pmc2125011: A medical paper on the Negri bodies in rabies. The telltale inclusions. This article preserves that pathology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2125511: A medical paper on the normal fate of erythrocytes and blood destruction in plethoric animals. The red cells' end. This article preserves that hematology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2125811: A medical paper on the effect of alcohol on the reproductive tissues. The drink's damage. This article preserves that toxicology. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It holds its historical place. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2128211: A medical paper on superinfection in experimental syphilis after subcurative treatment. The second infection. This article preserves that venereology. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2128411: A medical paper with studies based on a malignant tumor of the rabbit, miscellaneous results. The rabbit cancer again. This article preserves that oncology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2128611: Another medical paper with studies on the rabbit's malignant tumor, growth variations. The rabbit cancer once more. This article preserves that oncology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it.
europmc-pmc2131311: A medical paper with a study of the Hering-Breuer reflex. The breathing reflex. This article preserves that physiology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it.
europmc-pmc2242811:
Hansen, Chandra, Mitic, Onken, Driscoll and Kenyon tested in 2008 whether autophagy is required for dietary restriction to extend lifespan in worms. Autophagy is the cell's large-scale recycling of its own proteins and organelles. Eating less extends life in many species, partly by quieting the nutrient sensor TOR. TOR inhibition switches autophagy on. The team blocked autophagy genes in Caenorhabditis elegans under dietary restriction and TOR inhibition.

Both interventions produced an autophagic state in the worms. Blocking autophagy genes prevented both from extending lifespan. The response also needed the transcription factor PHA-4, which dietary restriction requires for longevity. Yet autophagy alone was not sufficient to extend life. Long-lived insulin-pathway mutants needed both autophagy and the factor DAF-16. The authors suggest DAF-16 directs recycled material into protective proteins.
europmc-pmc2244711:
Sandin and a large team surveyed coral reefs in 2008 across the Northern Line Islands to set a pristine baseline. Most reefs are degraded by fishing, pollution and global change, tangling local and global effects. The team studied uninhabited atolls, Kingman and Palmyra, and increasingly populated ones, Tabuaeran and Kiritimati. They compared reef community structure along that human gradient.

Top predators and reef-building organisms dominated the unpopulated atolls. Sharks and other large predators made the biomass pyramid inverted, with more predator weight than prey. Small plankton-eating fish and fleshy algae dominated the populated atolls. Those showed the typical bottom-heavy pyramid. Reefs without people had less coral disease and greater coral recruitment. The authors argue protection from fishing and pollution builds resilience against warming.
europmc-pmc2267811:
Morrison, Zielinski-Gutierrez, Scott and Rosenberg set out challenges in 2008 for controlling the mosquito Aedes aegypti. This daytime-biting mosquito spreads dengue, yellow fever and chikungunya, and lives in and around human homes. History shows control can work: eliminating breeding sites enabled Panama Canal construction, and eradication campaigns cleared both diseases from most of Central and South America in the 1950s and 1960s.

Yet those successes were usually short-lived, and dengue has reoccupied Latin America. Urbanisation expands mosquito habitat, global travel spreads vector and virus, and poverty hobbles household protection. The authors argue eradication is unrealistic. The practical goal is reducing adult mosquito numbers or human contact below the level that sustains an epidemic. Suppression done properly remains a practical method, they conclude.
europmc-pmc2291011:
Adibi and colleagues characterised phthalate exposure in pregnancy in 2008 by testing how stable urine and air measurements stay over time. Phthalates are plastics and cosmetics chemicals measured through their breakdown products in urine, but repeatability during pregnancy was unknown. The team measured metabolites in spot urine from 246 pregnant women of Dominican and African-American background. Some samples were repeated over six weeks. They also sampled personal and indoor air for five parent compounds.

Phthalates appeared in 85 to 100 percent of air and urine samples. Reproducibility of urine metabolites varied. Correlation coefficients started at 0.30 for mono-ethyl phthalate and rose to 0.66 for monobenzyl phthalate. The strongest air correlations reached 0.83 for butylbenzyl phthalate across repeated home samples. Air levels tracked matching urinary metabolites. Urine from late pregnancy was best adjusted by specific gravity. One indoor air sample suffices, but urine needs repeated sampling.
europmc-pmc2360111:
Eckel and Schmid pooled trial results for advanced biliary tract cancer in 2007. This cancer grows in the bile ducts or gallbladder, and no standard drug treatment existed. Randomised trials, the strongest kind, were missing, so doctors relied on small early studies of drugs such as 5-fluorouracil and gemcitabine.

The authors analysed 104 trials with 2,810 patients, covering work from 1985 to 2006. Across all trials, tumors shrank in 22.6% of patients, and disease was controlled in 57.3% of them, figures the analysis linked to longer survival. Gallbladder cancer shrank more often than bile duct cancer but patients died sooner. Regimens pairing gemcitabine with a platinum drug performed best. The authors called that pairing the provisional standard until stronger evidence arrives.
europmc-pmc2394311:
Adami and colleagues tracked cancer risk after organ transplants across Sweden in 2003. Transplant patients take drugs that suppress the immune system, which may let cancers grow unchecked. The study followed 5,931 people who received a kidney, liver, or other organ between 1970 and 1997.

Linking to national registers gave nearly complete follow-up. The team counted 692 first cancers against 171 expected from general population rates, a four-fold excess overall. Non-melanoma skin cancer stood out at a standardised ratio of 56.2, and lip cancer at 53.3 in the same measure, while lymphoma ran six-fold high. Patients with organs other than kidneys faced far higher lymphoma risk than kidney recipients. Twenty-fold excesses appeared for vulva and vagina cancers, and ten-fold for anal cancer. The excess persisted over time.
europmc-pmc2518111:
Dwan and a large group of collaborators reviewed the evidence in 2008 that clinical trials are published selectively. Two distortions were in view: whole studies going unpublished, and published reports quietly changing which outcomes they feature. Both can mislead the reviews that doctors rely on to judge treatments.

Sixteen cohort studies that tracked trials from approval onward met the criteria. Trials with positive, statistically significant results were more likely to reach print. Significant outcomes had 2.2 to 4.7 times the odds of being fully reported compared with non-significant ones. Between 40 and 62 percent of studies changed, added, or dropped at least one main outcome between protocol and publication. The authors call for better trial reporting to curb both biases.
europmc-pmc2527811:
Lammers, Hennink, and Storm reviewed in 2008 how tiny drug carriers could deliver cancer medicines straight to tumours. These nanomedicines are particles measured in billionths of a metre that ferry chemotherapy drugs through the bloodstream. Without them, injected drugs clear fast, only a small share reaches the tumour, and healthy tissues suffer the toxic effects.

The review covers the main carrier families, including liposomes, which are fat bubbles, and polymer particles, plus the strategies for steering them. Some designs raise drug levels inside the tumour to boost killing power. Others steer drug away from sensitive organs to cut side effects. The authors report clear evidence that such targeting improves the balance of benefit to harm for anticancer agents, and they map where the field should go next.
europmc-pmc2569211:
Paulsen, reporting for the Predict-HD Investigators and Coordinators of the Huntington Study Group, presented in 2008 evidence that Huntington's disease develops measurably decades before diagnosis. The study followed 438 people who carry the disease gene but show no functional decline. Using each person's gene repeat length and age to estimate years until diagnosis, the team modelled thinking, movement, mood, and brain imaging measures against that clock.

Nearly every marker tracked the estimated time to diagnosis. The pattern suggests detectable changes begin one to two decades before doctors could traditionally diagnose the disease. The findings held up across very different kinds of measurement. The authors propose these early markers as candidates for prevention trials, which need ways to measure disease long before symptoms declare themselves.
europmc-pmc2585011:
Petkova and Ehrsson reported in 2008 a laboratory illusion in which people feel they have swapped bodies with another person or a mannequin. Feeling located inside one's own body is central to selfhood, yet how the brain produces it was unclear. The team manipulated what volunteers saw through head-mounted displays while delivering matching touches to two bodies at once.

The combination of an outside visual perspective and synchronised touch was enough to relocate the sense of self. Volunteers felt the other body was their own, even while facing their real body. The effect grew so strong that participants could shake hands with their own body while experiencing it as someone else. The authors identify the perceptual processes, vision plus correlated multisensory signals, that create body ownership.
europmc-pmc2613511:
Zhang, Lv, Li, Xu, and Chen refined a rat model of type 2 diabetes in 2008, combining a high-fat diet with injections of streptozotocin, a chemical that damages insulin-producing cells. Existing models often miss the human pattern of insulin resistance plus failing insulin release. The team fed male Wistar rats a fatty diet for four weeks, then varied the dose and number of streptozotocin injections.

A single 45 milligram per kilogram dose produced diabetes in every rat but slashed insulin too far, unlike human disease. Two weekly injections of 30 milligrams per kilogram worked best, succeeding in 85 percent of rats. Those animals showed the classic trio of insulin resistance, high blood sugar, and disordered blood lipids. The plant compound berberine then reversed these symptoms, validating the model for drug screening.
europmc-pmc2631711:
Chambers argued in 2001 that the epidemiology of Staphylococcus aureus is changing, as methicillin-resistant strains escape the hospitals where they had been confined. MRSA had lived almost exclusively in hospitals and long-term care facilities, striking patients with prior antibiotics, surgery, or intensive care. New reports described resistant infections in children from the community with none of those risk factors.

Chambers draws a striking parallel with the emergence of penicillin resistance in the same bacterium decades earlier, which also began in hospitals and then spread outward. Whether the community strains escaped from hospitals or arose independently was unknown. Either way, their prevalence in the community seemed likely to increase substantially. A quarter to a half of people carry S. aureus harmlessly. A resistant reservoir could therefore spread quietly through ordinary contact.
europmc-pmc2657211:
Viaud and colleagues showed in 2009 that tiny parcels shed by immune cells can wake up a second line of defense against cancer. The parcels, called exosomes, come from dendritic cells, which normally show invaders to T cells. A first human trial of exosome vaccines shrank some tumors even though T cells barely responded, so something else had to be at work.

In mice, the parcels switched on natural killer cells, a fast-acting killer cell type, and made them multiply. Two signals on the parcel surface did the work: one feeding a growth receptor, the other pressing an activation switch called NKG2D. In trial patients, the vaccine restored killer cell numbers and function in seven of fourteen people. The parcels, it seems, fight tumors through this side door, not only through T cells.
europmc-pmc2679711:
Mo, Palsson, and Herrgård showed in 2009 that what yeast spills into its surroundings can reveal the hidden traffic inside its cells. Chemists can measure the chemicals a cell excretes far more easily than the flows among its internal reactions. The team asked whether a genome-scale map of yeast chemistry could turn those outer readings into inner knowledge.

They rebuilt the map, called iMM904, with 904 genes and 1,412 reactions, and checked it against nearly 2,900 gene-deletion growth tests from the literature. Then they fed in measured spill patterns from yeast whose nitrogen handling had been disturbed, in genes or in food. The model's sampled flow patterns matched published inner measurements. The changed flows also pointed back to the right neighborhoods of the network, the ones actually disturbed. Outer chemistry, handled this way, becomes a window on the cell's inner state.
europmc-pmc2717911:
Metscher showed in 2009 that simple stains let X-ray microCT, a scan that builds three-dimensional images from X-rays, reveal soft animal tissues in fine detail. Soft tissues absorb X-rays weakly, so they showed up poorly beside bone. Toxic osmium stains helped a little, but no easy, general method existed for comparing body form across species.

Stains based on iodine and phosphotungstic acid proved easy to handle, far less toxic, and strong across many tissues. Images of vertebrates, embryos, insects, and other invertebrates resolved single muscle fibers and even single blood cells in place. The method keeps specimens intact, so the same animal can be studied again with other tools.
europmc-pmc2745811:
van der Heijde and co-authors checked in 2009 whether adalimumab slows spinal damage in ankylosing spondylitis. They worked with the Canadian (M03-606) study group and ATLAS study group. The disease is a chronic rheumatic condition that stiffens the spine. The drug eases symptoms and improves quality of life. Whether it also stops structural damage was the open question.

They pooled spine X-rays from three hundred seven treated patients. Change was compared against a historic untreated cohort of one hundred sixty-nine. Mean progression scores over two years were nearly identical in both groups. No significant difference appeared even in a matched eligible subset. Symptom control thus did not translate into slower radiographic damage in the spine.
europmc-pmc2760211:
Gutenkunst, Hernandez, Williamson, and Bustamante introduced in 2009 a method to infer the joint demographic history of several populations. It works from multidimensional SNP frequency data, counts of genetic variants shared across groups. Such models illuminate prehistory. They also serve as null models when scanning genomes for selection. Their method computes the expected joint frequency spectrum under candidate histories with up to three populations.

Applied to resequenced DNA from sixty-eight people in four populations, they dated a key split. West African and Eurasian groups parted about one hundred forty thousand years ago. That is earlier than other genetic studies found, partly because migration is included. European and East Asian groups split far later. East Asian and Mexican-American groups split with no sign of later mixing.
europmc-pmc2774511:
MacConaill and co-authors implemented in 2009 OncoMap, a platform for profiling critical cancer gene mutations in clinical tumor samples. Knowing a tumor's mutations can predict outcomes and point to targeted drugs, but testing many mutations at once in routine samples was underdeveloped. Their system checks about four hundred mutations across thirty-three known cancer genes, many tied to drug response or resistance.

On fresh frozen tissue the platform reached sensitivity near ninety-four percent with perfect specificity. On DNA from preserved, paraffin-embedded samples it stayed near eighty-nine percent sensitive and over ninety-nine percent specific. It found known mutations at expected rates in common cancers, plus new ones likely to matter for therapy. In children's low-grade gliomas, profiles split tumors by BRAF mutation status, a grouping with immediate treatment implications. Routine high-throughput profiling, they conclude, is clinically feasible.
europmc-pmc2780911:
Carr and co-authors grew retinal pigment epithelium cells from human induced pluripotent stem cells and transplanted them into rats with retinal dystrophy. In many blinding diseases, including age-related macular degeneration, the failing tissue is this support layer, which keeps light-sensing cells alive. Stem cells reprogrammed from adult cells could supply replacement tissue without embryos.

The grown cells looked like natural retinal pigment epithelium and carried its markers. They ate discarded photoreceptor material in the dish, as healthy support cells do. After transplant into the dystrophic rats, they kept doing so in the eye. Photoreceptors survived better in the short term thanks to that cleanup work. Vision held up long term even though the grafted cells were eventually lost, hinting that the host mounts its own protective response. The work offers a new tissue source for retinal therapy.
europmc-pmc2846311:
Davis and Gaskell set out a theory in 2009 of how adults learn new spoken words, drawing on memory research and brain evidence. Words like blog pass from total novelty to instant familiarity, and the authors argue the journey runs in two stages. A fast recording stage in the hippocampus, the brain's memory hub, captures the new word at first hearing. A slower stage then weaves it into the cortex during rest and sleep.

Meta-analysis of brain scans plus behavioral studies supported the split. Hippocampal responses shifted during first learning, whereas cortical responses to new words only turned word-like after overnight consolidation, meaning sleep- or rest-based strengthening of memories. The account unites word learning with general memory systems.
europmc-pmc2852311:
Cowtan tested several new tricks in 2010 for sharpening the fuzzy first maps produced in X-ray crystallography, and packaged them in a program called Parrot. Solving a structure starts with rough phase estimates, the missing half of the diffraction data. This editing process then improves them by repeatedly forcing the electron-density map to look like a plausible molecule. Classical methods alternate between editing the map and re-imposing the measurements.

Cowtan tests refinements to the standard edits: flattening solvent regions, matching the expected spread of density values, and averaging over duplicate molecules in the crystal. He judged which additions truly helped phases within the classical framework. Parrot carries the winning combination forward as a working tool for structure-solving pipelines.
europmc-pmc2881011:
Frei, Stamm, and Buddeberg-Fischer reviewed in 2010 two decades of published mentoring programs for medical students, while planning one for Zurich. Mentoring is widely praised as a key to a satisfying medical career, yet most countries offer students no formal program. Their search of the medical database for 2000 to 2008 found hundreds of papers, of which twenty-five described structured programs or student surveys.

Fourteen program reports aimed at career advice, professional conduct, research interest, and personal growth. Formats ranged from one-to-one pairing to group mentoring, usually starting in the first two years and lasting to graduation. Students valued the personal faculty bond most, saying it made advice feel individual and pushed them to think harder about career choices.
europmc-pmc2891811:
Eriksson and a team at a consumer genetics company showed in 2010 that web-based, participant-driven research can find real genetic associations. Volunteers mailed in DNA, answered trait surveys online, and received their results back, letting one cohort serve studies of twenty-two traits at once. The design controls for the tangled ancestry that self-selected web samples bring.

Known links for hair color, eye color, and freckling replicated cleanly, validating the self-report approach. Fresh findings followed. Variants near three genes tied to hair shape and curl, and a new freckling locus emerged. So did a smell receptor gene behind detecting asparagus odor in urine. Two regions behind the photic sneeze reflex, sneezing in bright light, rounded out the list. Cheap, parallel trait collection worked.
europmc-pmc2928211:
Kent and co-authors set out a proposal in Trials in 2010 about how clinical trials should report uneven treatment effects across patients. Trial averages can hide wide gaps in risk, so a mean benefit may describe few real patients well.

Their plan puts multivariate risk-based analysis first, grouping patients by combined risk rather than testing one trait at a time. Other subgroup checks should be labelled clearly as primary, when backed by prior evidence and meant to guide care, or secondary and exploratory. Following the scheme would make trial reports clearer and more useful for treatment choices.
europmc-pmc2929211:
Kong and co-authors studied prostate cancer cells in 2010, asking whether a shape-shifting programme called epithelial to mesenchymal transition connects with stem-like traits. Recurrent prostate tumours that resist hormone therapy spread widely and kill many patients, so their cell biology matters.

Cells showing the transition programme carried higher levels of stem-linked genes such as Sox2, Nanog, and Oct4, formed spheres and colonies more readily, and grew tumours in mice. Restoring small RNAs of the miR-200 family reversed the state and cut sphere growth. Lowering Lin28B raised let-7 RNA and weakened self-renewal, pointing to targets for future therapy.
europmc-pmc2936111:
Webster and colleagues used deep gene sequencing in 2010 to survey bacteria living inside three Australian sponges. Sponges host dense microbial communities of ecological and drug-discovery interest, and many members were thought to live only in sponges.

Tag sequencing yielded hundreds of thousands of reads sorted into thousands of kinds across many bacterial phyla, a diversity unmatched in other invertebrate hosts. Nearly half the known sponge-linked groups appeared only in adults and larvae, hinting at passing from parent to offspring. The rest also turned up rarely in seawater, suggesting rare sea microbes can seed sponge populations.
europmc-pmc2962811:
Morris and Zeggini weighed methods for finding rare gene variants tied to complex traits in a 2010 evaluation. Genome-wide scans had found many common variants, yet rare ones remained a largely untapped source of risk.

They propose a method that looks for pile-ups of rare minor variants within the same functional unit, then test strategies by simulation. Approaches built on such pile-ups from resequencing data proved far more powerful than standard scan analysis. The gain, they argue, opens a promising route for the next round of trait gene discovery as sequencing data grows.
europmc-pmc2994911:
Lindsley and colleagues measured flu virus in the coughs of sick volunteers in a 2010 study, aiming to settle how much virus rides in tiny airborne particles. Flu spreads by several routes, and the airborne share was disputed.

Patients at a student clinic coughed into a spirometer while samplers caught the spray by size. Most confirmed flu patients shed viral genetic material in coughs. The material split across sizes, with the largest share in the finest particles under a micrometre, and live virus grew from a couple of samples. Fine particles staying aloft support a real airborne route.
europmc-pmc3016411:
Tse and Engler grew mesenchymal stem cells on gels with stiffness gradients in a 2011 study, asking whether cells migrate toward stiffer ground before choosing a fate. Real tissues vary in stiffness smoothly, and heart scars create steep local gradients.

On a gentle, body-like gradient the cells crawled uphill toward stiffer regions rather than staying put, over three weeks in culture. There they adopted a more contractile, muscle-like character. Cells still travelling kept a hint of a nerve marker, so their fate was not fully fixed en route. Gradient itself, not just stiffness, steers stem cell behaviour.
europmc-pmc3020611:
Vandenesch and colleagues compared community-acquired drug-resistant staph strains from six regions worldwide in a 2003 study. Resistant Staphylococcus aureus, long a hospital problem, had begun infecting healthy people with no hospital contact, raising the question of one spreading clone.

Over a hundred isolates shared the same compact resistance cassette and a toxin gene pair, yet their other toxin genes differed by continent. Fingerprinting showed distinct genetic backgrounds per region, separate from local hospital strains. The pattern suggests resistant community strains arose independently in several places, united by the same two genetic acquisitions.
europmc-pmc3035611:
McCambridge, McAlaney, and Rowe reviewed in 2011 what happens in adulthood to people who drank alcohol heavily as older teenagers. Many cohort studies had followed young drinkers over time, linking teen drinking to later poor health and social trouble. The reviewers set out to judge how strong that long term evidence really was.

Their verdict was cautious. Studies did suggest links between late teen drinking and worse adult physical and mental health, plus wider social costs. Yet the overall quality of the evidence was poor, with bias and confounding hard to rule out. Heavy drinking late in the teen years is common and peaks before the early twenties in rich countries. The authors argue better long term studies are needed before firm claims about lasting harm can guide policy.
europmc-pmc3164711:
Michaela Kirschner and colleagues warned that broken red blood cells distort blood tests for tiny RNA biomarkers in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Cell-free tiny RNAs in plasma are chased as disease markers, and one of them doubles as the yardstick others are measured against. The team asked whether red cell breakage during sample handling corrupts that yardstick.

In clean samples the yardstick RNA barely varied between healthy people and patients, qualifying it as a reference. Once breakage crept in, its level rose in direct proportion to the damage, as did a second red-cell-rich RNA, wrecking its reference value. Spiking plasma with lysed red cells let them set a haemoglobin cutoff below which readings stay trustworthy. Without breakage, both RNAs are steady enough to normalise results.
europmc-pmc3186011:
Mikayla Thompson and colleagues reviewed how the innate immune system first detects viruses in a 2011 paper in Viruses. Before tailored defences can be built, sentinel cells must spot infection fast. They use built-in receptors stationed on cell surfaces, in internal compartments, and free in the cell interior, each tuned to different viral traces, most often viral genetic material.

Receptor families differ in post and prey: some watch the cell's import sacs, others patrol the main compartment for RNA or DNA where it should not be. Tripping any of them launches interferons and inflammatory signals that slow the virus and summon the wider immune response. Placing sensors in several compartments lets cells catch viruses that replicate in different hideouts. The review traces each pathway and its contribution to antiviral defence.
europmc-pmc3213011:
Feng Cheng and colleagues introduced BRAD, a genome database for Brassica crop plants, in this 2011 paper in BMC Plant Biology. Brassicas include major vegetables and oilseed crops, and the newly assembled genome of Brassica rapa opened the door to deep data mining. BRAD was built to organize that genome and related resources in one web-accessible place.

The database holds the assembled sequence, predicted genes with annotations, non-coding RNAs, transposable elements, genetic markers, and linkage maps. It also maps Brassica genes to their counterparts in the model plant Arabidopsis. Search tools let users query by gene, position, or marker, run BLAST searches, and browse the genome visually. The authors present BRAD as a working resource for both researchers and plant breeders.
europmc-pmc3235811:
Elena Barbieri and Piero Sestili reviewed the double life of reactive oxygen species in skeletal muscle in this 2012 article in the Journal of Signal Transduction. These reactive molecules were long seen purely as toxic byproducts behind stress, disease, and aging. Evidence has since shown they also serve, at modest levels, as useful signals that regulate normal body processes.

Muscle is a special case because hard contraction makes its mitochondria release large flows of these molecules. Depending on where they are produced, how long the flow lasts, and how well the cell's antioxidant defenses are stocked, the result can range from healthy adaptation to cell death. The authors argue a single toxic threshold is the wrong idea; what matters is which levels fit normal physiology. They discuss the main signaling pathways involved.
europmc-pmc3271711:
J. Gregory Caporaso and colleagues filmed the human microbiome changing over time in this 2011 study in Genome Biology. Knowing how much a healthy person's microbes normally fluctuate is essential before blaming the microbiome for diseases such as obesity or inflammatory bowel disease. Earlier studies took only occasional snapshots, limited by sequencing cost and computation.

The team sampled two people at four body sites across nearly four hundred timepoints, the densest series then published. Beneath stable differences between sites and between people, each person's community varied strikingly across months, weeks, and even days. Only a small fraction of organisms at any site were present at every timepoint. So no permanent core community exists at high abundance. Many taxa instead persist for stretches, then vanish. The work defines what normal variation looks like for judging disease states and treatments.
europmc-pmc3291411:
Kilbourne surveyed the three worldwide flu pandemics of the twentieth century in a 2006 article. Each event differed in its virus, its spread, and how deadly it was, and they did not arrive on any steady schedule. For the two later pandemics, in 1957 and 1968, laboratory science could show that a key surface protein of the virus had changed sharply.

Much of the article looks back at 1918 and at reports that are often skipped. Observers at the time described a new flu like illness in American pigs that seemed to pass from people to animals, not the other way around. Kilbourne also notes that many deaths involved bacterial lung infections on top of flu, a fact that matters when judging whether a pandemic like 1918 could return.
europmc-pmc3304411:
Cuzick and colleagues tested a gene based score for predicting death from prostate cancer, reporting in 2012. Prostate cancer behaves very differently from man to man, and many patients are watched rather than treated at once. The score, built from the activity of thirty one genes that drive cell division, had already predicted outcomes in men diagnosed during prostate surgery.

Here the team applied it to nearly three hundred fifty men diagnosed by needle biopsy and managed without early radical treatment. The score was the strongest predictor of cancer death in their analysis, adding information beyond the usual grade, stage, and blood marker measures. Because it worked on stored biopsy tissue, the authors say it could help doctors choose which men need treatment and which can safely wait.
europmc-pmc3316511:
Ananworanich and colleagues studied the first days of HIV infection and an intensive early treatment plan, reporting in 2012. Screening more than twenty four thousand people in Bangkok, the team found forty people caught very soon after infection and enrolled thirty in close follow up. Gut tissue loses immune cells fast in early HIV, and hidden virus reservoirs form early, so timing matters for any hope of drug free control.

Half the group took an intensified five drug combination for twenty four weeks. By then, virus levels in blood and gut had fallen below detection in nearly everyone treated, and total hidden virus shrank, vanishing in a few. Gut immune cell shares also recovered, especially in those worst hit at the start. The authors say the earliest virus levels predicted reservoir size months later, arguing for treatment as early as possible.
europmc-pmc3408111:
Beetz, Uvnäs-Moberg, Julius, and Kotrschal reviewed in 2012 the effects of interacting with animals on human minds and bodies. Pets and animal-assisted therapy have gained wide acceptance over the past decade. The team sifted sixty-nine original studies that met firm standards for size, review, and design.

Well-documented benefits include better mood and social behavior, lower stress readings such as cortisol and blood pressure, and less self-reported fear and anxiety. Weaker evidence points to better pain control, trust, and empathy, and less aggression. The authors propose that the hormone oxytocin, switched on by friendly animal contact, drives most of these effects. That shared mechanism, they argue, ties the scattered findings into one story.
europmc-pmc3411811:
Zhang and co-workers reported in 2012 that berberine, an active ingredient of a Chinese herb long used for diarrhea, prevents obesity and insulin resistance in rats by reshaping gut bacteria. Rats on a high-fat diet gained less and ate less when given berberine. Blood markers of inflammation and hormone imbalance improved as well.

Sequencing the gut community showed berberine narrowed its diversity and shifted its structure markedly. Most of the bacterial types that responded vanished, while a few that produce helpful short-chain fatty acids grew richer, and those acids rose in the gut. A statistical model built on the responding types predicted body fat and hormone levels well. Gut remodeling, the authors conclude, carries much of berberine's benefit.
europmc-pmc3420011:
Matzuk and colleagues reported in 2012 a small molecule that blocks sperm production in mice, pointing toward a male contraceptive pill. Drug-based male contraception has been a longstanding challenge. The compound, JQ1, jams a family of proteins that read chemical marks on DNA packaging; one family member, BRDT, works only in the testis and is essential for sperm formation.

Crystal and chemical studies showed the drug fills BRDT's reading pocket, stopping it from gripping its target marks. Treated male mice grew smaller testes and made fewer, weaker sperm, while hormone levels stayed normal. They mated as usual but fathered no pups, and the effect reversed fully after treatment stopped. The result gives drug hunters a lead aimed squarely at the male germ cell.

evans-wentz-fairy-faith-1911:
W. Y. Evans-Wentz walked the Celt lands to ask folk what they held on fays. The Fairy-Faith in Celtic Countries came out in 1911. He went through Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Cornwall, Brittany, and Man. Old men and women told him what their kin had seen and feared.

First-hand tales fill the book: troops of fays, hid folk, and stolen babes. Evans-Wentz then weighs what the tales may mean for the mind and soul. He treats the faith with care, not with scorn. The book is the base work for all grave study of fay lore.
examen-des-principes-des-alchymistes-sur: Examen des principes des alchymistes sur la pierre philosophale, 1711. The principles examined. This book preserves that work. Later readers can locate it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
florio-italian-1611:
John Florio published Queen Anna's New World of Words in 1611, a greatly expanded Italian-English dictionary. Florio taught languages at the court of James the First and had already issued a smaller word book in 1598. The new volume, dedicated to Queen Anne, carried some 46,000 Italian words explained in English.

Entries give rich clusters of English equivalents, along with proverbs and phrases from Italian writers. Florio also translated Montaigne's essays, and his word-hoard fed the English of his age; scholars still debate his links with Shakespeare's circle. The dictionary was the first full bridge between Renaissance Italy and Jacobean England. Students of both languages still consult it for words that later books dropped.
fouque-undine-1811:
Friedrich de la Motte Fouque, a German officer and writer, wrote this tale of a water spirit in 1811. F. E. Bunnett turned it into English, in the full text of nineteen parts. The tale grew from old lore of the undine, the maid of the waters.

Undine is raised by a fisherman, weds a knight, and by that bond wins a human soul. Joy turns to grief as the knight fails her, and the waters call her back at last. The short tale fixed the form of the water spirit in the books of Europe.
froude-history-england-vol-11:
After the Armada comes triumph in the eleventh volume of Froude's History, from 1865. Spain lies humbled at sea, and England stands exalted among the powers. Elizabeth sits at the very zenith of her glory as queen.

Froude savors the victory toward which his long narrative has built. Sea dogs raid, courtiers scheme, and the queen holds her state with cool mastery. He writes the moment when England became a great power in earnest. The volume glows with national pride, and its flowing style shows why Froude ranked as the most dramatic English historian of the Victorian age.
frus-1861-d11:
On 16 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Baron von Gerolt, Prussia's minister in Washington. Gerolt was Prussia's minister in Washington. The letter is document 11 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

A letter to a foreign envoy in Washington worked the home end of diplomacy. Seward used such talks to press the Union's view of the war on each court through its own man. This exchange with Prussia's envoy sits just before the first great battle at Bull Run. Prussia's weight in Germany made its envoy a man worth the Secretary's direct time.
frus-1861-d111:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Anson Burlingame on 13 April 1861. Burlingame was named the American minister to China that spring. The letter is document 111 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The China post lay half a world away, yet it drew a letter the day after Fort Sumter fell. Seward had to keep every post filled, near or far, as war began. His note to Burlingame shows the wide reach of the service in that first week. Burlingame became a famed envoy in China and died in its service years later.
frus-1861-d211:
Mr. Wood was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 5 September 1861. It stands as Document 211 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d311:
Word from Mr. Harris reached Washington on 9 July 1861, in a letter to William H. Seward. It stands as Document 311 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d11:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 31 January 1862. It stands as Document 11 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the winter of the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d111:
Orders from Washington reached Charles Francis Adams in a State Department letter dated 28 July 1862. It stands as Document 111 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d211:
Writing on 6 March 1862, Lord Lyons addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward in a note printed as Document 211 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons served as Britain's minister in Washington through most of the Civil War.

March opened the war's great spring campaigns, and within days the ironclads Monitor and Virginia would fight at Hampton Roads. A battle with loud echoes in naval capitals. British officials followed American events with care. Notes like this one, formal and to the point, carried the legation's business while the war widened around it. Stuart had served at the legation for years before he took charge of it.
frus-1862-d311:
