Two Seward dispatches to Paris are dated 19 September 1862, and the first is Document 311 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

Seward wrote two days after Antietam, with the battle's scale known but its meaning still argued over. For Paris, the key fact was that Lee's invasion had been stopped. Seward's paired letters that day carried Washington's account to the French capital. There, the truce plan's fate depended heavily on how the Maryland campaign was read. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d411:
On 21 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Gustav Koerner, the American minister in Madrid. The dispatch is Document 411 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

By October 1862 the fighting at Antietam had slowed talk of foreign intervention, and Lincoln had announced his emancipation plan. Koerner's work in Spain shifted toward keeping that gain: holding Madrid to neutrality and watching Cuba, where Spanish rule sat close to Confederate shores. Seward's instruction belongs to the autumn effort to turn a military reprieve into lasting diplomatic safety for the Union.
frus-1862-d511:
August 1862 opened at The Hague desk with this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to James Shepherd Pike, dated 4 August. It is Document 511 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

August was the month of the second call for troops and of rising talk in London and Paris about stepping between the combatants. Seward's orders stiffened his ministers against any hint that the Union would accept mediation. Pike, in a small and friendly capital, had the easier version of that task, but the line had to be identical everywhere. The dispatch shows the Department keeping its whole European front in step as the war entered its most dangerous diplomatic season.
frus-1862-d611:
George G. Fogg, the American minister in Switzerland, received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 March 1862. It is Document 611 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, opening the Swiss file.

Switzerland was a small republic whose example Americans liked to cite and whose neutrality was absolute. Fogg, a New Hampshire editor and abolitionist, held the post at Berne. Orders to such a mission dealt with the standing courtesies and the war's presentation in a friendly, watchful little state. The dispatch begins one of the volume's shortest files. It is a reminder of the Department's reach. That care extended to every flag under which an American minister served, however quiet the post.
frus-1862-d711:
From Washington on 6 October 1862 came this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Andrew B. Dickinson. Dickinson was the American minister in Nicaragua. The letter is document 711 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, answering Dickinson's September reports.

Seward's answers gave envoys their marching orders and told them how Washington read their news. For Nicaragua, the transit route and the republic's steadiness sat at the heart of the brief. This letter is one turn in that exchange. It shows the State Department keeping its grip on a distant post whose ground mattered far more than its size.
frus-1863p1-d11:
William H. Seward sent this second letter of 8 December 1862 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 11 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, right after its twin. The two letters split the day's London business between them.

A secretary's mail often came in such pairs: one letter for the record of a talk, one for fresh orders. Seward's sheets to Adams kept the legation in step with a government whose war news changed by the week. Read beside document 10, this one shows the grain of that work — brief, plain notes that added up to a policy.
frus-1863p1-d111:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward a second time on 6 March 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 111 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The mate to a same-day letter often held the overflow: a talk in full, a set of facts, a press view. Adams's pair of 6 March fits that mold. This letter is its second half, sent as the ship fights in Britain's yards grew warm. With its twin, it shows the London brief at full stretch in the first week of spring.
frus-1863p1-d211:
Washington's orders to London on 5 June 1862 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 211 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d311:
Mr. Stuart, an officer of the British legation in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 November 1862. His note is document 311 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Small cases fill this part of the volume: a vessel, a cargo, a British subject under arrest. Together they show how a war at sea kept landing on diplomats' desks. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d411:
The American answer to London on 6 March 1863 took the form of this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 411 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

For historians, this exchange shows Anglo-American tension being managed day by day. It is the paper record of a war that never happened between the two countries. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d511:
A letter of 14 May 1863, from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, stands as document 511 in the printed record. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports.
frus-1863p1-d611:
Document 611 in the volume is a letter of 13 August 1863 from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d11: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on June 20, 1943, two days after the president's paired letters to London and Moscow. His message is Document 11 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The summer correspondence between the two men ran at a pace that matched the war itself. What this note carried, the catalog does not say. It survives in the Foreign Relations series as one link in the long exchange behind the autumn summits.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d111: Roosevelt wrote to Chiang Kai-shek on November 10, 1943, his last letter to China's leader in this series before the journey. It is Document 111 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Cairo Conference opened twelve days later. The record supplies the date and the names and leaves the subject to the text. The letter is part of the Foreign Relations series' account of how the Cairo meeting was arranged.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d211:
Ambassador Averell Harriman sent President Roosevelt a secret cable from Moscow on 11 November 1943, numbered SD 1. He warns that a thorny subject is almost sure to come up at the coming conference: Soviet pressure on Sweden to help in the war. Molotov had raised the point more than once since the Moscow conference ended.

Harriman reports a talk with Sweden's minister in Moscow. Finland, the minister said, would quit the war quickly if sure Soviet troops would not occupy her afterward, and Sweden could feed Finland for six months once German shipments stopped. But he doubted Sweden could move either Moscow or Helsinki in time, and he noted the Swedish king hoped to spare his people the suffering of joining the war.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d311:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote a most-secret memorandum at Cairo on 25 November 1943 attacking the American plan for a supreme commander over the war against Germany. He sets out, point by point, why the appointment would not cure the troubles seen since the Salerno landing.

The real divergences, Churchill argues, are political as much as military. Only governments and the Combined Chiefs can settle them. A supreme commander would thus be squeezed into a narrow strip of work, or else supplant the chiefs entirely. No single officer, he doubts, could decide across so vast a range. His own rule is that command in each theater should go to the ally with the largest forces there: the Mediterranean British, Overlord American. A merged command, by force counts, would fall to a Briton, an outcome he calls invidious and refuses to impose.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d411:
The agreed text of the Tehran communiqué, is dated 4 December 1943. It is the version Churchill and Stalin accepted. It is printed with its handwritten deletions, and with Harriman's note in the corner of the single sheet. An editorial headnote explains how this copy differs from both the third draft and the text finally released.

The text is headed Declaration of the Three Powers. It is timed for release at eight in the evening, Moscow time, on 6 December. It declares the three nations' determination to work together in war and in the peace that follows. Complete agreement was reached on the scope and timing of operations from the east, west, and south. The leaders claim the supreme responsibility of making a peace. The peace must command the good will of the overwhelming mass of the world's peoples. They close as friends in fact, in spirit, and in purpose.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d511:
Charles E. Bohlen, first secretary at the American embassy in Moscow, wrote this memorandum dated December 1, 1943, the final day of the Tehran Conference. Bohlen spoke Russian and served as President Roosevelt's interpreter with Stalin, taking notes at talks where no other American record was made. The State Department printed his memorandum in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Bohlen's papers are prized because he sat between the leaders, hearing both languages at moments that shaped the postwar world. A memorandum from the last day of Tehran carries the closeness of that seat. For readers, it offers the conference through the eyes of the man who made its conversations possible.
frus-1944-quebec-d11:
Two weeks after the Normandy landings, Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on June 20, 1944. The beachhead was secure but the breakout had not yet come. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

With the invasion ashore, the leaders' agenda shifted: reinforcing France, finishing in Italy, and looking toward the autumn meeting that became the Second Quebec Conference. Churchill's June letters worked that transition. For readers, this message shows the alliance moving from the question of whether the invasion would succeed to the harder politics of what its success would mean for Europe's future.
frus-1944-quebec-d111:
Trade barriers are the subject of this short note from Harry Hopkins to President Roosevelt, dated September 8, 1944. Hopkins, the president's closest aide, wrote just before Roosevelt left for the Quebec Conference with Winston Churchill. He worried Churchill saw freer trade as Secretary Hull's pet project, not the president's own policy.

Hopkins urged Roosevelt to correct that idea in person at Quebec. Making clear the president himself backed lower trade barriers would strengthen America's hand in later bargaining with Britain, he argued. The note is brief, but it shows how personal diplomacy was prepared. Even a prime minister's assumptions were worth fixing before the talks began.
frus-1944-quebec-d211:
A verbatim transcript of the Quebec press conference survives in the Roosevelt Papers, the editors note, and a substantively complete text is printed in Rosenman's edition of the president's papers. Roosevelt first reviewed the Second Quebec Conference in very general terms. He expressed hope for Germany's surrender and discussed joint action against Japan and Pacific logistics.

He stated specifically that questions of command in the Pacific war had not been discussed. Instead he described the existing division of responsibility among Mountbatten, MacArthur, and Nimitz. Churchill then commented on the conference results and on British and Canadian participation against Japan, and Mackenzie King made brief closing remarks. The conference communiqué was released to the press the same day, September 16.
frus-1945-50-intel-d11:
Arnold Miles of the Budget Bureau staff wrote to Stone, the bureau's assistant director for administrative management, on 19 September 1945. The paper moved inside the bureau on the eve of a landmark order. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Budget Bureau staff work decided much of what presidents finally signed, since the bureau drafted the orders themselves. Miles wrote one day before Executive Order 9621 ended the OSS. Readers should read his paper as part of the penumbra around that order. In such memos, officials weighed where the OSS's people, files, and duties should land. Small staff papers like this one are where big decisions take their final shape.
frus-1945-50-intel-d111:
Ladd of the FBI wrote to Hoover on 14 May 1946. Ladd's memoranda kept the director informed on the bureau's intelligence fronts, the central group among them. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

By May the CIG under its new leaders was reaching toward the Latin American field the FBI regarded as its own. Ladd's paper belongs to the bureau's watch on that reach. Readers following the FBI thread can see its method again: steady reporting, claims restated, and a director who answered encroachment with paper of his own. The border war between the bureau and the group, fought in memoranda, is one of the volume's most instructive threads.
frus-1945-50-intel-d211:
A memorandum dated 17 April 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Eddy). The reader was Acting Secretary of State Acheson. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 211, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d311:
A memorandum dated 7 September 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was Robert P. Joyce of the Policy Planning Staff. The reader was the Counselor of the Department of State (Kennan). Readers meet it as document 311 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d411: A short paper dated 19 January 1950 carries only the heading Memorandum for the Record, with no writer and no reader named. It is document 411 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Papers of this kind set down what was said or decided at a meeting. The file would then hold it, even when no order followed from it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d11: On 19 October 1944 Stalin sent Roosevelt another message, the third Soviet letter in this opening run of papers. It stands as document 11 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering the Malta and Yalta conferences. The full text appears as the Office of the Historian published it, in sequence with the replies it answered and prompted in return.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d111:
Ambassador John Winant wrote to the President from London on 10 January 1945 about three papers awaiting approval. His personal and secret message, number 2047, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. All three concern how the allies would control Germany.

The control machinery agreement, Winant reports, already has State Department and Joint Chiefs approval. The zones protocol waits only on allied agreement for American control of Bremen and Bremerhaven, the ports feeding the American zone. Britain has approved both papers, and the Russians, he hears, are looking on them with favor. Winant hopes the surrender instrument and both agreements can be settled by 14 January, one year after the European Advisory Commission began.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d211:
H. Freeman Matthews briefed the Secretary on France's German claims on 19 January 1945. His secret memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, was written for Stettinius's Sunday talk with the President. The Rhineland and a French zone head the agenda.

The five French proposals, Matthews recalls, already have the President's approval in principle, from signing the surrender to a share of Berlin. Paris has also formally told the three allies, in a note of 13 January, that it wishes to join the coming three-power conference. London, he judges, will answer with favor. If Moscow grows sure that Washington will oppose an invitation, the picture changes. The paper goes on to weigh the play of the three capitals.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d311:
British chiefs of staff put their case on Asia in writing at Malta on January 31, 1945. Their memorandum covers the split of resources between the India-Burma and China theaters. London granted the scale of American pledges to China, both political and military. It asked Washington to grant the weight of Britain's stake in Burma in return.

The British argued that the ground had shifted since an earlier American reservation was accepted without debate. British land forces in Burma now leaned heavily on air transport for their safety. China, meanwhile, faced a far more urgent crisis than a year before. The paper is a frank bid for a fairer share.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d411:
An invitation with blanks stands at the center of this American proposal of February 9, 1945. The United States, speaking for itself and for Britain, the Soviet Union, China, and France, invites the government of a named state to send representatives. The conference of the United Nations would meet on April 25, 1945, or soon after. The city is left blank in the draft.

Its task: prepare a charter for a general international organization to keep peace and security. The sponsors suggest the conference build on the Dumbarton Oaks proposals, made public the past October. The blank spaces show history caught mid-decision — San Francisco not yet named, the date already fixed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d511:
Dictated at San Francisco on June 3, 1945, this memorandum by Hiss rebuilds a Yalta moment from his own longhand notes. It covers the plenary session of February 6, 1945, at Livadia Palace. Roosevelt asked Stettinius to explain the American proposal on the voting formula. Stettinius, he noted, had been at Dumbarton Oaks; none of the three delegation heads had.

The President felt strongly, Hiss records, that people would insist on something insuring peace — not for all time, but say for fifty years. Stettinius then read the American statement on voting in the Council. The memo, dictated four months later, shows the record of Yalta still being assembled at the founding conference itself.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d11:
Relations with Russia are the number one problem affecting the future of the world. Harriman made that case at the White House on May 15, 1945, in Grew's memorandum of the conference. The President, Grew, Harriman, and Bohlen took part. The State Department, Grew said, held it vital that the Big Three meeting come as soon as possible, not be postponed until July.

Harriman argued that the two countries were getting farther and farther apart at the present moment. Beyond the general picture stood specific questions, such as treating Germany on a tripartite basis. The memorandum shows the Moscow embassy pressing Washington for speed, with the alliance drifting.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d111:
The British Chiefs of Staff accepted the American line on small staffs in a memorandum dated June 30, 1945. The paper, C.C.S. 880/6, is document 111 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It reports London's answer to the U.S. memorandum of June 28, which had argued against big military staffs at Terminal.

The British agree that large staffs will not be required. Each of their chiefs will bring his personal staff plus four or five staff officers. The secretariat will take only enough people to run the conference's normal paperwork and administration. The brief memo closed the question of military manpower for Potsdam and matched the lean approach both sides wanted for a summit meant to be short.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d211:
Ambassador Kirk passed on Field Marshal Alexander's news about Yugoslavia in a telegram from Caserta on July 12, 1945. The message is document 211 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Alexander had learned the British government's intentions while in London.

The British expected to discuss the Tito-Šubašić agreement at the coming Big Three meeting, Alexander said. Churchill would make it quite clear that his government was not satisfied with how the accord had been carried out so far. Britain would hold Tito to strict account for putting it into effect. The agreement was meant to unite Tito's movement with the royal government and open the way to free elections, and London judged Tito to be stalling.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d311:
Budapest reported a Soviet move on July 13, 1945, in Schoenfeld's cable to the Acting Secretary of State. General Key had received a note from Marshal Voroshilov, dated July 11, setting out Moscow's decision on new procedure for Hungary's Allied Control Commission. A first translation was already in hand.

The new procedure seemed to follow, in the main, lines Washington had suggested in May, with details added by the American mission. Yet Schoenfeld found much ambiguity in Voroshilov's wording. Key meant to take the unclear points up with the Marshal directly. The cable holds a rare note of cautious hope from Hungary.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d411:
Moscow's own formula arrived in Winant's top secret cable from London of July 11, 1945. The Soviet delegation to the European Advisory Commission that night communicated new wording for the disputed final paragraph of the report on the French zone agreement. The formula had been sent from Moscow after Gousev's return there.

The Soviet text recommends that the question of fixing the boundaries of the French area in greater Berlin go to the Control Council. It states that the French area, since the Soviet area of the city suffered the greatest destruction, will be formed from the American and British areas. The formula also went to the British and French delegations, for a meeting on July 12.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d511:
Eastern Poland's boundary is fixed in a briefing book paper dated July 3, 1945. Its recommendation restates the Crimea settlement. The United States, in the Big Three agreement of February 11, 1945, approved the Curzon Line. With Extension A, that line forms the boundary between Poland and the Soviet Union. Deviations of five to eight kilometers in Poland's favor are to be allowed in some regions.

The basic data trace the land between the Riga and Curzon lines. It includes pre-1914 Austrian and Russian territory. Eastern Galicia was renounced by Austria in the Treaty of St. Germain in 1919, and awarded to Poland in 1923. The former Russian territory came to Poland by the Treaty of Riga of 1921. In September 1939 the Soviet Union occupied both parts.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d611:
The United States Chiefs of Staff replied to the British on sharing war facts with Russia, July 8, 1945. Their top secret memo is document 611 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It answers the British proposal printed as document 609.

The U.S. chiefs say the matter is not a fit one for a joint Allied agreement. Each side, in effect, may set its own rule for what it tells Moscow. They add one firm pledge of their own. They will not pass to the Russians any facts on British forces or plans without prior British consent. Nor will they pass on facts that came from a British source. The Combined Chiefs took up the paper at Potsdam on July 19, where the British pressed their case again.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1011:
Collado drafted this agreement on the German fleet and merchant marine at Babelsberg on July 29, 1945. The fleet would be split equally at once among the Soviet Union, Britain, and the United States. Most German submarines would be destroyed. A few would be kept for tests and training, under a mixed commission's eye.

The merchant marine would also be split in equal thirds in the end. Until Japan falls, though, every German merchant ship stays at work in the war, run by the joint shipping boards. Final division would come six months after Japan's defeat. Officers of the three powers could inspect vessels wherever they are held.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1111:
Alexander Kirk, the American ambassador in Italy, cabled the Acting Secretary of State on 17 July 1945. That was the opening day of the Potsdam Conference. Kirk reported from Rome, where he watched a beaten country try to build a new order after the fall of Mussolini.

Italy was a live question at the summit. Its peace treaty, its borders, and the shape of its new state all waited on the talks. Kirk's dispatch fed the view from Rome into the bargaining in Germany. Cables like his kept the men at the table supplied with facts from the ground, not just claims from other teams.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1211:
The Soviet team tabled this proposal on 30 July 1945, with three days of the conference left. By that stage, fresh papers were rarely opening bids. They were endgame moves, put forward when the deal's shape was set and each side hunted last gains.

Moscow's late papers deserve close reading for that reason. A demand repeated at the end marks a point the Soviet side prized. A demand dropped marks the price of the deal. This proposal stands in the record as one such move. It gains meaning from its neighbors, the replies and drafts that surround it in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1311:
Harrison wrote to Stimson on 23 July 1945, one of two committee-channel papers of that date in the volume. The acting chairman's notes came thick as the summit and the atomic file both neared their peaks. Each carried Washington's end of the secret to the war secretary in Germany.

The exchange between these two men is the policy spine of the bomb's story at Potsdam. Tests, targets, warnings, and timing all passed along it. This message is a link in that spine. It shows the committee's work feeding the summit at the moment the final choices about the weapon were being formed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1411:
The sixth Caffery cable to Secretary Byrnes dated 6 August 1945 closes the day's run from Paris. Six cables to the secretary in one day is a remarkable count in any foreign service. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

A run's last cable often carries the day's summing-up or its sharpest ask. Whether this one does, readers can judge by setting it at the end of the sequence where the editors placed it. The whole cluster marks the high point of French pressure in the volume. A freed ally, shut out of the summit, demanding its place in the peace by sheer weight of well-aimed paper.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-11:
Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes for July 18, 1945, record the U.S. military team's morning session at Potsdam. The top secret extracts are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. Three items stand out in the part printed here.

First, the chiefs reviewed and amended a memo to the President on the surrender formula for Japan. They approved it as amended during the discussion. Second, Admiral Leahy reported a talk with the President on staff relations with allied nations. Truman thought it undesirable to raise a military alliance with Britain just then. Allied relations, he held, were not settled enough to warrant a permanent link between commands. Third, Admiral King and General Marshall each proposed changes to the draft memo on French and Dutch participation in the Japan war.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-111:
Dated July 25, 1945, this rapporteur's report carried a Potsdam working group's results to a higher level of the conference. Subcommittees did the detailed labor at Potsdam. Their rapporteurs then had to state, in short compass, what had been agreed and what had not. The report entered the record printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Inside is the state of a negotiation at one point in time. Settled lines appear beside open brackets and rival drafts. For leaders scanning many files, such a report was the quick way to see where work stood. It shows the conference's layered method: detail below, decision above.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d711:
Document 711 is a proposal tabled by the United States delegation on July 17, 1945, the opening day of the Potsdam Conference. Delegations opened by putting written proposals on the table. Each one marked out ground its side wanted the talks to cover. The text was printed at the head of this run in the second Potsdam volume.

An opening-day proposal shows intent before bargaining began. Readers can set its lines beside the final protocol and see what survived. That gap between ask and outcome is where the conference happened. The document also shows the American team's method: arrive with texts ready, and force the talk onto paper early.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d811:
Melbourne wrote from Rumania on July 23, 1945, in document 811. The acting representative in Bucharest reported to the Acting Secretary of State. Two Rumanian letters in two days mark an active file. This one joined the second Potsdam volume beside its fellows.

Frequent reports from one post trace a situation in motion. Melbourne could correct and extend his own record. Readers follow Bucharest's politics almost day by day. The document shows the value of a resident observer over a visiting one. He knew the players, and his letters carry that knowledge to the summit's readers then and now.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d911: American staff drafted this undated memorandum, filed with the July 22, 1945 papers, as an alternative reply to the Soviet stand on war booty. It quotes the Soviet definition of war trophies. Under that idea, the paper argues, any occupying power could strip its own zone and call the goods booty. Overall reparations planning for Germany then becomes meaningless. The United States would accept the position. It would remove plants and goods from its own zone, for itself or for others, and expects the other powers to do the same.
frus-1952-54Guat-d11: A 1952-1954 FRUS editorial note on Truman's 1952 authorization regarding Guatemala. The covert operation took shape. This note provides that context. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
frus-1961-1963-cuban-missile-crisis-vol-:
Volume eleven of Foreign Relations of the United States for 1961 to 1963 is devoted to the Cuban Missile Crisis and its aftermath. The Office of the Historian compiled it from declassified records. For thirteen days in October 1962, the world stood at the edge of nuclear war.

The documents follow the Executive Committee's secret debates as Kennedy weighed invasion, air strikes, and blockade. The naval quarantine, the downed U-2, and the near accidents at sea all stand in the record. Behind the public standoff runs the secret deal: Soviet missiles out of Cuba, American missiles quietly out of Turkey. The volume is the crisis in its makers' own words.
gao-gaoreports-b-295911: Two firms, one fight: Public Facility Consortium I and JDL Castle both protested in May 2005 — dockets B-295911 and B-295911.2 — and GAO's combined ruling settles each claim. The calls get weighed side by side, with one verdict for both. The gavel fell once.
gao-gaoreports-b-298011: American Printing House for the Blind took its May 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298411: Advanced Systems Development doubled its September 2006 protest — two case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-309911: A 2007 GAO ruling on a contract fight from the FitNet Purchasing Alliance, a frequent name in that year's protest docket. The group challenged how a federal buying pact was set up; the ruling parses the legal fine print. The call adds one more marker to the map of what agencies may and may not do when they buy.
gao-gaoreports-b-310611: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Merlin International, Inc. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-211: Endangered species recovery dollars got a GAO check in 2005, and the report says the wildlife service mostly funded the high-priority animals, though needs remained. The review grades the triage. The rarest creatures deserved the help. The focus was mostly right.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-611: DOE's under secretary office needed prompt action in 2005, and GAO's report says coordinated steps were required on nuclear security. The findings demand the urgency. The report warns that the bomb material deserved guarding. The action had to be prompt. The bomb material deserved guarding.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-711: The Middle East Partnership Initiative got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says the tools supported reform, though project monitoring needed work. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the reformers deserved watched aid. The monitoring had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1011: Combat pay and tax breaks needed better management in 2006, and GAO's report says the benefits for danger pay and tax relief wanted strengthening. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the troops in harm's way deserved accurate pay. The benefits had to be right.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-11: HHS's IT investment management was partial in 2005, and GAO's report says several capabilities existed, though key weaknesses needed addressing. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the health department's tech dollars deserved managing. The weaknesses had to be fixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-111: Army National Guard equipment readiness needed plans in 2005, and GAO's report says plans were needed to improve readiness and integration. The findings demand the strategy. The report warns that the citizen-soldiers deserved working gear. The plans had to be made.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-211: The Pentagon's global info grid needed better management in 2006, and GAO's report says the approach was not well-suited to support development. The findings diagnose the mismatch. The report warns that the war net needed proper building. The approach had to change.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-311: Fighting nuclear smuggling abroad hit corruption and maintenance woes in 2006, and GAO's report says the problems challenged U.S. radiation detection efforts. The findings target the rot. The report warns that the atomic gateways abroad needed guarding. The problems had to be fixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-511: Surplus federal property giveaways mostly worked in 2006, and GAO's report says most public benefit conveyances were used as intended, though federal oversight could improve. The findings balance credit and prodding. The report shows the hand-me-down buildings served the public. The oversight had to be enhanced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-811: Federal cyber research needed coordinating in 2006, and GAO's report examines the coordination of cybersecurity research and development. The findings map the efforts. The report warns that the scattered labs needed a common direction. The research had to join up. The labs had to pull in one direction.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-911: Small businesses and e-travel got a GAO look in 2006, and the report examines small-firm participation and estimated savings. The findings measure both. The report shows the digital booking was supposed to save money and share work. The savings had to be real.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-11: Servicemembers' college benefits needed better data in 2007, and GAO's report says more information could show how many eligible troops were served. The findings demand the numbers. The report warns that the education promise needed proof. The troops deserved the count.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-211: Floating bases needed a real plan in 2007, and GAO's report says the joint seabasing concept wanted comprehensive management and rigorous testing. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the sea-base dream needed more than blueprints. The fleet had to prove it could float the idea.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-411: The nation's emergency siren was aging in 2007 — GAO's report says the current alert system had limits, and the new integrated one needed building. The findings sound the warning. The report's plea: the alarm that warns America should actually reach America.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-611: The thrift board wore many hats in 2007 — GAO's report maps the many duties Congress piled on the overseers of federal retirement investments. The findings inventory the sprawling mandate in plain terms. The report asks whether one board could sanely mind so many billions at once.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-711: American guns for Iraqi troops were vanishing into the fog in 2007 — GAO's report says the Pentagon could not prove U.S.-bought gear reached Iraqi forces. The findings describe an accountability black hole in the middle of a war. Weapons paid for by taxpayers, the report warns, were wandering without a paper trail.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-11: This 2007 Government Accountability Office report examines the Office of Personnel Management — the federal government's HR agency — and finds opportunities to build on recent progress in its own workforce capacity. OPM advises agencies on hiring and talent, so GAO's review of its internal human-capital strength carried a certain symmetry. The report credits gains while pointing to unfinished work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-211: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at information Security: IRS Needs to Address Pervasive Weaknesses. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-311: GAO published its findings on homeland Security: Enhanced National Guard Readiness for Civil Support Missions May Depend on DOD's Implementation of the 2008 National Defense Authorization Ac in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-511: The Government Accountability Office dug into unmanned Aircraft Systems: Federal Actions Needed to Ensure Safety and Expand Their Potential Uses within the National Airspace System in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-02-1911:
James George Frazer published Volume 2 of the third edition of The Golden Bough in 1911, subtitled The Magic Art and the Evolution of Kings, Part 2. Frazer, a Cambridge scholar, built his vast study of magic and religion from reports across the world. The third edition ran to twelve volumes.

Part 2 of The Magic Art presses on with charms, rites, and the rise of sacred kings. Frazer argued that magic came before religion in human thought, and that kings began as magicians. His examples range from rain makers to tree spirits on every continent. The volume shows his method at full scale: one custom matched against hundreds of kin worldwide.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-03-1911:
Volume 3 of Frazer's Golden Bough, third edition, appeared in 1911, under the title Taboo and the Perils of the Soul. James George Frazer gathered customs from peoples worldwide to show how taboo worked. Taboo, a word from Polynesia, named things and persons set apart as dangerous and holy.

Chapters cover taboos on kings, strangers, food, words, and the dead, and beliefs about the soul leaving the body in sleep or shadow. Frazer argued that taboo guarded early societies where law did not yet reach. His mass of examples, drawn from travelers and missionaries, made the volume a storehouse for later students of religion, even those who rejected his theories.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-04-1911:
Volume 4 of the third edition of The Golden Bough appeared in 1911, titled The Dying God. James George Frazer's theme was the god who dies and returns, a figure he found in rites across the ancient world. The priest of Nemi, slain by his successor, stood behind the whole work.

Frazer traced dying gods through grain rites, sacred kings, and seasonal festivals in many lands. He held that such rites acted out the death and revival of plant life each year. Critics later doubted his single pattern, but the evidence he gathered stayed valuable. The volume is central to his claim that myth and ritual grow from the same root.
govdocs-archive_org-TheSpotlightVolume27:
The Spotlight was a populist weekly newspaper published in Washington, and this file holds a single issue: volume 27, number 11, dated March 12, 2001. Single issues are kept as issued, so the paper can be read exactly as its subscribers saw it.

Inside are the paper's news stories, commentary, and notes from its own distinct perspective, which favored economic nationalism and deep suspicion of global institutions. The Spotlight spoke to readers who distrusted the mainstream press, and it kept a loyal following for decades. As a record, the issue shows what that audience was reading in the spring of 2001.
heindel-rosicrucian-mysteries-1911:
Max Heindel put out The Rosicrucian Mysteries in 1911. The book is a plain first step into the scheme of the Rosicrucian Fellowship. Heindel had set up that group in the United States not long past. He calls the book a first exposition, made for new hands.

Seven worlds stack up in his scheme, from dense flesh to pure spirit. Man has more than one body in his count, and death is a shift, not an end. Steps of growth lead the soul to full sight of hid things. The book is the gate text of Heindel's whole school.
hill-new-evidences-psychical-research-19:
J. Arthur Hill adds fresh proof to the pile in New Evidences in Psychical Research, his book of 1911. Hill was a keen hand in the chief band for such study. He prints his own tests. Sittings with seers sit by tales that checked out true. Some talks seemed to come from the dead through more than one voice in far towns.

His tone is calm, fair, and shorn of wild zeal. He asks fans to weigh, not to swoon. The book is a fair flag of the field in its prime age. It shows its care at work.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume eleven: the enemies gather, Austria, France, and Russia arrayed against little Prussia. Carlyle builds the drama of the coming storm with gathering power. The vast work's tension mounts toward the Seven Years' War. The clouds gather in this volume of Carlyle's vast history.
hobhouse-liberalism-1911:
L. T. Hobhouse set out the new liberalism in Liberalism, a compact book of 1911. Older liberal thought had stressed freedom from state meddling above all. Hobhouse argues that real freedom needs food, schooling, and fair terms of work. The state, used with care, becomes a tool of liberty rather than its foe.

He traces liberal ideas from early toleration to his own social program. Each stage widens the circle of who counts as fully free. The book became the classic statement of social liberalism's case for state action. British reform in his century ran on lines he helped draw. It remains a clear, brief classic.
husserl-philosophie-als-strenge-wissensc:
Edmund Husserl published his essay Philosophy as Rigorous Science in the journal Logos in 1911, and the German text is given here. Husserl taught at Göttingen and had founded phenomenology, a method that studies how things appear to the mind. The essay served as a public call to rebuild philosophy on firm ground.

Two foes draw his fire: the view that thought is just brain work for science to explain, and the view that truth shifts with each age. Both, he argued, end in doubt about all knowledge. His fix was a strict method that sets aside rash claims and studies experience itself. The piece set the course for much of later European thought.
ibn-arabi-tarjuman-1911:
Ibn Arabi was the great Sufi sage of Spain and the East. His Tarjuman al-Ashwaq, the Interpreter of Desires, holds his love poems. R. A. Nicholson turned them into English in 1911, with the Arab text at hand. A young woman of Mecca first woke the poems in him.

On their face, the odes praise her grace in rich, warm lines. Ibn Arabi then adds his own notes to bare the hid sense. Each grace, he says, points to God and the soul's love for Him. The book is a core text of Sufi thought on love.
ibsen-a-dolls-house-sharp-1911:
Henrik Ibsen wrote A Doll's House in Norwegian, and R. Farquharson Sharp made this Dent version in 1911. The play detonated modern drama when its last scene first stunned audiences in Copenhagen and beyond. Nora's door slam at the end was heard, as the phrase goes, round the world.

Nora Helmer seems a gay, childish wife in a snug and prosperous bourgeois home. A secret loan and a forged name rise to threaten her husband's new bank post. Torvald's rage at the scandal shows Nora she has lived as a doll, not a person. She walks out on husband and children to find herself, in a shocking close. The play still sparks debate on marriage, duty, and a woman's right to selfhood.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-11:
Archer's eleventh and final Ibsen volume gathers the last plays: Little Eyolf, John Gabriel Borkman, and When We Dead Awaken, in 1908 translations. Guilt, age, and the unlived life haunt all three. An old man facing death wrote these spectral dramas, and they read like reckonings.

A drowned child accuses his parents in Little Eyolf; a ruined banker paces his room in Borkman, dreaming of lost empire. When We Dead Awaken lets a sculptor and his model count what their art cost their lives. The volume completes the English edition that defined Ibsen abroad. It also closes the career of the father of modern theater on a note of strange, cold beauty.
james-memories-studies-1911:
Memories and Studies, published in 1911, is a posthumous gathering of James's essays, memorial pieces, and addresses. It shows the philosopher among his dead: teachers, friends, and fellow workers remembered with unusual tenderness.

The volume includes his memorial of Louis Agassiz, his Harvard teacher, and his celebrated address on Emerson. Other pieces take up the moral equivalent of war's themes, the energies of men, and the will to believe's echoes. James writes of persons as he wrote of ideas, with sympathy and precision. The book is the most personal of his volumes, a portrait of a mind through its attachments.
james-more-ghost-stories-1911:
More lore and more curses fill M. R. James's next set of ghost tales, from 1911. Its best known tale sends a curse by runes on a scrap of paper. A proud man who spurned a scholar's work finds dread dogging each step he takes.

James keeps his dry wit and slow build. Old halls, inns, and church tombs hide each threat. Facts pile up till doubt fails. The set shows his craft at full strength. It fixed his name as the chief of the form. A lost maze, a cursed inn, and a school tale with a grim well fill the set. Each shows James at ease with pace, lore, and shock.
james-some-problems-philosophy-1911:
Some Problems of Philosophy, published in 1911 after James's death, is the unfinished introduction to philosophy he was writing at the end. It is subtitled a beginning of an introduction. The book breaks off mid-course, brought to print by his son's care.

James takes up substance, design, free will, and the quarrel between monism and pluralism. He tests each against his pragmatic method: what difference would the answer make in experience? The writing has his late clarity and charm. Though a fragment, it serves as the best short doorway into his thought. Readers meet the philosopher mid-argument, still working.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-11:
Side by side, the Huron and Quebec missions run through Volume 11, from 1898. Thwaites sets the later 1630s on two fronts of one shared enterprise. While Brébeuf builds among the Hurons, the St. Lawrence colony takes shape below.

Letters from bark chapels sit beside reports from the river towns. Both tell of scarce food, hard travel, and slow gains in faith. The writers count each baptism and mourn each early death. Year by year and letter by letter, the record keeps its march. It shows French America's bold age from two ends at once.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lyon-robert-102:
Robert Lyon, an American journalist, is the subject of an entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in London on January 15, 1810, he tried business there first. In 1844 he emigrated to the United States. A manufacturing venture failed, and he turned to publishing. He died in New York City on March 10, 1858.

The article remembers him for one paper above all. On October 26, 1849, he launched The Asmonean, the first American Jewish weekly of its kind. He ran it until his death, while also editing the New York Mercantile Journal. Writers such as Isaac M. Wise contributed to the paper regularly. The Asmonean never won more than local fame, the entry admits. Still, the piece preserves the start of the American Jewish press and the editor who began it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-makai-emil-1031:
Emil Makai, a Hungarian poet, receives a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Mako on November 17, 1871, he was the son of Rabbi A. E. Fischer. He studied at the Rabbinical Seminary in Budapest. There he stood out early for his poetical talent. He died at Budapest on August 6, 1901.

The article praises his gift for carrying Hebrew poetry into Hungarian. He rendered medieval poets such as Gabirol, Ha-Levi, Moses ibn Ezra, and Al-Harizi. Immanuel of Rome also found a voice through him. His own works include Absalom, a biblical drama, and a collection drawn from the Hebrew poets in 1891. The Song of Songs followed in 1892, beside volumes of his own lyrics. The brief entry preserves a poet who died at twenty-nine, having spent his short life as a bridge between two literatures.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marhab-ibn-al-h:
Marhab ibn al-Harith, a Jewish warrior of Arabia, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was killed during Mohammed's invasion of Khaibar about 628. Of Himyarite descent, he won fame for bravery in defending one of Khaibar's forts. The sources picture a giant of a fighter.

The article lingers on his last combat. Marhab wore two cuirasses, a double turban and helmet, with a sword at each side and a three-pointed lance. Following Arab custom, he sent out a poem challenging any of Mohammed's heroes to single combat. One account gives the answering fight to Ali, Mohammed's cousin. Ibn Hisham instead names Mohammed ibn Maslamah, avenging his brother. In that telling the two men fought around a tree until its branches were cut away. Marhab dropped his sword, and his foe struck the fatal blow. The entry weighs both versions of a famous duel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mem-10611:
Mem is the thirteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Crawford Howell Toy and M. Seligsohn describe it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its name means "water." Its early shape is said to have looked like waves. Like some Hebrew letters, it has two forms, one for the start and middle of a word and a final form for the end. In post-Biblical reckoning its value is forty.

The second half of the article is grammar. As a labial, mem swaps with the other labials. This happens across the Semitic tongues. At times it swaps with the liquids too. In word building it works as a prefix. It marks place, time, instrument, or agent. It builds the participles of most Hebrew verb stems. It builds a large class of nouns too. One short paragraph carries the whole entry, cross-referred to the article on the alphabet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshullam-ben-i:
Meshullam ben Isaac, called in full Salem ben Joseph, was an Italian poet of the Hebrew printing houses. Richard Gottheil and Isaac Broydé enter him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Mantua and Venice around the turn of the seventeenth century. Like his father before him, he worked as a corrector in the Hebrew presses of those cities. He graced the trade by supplying the books he corrected with laudatory poems of his own, printed at their heads.

Three liturgical poems of his are named. One is a kinah, an elegy on the great fire at Mantua in 1610, which dates his activity. One treats the Exodus from Egypt. One is a selihah built as a fourfold alphabetical acrostic. The entry rests on Steinschneider's catalogue and Zunz's history of the liturgical poets. It preserves a working poet of the press room rather than the academy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-modona-leonello:
Leonello Modona was an Italian Orientalist born at Cento in 1841. Isidore Singer and Vittore Castiglione give him a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He was educated at Florence's Istituto degli Studi Superiori. His working life joined two trades. He compiled library catalogues. He also wrote studies that range across classics, folklore, and Jewish letters.

His titles show the range. L'Uomo e la Natura treats man and nature. Another study covers the historical Sappho and the myth of Sappho and Phaon. A third reads the Christian legend of the fall of the angels against two British Museum tablets. For Jewish readers he wrote on Sara Copia Sullam, the Venetian poetess. He also wrote on an edition of the prayer-book. The entry rests on De Gubernatis's biographical dictionary alone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moreno-morenu-1:
Moreno, or Morenu, began as a proper name, by Moses ibn Ḥabib's account. Spanish-Portuguese Jews adopted it as a family name, as the Jewish Encyclopedia records in 1906. It travels in company with Paz, Shalom, and Henriquez. Families of the name appear in the seventeenth century at Bayonne, London, Amsterdam, and Hamburg. Others still live in Turkey.

The entry's notices are brief lives. David Shalom Moreno of Bayonne was celebrated for wisdom and Talmudic learning. Gabriel Moreno belonged to Amsterdam's Academia de los Floridos. Jacob Isaac Morenu was an Amsterdam physician who died in 1667. His tombstone was carved with a count's coronet for arms. A surname entry doubles as a map of the western Sephardic diaspora.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-mesharshe:
Moses Kahana ben Jacob, called Mesharsheya, was gaon of Sura from 832 to 843. Wilhelm Bacher and Max Schloessinger wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He was the son of an earlier gaon, Jacob ha-Kohen ben Mordecai. Tradition also makes him a student of the Cabala who used amulets and charms.

His fame rests on two surviving responsa. One treats questions of inheritance and was drawn on by Alfasi and other later authorities. In the other he allowed a Torah scroll to be written on untanned skin when no tanner could prepare parchment. He was the only gaon to allow it, and many Babylonian communities acted on his ruling.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-muller-gabriel-:
Gabriel Müller was a dayyan, a rabbinical judge, at Mattersdorf in Hungary, born at Nadas in 1836. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He learned much of his Torah in his father Hayyim's yeshiva. In 1860 he was appointed dayyan of the community of Mattersdorf.

His books are working tools for rabbis. Birkat ha-Mizwot sets out the laws of the benedictions, and Shi'ure Mizwot treats the weights and measures of the Talmud. His Ozar Agadot gathers haggadic passages from the Talmud in four parts, issued over twenty-five years. A late work, Ma'gele Zedek, turns to ethical reflection.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naphtali-ben-da: Naphtali ben David was a German Hebrew author who lived at Amsterdam in the early eighteenth century. Solomon Schechter and A. S. Waldstein give him a short Jewish Encyclopedia notice. He came of the family of Moses Isserles, was a distinguished Talmudic scholar, and won great fame as a cabalist. His one book, Ben Dawid, printed in 1729, criticizes Lonzano's cabalistic Omer Man.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-necromancy-1141:
Necromancy is divination by aid of the dead. Joseph Jacobs and Ludwig Blau wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Persians, Greeks, and Romans all practiced the dark art. Israel may have borrowed it from Persia. The Bible bans it again and again in strong terms.

Three kinds of workers are named in the sources. The ob spoke as if from joints and arms. The yidde'oni used a bone held in his mouth. At Endor, Samuel rose as an old man in a mantle. Only the witch saw him; Saul heard just the voice. Saul had banned such workers, yet he sought one out. The art lived on into Talmudic times regardless.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-novogrudok-1161:
Novogrudok is a Russian town in the Minsk government. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews first appear there in a deed of 1484. King Casimir leased its customs to four Troki Jews. Royal tax farming shaped its early Jewish life.

In 1529 its Jews shared a special military tax. A royal edict of 1563 fixed their quarter. They were to settle below the castle there. Building on Podlyaskaya street was barred to them. Slow removal brought a fine of 1,600 ducats. Stephen Bathori renewed their charter in 1576. The Orientalist Albert Harkavy was born in Novogrudok. Of 13,656 souls in 1897, 8,137 were Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-onias-honi-ha-m:
Onias, called Honi the Circle-Drawer, was a teacher and wonder worker. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the first century before Christ. Some tales make him kin to Moses himself. He was an Essene, a man of strict faith.

Honi was held in high regard for his pure life. When he entered the school house, all grew clear. He gave plain replies to hard points of law. Yet no rule of his has come down to us. His fame rests on his wonders, the piece says. In a dry year, men begged him to pray for rain. He drew a circle and stood in its midst. Rain came at once at his word of prayer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottinger-joseph:
Joseph Öttinger was an Austrian doctor from Tarnow, in Galicia. Isidore Singer and A. Beck wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born on May 7, in 1818. He died at Cracow on October 2, 1895. He read at the University of Cracow in youth.

Joseph took his first degree in the year 1843. He took a surgeon's degree in the year 1850. In 1851 he took charge of talks at the school. Those talks were on the past of cures and their law. The right to teach was kept from him for years. His love of Poland stood in the way, men said. In 1867 he won that right at long last. He was chief doctor at the Jewish hospital of Cracow.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-parhon-solomon-:
Solomon ben Abraham ibn Parhon was a Spanish word scholar. Crawford Howell Toy and Wilhelm Bacher wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the twelve hundreds in Spain. He was born at Kal'ah, a town in Aragon land. Two great Spanish scholars were among his teachers.

Those teachers were Judah ha-Levi and Abraham ibn Ezra. Solomon tells of talks held with Judah ha-Levi in person. He tells of their stays in North Africa in past days. One work of his has lived to our own time. That one work is his word book, or lexicon, in full. In it he stands as a true pupil of Ibn Ezra. He spread the Hebrew word lore of Spain to new lands. At Salerno he found folk who knew none of that lore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pentateuch-1201:
The Pentateuch is the five books of Moses. Emil G. Hirsch and Joseph Jacobs wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its name is Greek for the five scrolls of the Law. In Hebrew its name means the five fifths of the Law.

The five books run from Genesis to Deuteronomy. Tradition gave their writing to Moses himself. Only the last eight verses, on his death, were excepted. Later readers spotted clashes inside the text. Ibn Ezra hinted at doubts in the Middle Ages. Spinoza later gave the work to Ezra instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phillips-george:
George Lyon Phillips was a leading politician in Jamaica. He was born in 1811 and died at Kingston in 1886. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He ranked among the island's most trusted men.

Phillips held the chief magistracy of the privy council. He filled other high executive posts on the island too. His hour of trial came in the Saturnalia of Blood. That was a season of panic and harsh rule. His calm and gentle manner steadied the councils. The colony owed much of its safety to him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-plotke-julius-1: Julius Plotke was a Frankfort lawyer and communal trustee. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Borek in 1857 and died in 1903. He practiced first at Bockenheim, then in Frankfort itself. He sat on the board of the Frankfort congregation. He served as trustee for several great relief bodies. His pamphlets described the Jews of Russia and Rumania.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-psalms-of-solom:
The Psalms of Solomon are songs that stand outside the Bible. Crawford Howell Toy wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The work is not in the Greek Bible of old. So it forms no part of the Apocrypha either. It comes down to us in Greek alone. Versions made from that Greek exist as well.

The work was most likely written in Hebrew first. It is a Palestinian work, and Hebrew was its natural tongue. Its Greek is rough and at times hard to grasp. Many dark spots come from Greek misuse of Hebrew words. That fact points back to a Hebrew source. The article weighs the songs' age, place, and faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabinovitz-samu:
Samuel Jacob Rabinovitz was a Russian rabbi and author, born in 1857. Herman Rosenthal and Benzion Eisenstadt wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Chelm in the Kovno government. In 1887 he became rabbi at Jevije. That same year he was called to Alexoty instead. His pen was as busy as his pulpit in those years.

Rabinovitz wrote many pieces for the paper Ha-Meliz. They were later made into a book at Warsaw. The book came out in 1900 on faith and nation. In 1897 he sat as a delegate at Basel. That was the first Zionist Congress of Theodor Herzl. In 1900 he became rabbi of Sopotkin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-revai-mor-12711:
Mór Révai was a Hungarian publisher and deputy born at Eperies in 1860. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied at the universities of Budapest and Leipzig. In 1880 he joined his father's publishing house.

The article says that firm was Révai Brothers, founded in 1869. Révai gave great service to popular education in Hungary. He edited a fiction magazine from 1880 to 1885. He helped issue a grand work on the Austro-Hungarian monarchy. He introduced book canvassing into Hungary, they say. His lexicon drive won twenty thousand subscribers. His hundred volume Jókai edition won a Paris grand prize. In 1901 the Szék district sent him to Parliament.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-romaner-benjami:
Benjamin Zeeb Wolf Romaner was a rabbi and preacher. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He worked in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. He served as darshan, or preacher, at Semigrod.

The article says he later preached at Dessau. In his old age he lived at Metz. His book is called Ir Binyamin. It treats the haggadot of both Talmudim in two parts. Part one appeared at Frankfort on the Oder in 1698. Part two appeared at Fürth in 1722. Four bibliographies support the short entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rothschild-mena:
Menahem Mendel Rothschild was a German rabbi born in Frankfort-on-the-Main about 1650. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was a grandson of Isaac, the Rothschild family's forebear.

Menahem preached for several years at Prague, in Bohemia. In 1686 he became chief rabbi of Bamberg, serving Bayreuth and Baiersdorf as well. He stayed at Bamberg until 1718, then moved briefly to Hesse. His last post was the old community of Worms, held until his death in 1731. Like many rabbis then, he was a man of considerable wealth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-jaco: Samuel ben Jacob of Troyes was a French Talmudist of the first half of the thirteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and A. Peiginsky wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was a descendant of Rashi. In his youth he addressed a circular letter, probably cabalistic in nature, to Asher ben David in Provence. Asher later alludes to it in his own cabalistic work on the thirteen attributes of God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sarug-saruk-isr:
Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Israel Sarug. He was a cabalist of the sixteenth century, also called Ashkenazi. Sarug was a pupil of Isaac Luria, the great mystic of Safed. When Luria died, Sarug spread his master's system. He won followers for it in many parts of Italy.

His leading Italian disciple was Menahem Azariah da Fano. Sarug persuaded him to spend large sums buying Luria's manuscripts. Aaron Berechiah of Modena also joined his circle. Sarug lectured in Germany and in Amsterdam as well. Abraham de Herrera was among his Amsterdam pupils. His writings include a cabalistic essay printed in 1629. Another work teaches an ascetic way of life. He also commented on three of Luria's Sabbath hymns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schottlander-ju:
Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on a second Julius Schottländer. He was a German gynecologist, a doctor for women's diseases. Schottländer was born at St. Petersburg on April 12, 1860. He studied medicine at Munich and Heidelberg. He took his doctorate in 1887. He then assisted Kehr at Halberstadt and Martin at Berlin.

In 1893 Schottländer settled at Heidelberg as a physician. He became a privat-docent in gynecology at the university there. In 1897 he was appointed assistant professor. He has written several essays for the medical journals. His book Eierstocktuberculose, on tuberculosis of the ovary, appeared at Jena in 1896. The entry rests on Pagel's lexicon of physicians. The shared name with the Breslau merchant is a coincidence of the catalog.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-semiatitsch-ged:
Gedaliah Semiatitsch was a Lithuanian Talmudist who lived in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. In 1700 he joined a Hasidic party that sailed for Palestine under Judah Hasid. That journey became the subject of his best known book.

His work, printed at Berlin in 1716, tells the full story of the pilgrimage. It covers the party's adventures and the death of Judah Hasid. It also describes Jerusalem, its ruins, and holy burial places across the land. The entry preserves the memory of a traveler whose book outlived him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-she-heheyanu-13:
She-heheyanu is the blessing that thanks God for keeping Jews alive to reach a season. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Its words praise God who sustained us and brought us to this time. People first said it on meeting a loved one after long parting.

The blessing also fits good news and first uses of new things. A new house, garment, utensil, or book called for it. Trivial goods did not, unless the buyer was poor and glad. In modern use it marks first fruits of each season. It is also said after Kiddush on festival first nights. The entry traces a thank-you prayer from reunions to holidays.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-showbread-13611:
Showbread, better called presence-bread, was twelve cakes set before God in the sanctuary. Joseph Jacobs and Emil G. Hirsch wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the offering. Each cake held two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour. The cakes stood in two rows on a pure table.

There they stayed exposed to view for a full week. Each Sabbath fresh cakes replaced the old ones. Priests then ate the old bread in a holy place. Cups of frankincense rested on the rows of cakes. That incense served as a memorial offered on the altar. Kohathite priests had charge of baking and arranging the bread. Their method was kept as a family secret, later writers said. The entry explains a quiet weekly rite at the Temple's heart.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ha-pakol: Simeon ha-Pakoli was a tanna of the second generation, a contemporary of Gamaliel the Second at Jabneh. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He arranged the eighteen benedictions of the daily prayer, the Shemoneh Esreh. He set them in the sequence handed down ever since. His name Pakoli likely came from his trade. Rashi explains that he dealt in flax and wool. Nothing further is known about his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-smolensk-13811:
Smolensk was the capital of the government of Smolensk in Russia. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It stands on the Dnieper, 250 miles from Moscow. Jews lived there as early as 1489. A letter of that year names Jewish customs collectors there.

The city changed hands again and again over time. Russians, Poles, and Lithuanians held it in turn. Its Jewish people suffered greatly from those changes. In 1654 Russia annexed Smolensk for good. By 1899 Jews numbered 4,567 of 56,389 people. Their numbers had fallen since 1896 under residence laws. The town then had two synagogues and five hadarim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steindorff-geor:
Georg Steindorff was a German Egyptologist born at Dessau on November 12, 1861. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. Steindorff studied Oriental languages at Leipsic and Berlin. In 1893 he succeeded his teacher Georg Ebers as professor of Egyptology at Leipsic. He later embraced Christianity.

Steindorff served as associate editor of a leading journal on Egyptian language and antiquities. His books include a Coptic grammar first printed in 1894. He also wrote on burial finds from the Middle Kingdom in Berlin museums. Other works cover Egyptian art and the glory days of the pharaohs. He edited Baedeker's guide to Egypt as well. The entry maps the output of a busy scholar of ancient Egypt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sumptuary-laws-:
Sumptuary laws limit what people may spend on food and clothing. Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The Mishnah records such limits from times of war. Hard times led sages to ban costly wedding customs. The rules aimed to cut display in dark days.

During Vespasian's war, grooms lost their crowns and wedding drums. Titus's war banned the crowns of brides as well. In the last war brides could not ride in curtained litters. Teachers debated crowns of salt, myrtle, or plain reeds. One bride's crown pictured a golden city wall. Modesty later brought the litter back into use. The entry shows law trimming luxury after national disaster. It ties private spending to public mourning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tally-14211:
A tally was a wooden stick that recorded a debt. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Notches along its edge marked the sum due. The stick was then split lengthwise in two. Each half kept part of every notch.

The debtor took one half and the creditor the other. In medieval times this was the standard receipt. Jews and others used tallies for loans. Some survive at Westminster from before the Expulsion. When a debt was claimed, the halves were joined. Any mismatch in the notches exposed fraud at once. The exchequer's stored half settled disputes as decisive. Britain's exchequer used tallies for general receipts too. The entry explains a receipt that could not be forged easily.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-templer-bernhar:
Bernhard Templer was an Austrian theologian born at Brzesko, Galicia, in 1865. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Templer studied at the University and Bet ha-Midrash of Vienna. He also studied at the Berlin Hochschule for Jewish learning.

Templer began writing for Hebrew periodicals at age fifteen. Two years later he published a book on hard Talmudic passages. Other books treated Bible passages and medieval Jewish views of the soul. His 1895 work covered immortality, messianic belief, and the world to come. It drew on Jewish philosophers of the Middle Ages. The entry is short, but it maps a young scholar's early career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-titles-of-honor:
Titles of honor marked birth, rank, learning, and piety in Jewish life. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. In the Bible, adon, or lord, named a master of property. Guests of honor and benefactors received the word too. Abraham was called lord and mighty prince.

A people's leader bore the title melek, or king. Dukes, called aluf, ruled clans under a tribal head. The king's second was the mishneh. Joseph held that rank under Pharaoh in Egypt. Moses earned the titles man of God and servant of the Lord. Other prophets shared those same honors. First-born sons held the title bekor, with its rights. Priests and Levites carried titles by descent.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trier-herman-14:
Herman Trier was a Danish educator, writer, and politician of Copenhagen. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born in 1845, he studied law briefly at the university. In 1864 he turned to pedagogics, his life's field. In that field he won international fame.

From 1876 he published studies of cultural and historical figures. His first pedagogics book argued it was a true science. With P. Voss he ran a youth periodical from 1879. He also wrote on medieval Copenhagen's history. Voters sent him to the Danish Folkething in 1884. In 1898 he joined Copenhagen's board of aldermen. The entry catches a reformer mid-career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-visontai-soma-1:
Soma Visontai was a Hungarian lawyer and member of parliament. He was born at Gyöngyös on November 9, 1854. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He studied at Budapest and became an attorney in 1882. As a student he wrote papers on political economy.

Visontai won fame as a courtroom speaker in 1890. He defended a Serbian newspaper editor in a political murder trial. The defense succeeded, and grateful voters sent him to parliament. Since 1899 he has represented his native town. He is an expert on criminal law. He also helped draft large parts of Hungary's criminal code.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wiesbaden-14911:
Wiesbaden is a German town, capital of former Nassau. Gotthard Deutsch and Moritz Silberstein wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A local history claims Jews lived there in the thirteen hundreds. No documents support that early claim. No record shows persecution in Nassau either. Neither the Armleder riots nor the Black Death struck there.

A Judengasse, or Jews' street, proves their early presence. During the Thirty Years' War, Jewish families found shelter there. Clergy pressed for their removal afterward. Many citizens and officials protected them instead. Friendly feeling toward Jews grew in the town. One citizen in 1700 even adopted Jewish rites. The entry follows the community into modern times.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-woolf-sidney-15:
