Sidney Woolf (1844-1892) was an English lawyer famed for cases on failed firms. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in London, he schooled at a private school and University College. He first worked with his brother in a law firm.

He then read law and joined the bar in 1873. He pled trade and crime cases at first. In time he led the bar in cases of failed firms. In 1890 he was made queen's counsel at last. His first law book treats bad food sold in shops. Later books treat pay for loss and firm wind-ups. He gave time to Jewish schools and synagogue work too. He sat on the board of the Anglo-Jewish Association.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhaki-abraham:
Abraham Yizhaki was a Turkish Talmud scholar at Salonica in the late 1500s. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served as a judge in that town's court. He served under Rabbi Solomon ha-Levi in that role.

His name stands third on a court writ of 1597. It stands second on a writ of the next year. He wrote a work with the name Ahot Ketannah. That work is quoted in two books of later men. It was bound at the end of a book by Jacob Hagiz. Some lists give that work to the wrong man by slip. The work has four parts on the laws of one writ. That writ is the bill that frees a wife who is a minor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zedekiah-ben-be:
Zedekiah ben Benjamin was an Italian Talmud man and hymn scribe. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Rome in the thirteenth century of this era. He died at a date past the year 1280.

He was the elder cousin of Zedekiah ben Abraham Anaw. That man quotes him oft in his great rite book. He was a pupil of Meir ben Moses at Rome. He went to Germany to sit with a top tosafist there. That man was Abigdor ben Elijah ha-Kohen of that land. He kept in touch with that teacher in late years. One peer calls him a mate in a note of that book. Some hold he was a pupil of Abraham Abulafia as well. His own hymns of pardon live on in one draft set.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zweifel-paul-15:
Paul Zweifel was a German gynecologist who taught at Erlangen and then at Leipsic. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Höngg, near Zurich, on June 30, 1848, he took his medical degree at Zurich in 1871. That same year he won the right to lecture at Strasburg.

Erlangen made Zweifel professor of gynecology in 1876, and Leipsic called him in 1887. He held the title of Geheimer Medizinal-Rat, a senior medical honor. He wrote over one hundred papers for medical journals. His books include a textbook of operative obstetrics, often reprinted, and studies of digestion in newborns and of rickets, its causes and cure.
journal-of-discourses-vol-11:
Volume Eleven, from 1865, greets the Civil War's end from Utah's pulpits. Young reads the slaughter as the nation's chastisement, long foretold. The prophet who warned of judgment now watches it fulfilled.

Vindication brings no triumph in the sermons' sober, watching tone. Speakers turn the Saints toward building, gathering, and the years ahead. The republic counts its dead while the mountain kingdom endures intact. Old prophecies get reread in light of smoking battlefields back east. The discourses close one age of warning and open one of patient work. Grief for the nation mixes oddly with pride in Zion's peace.
justice-pg2911:
Justice is John Galsworthy's play, first produced at the Duke of York's Theatre on February 21, 1910. Its people include two solicitors named How, their managing clerk Cokeson, and junior clerk William Falder. A judge, advocates, a prison governor, chaplain, doctor, and warders fill the cast. Ruth Honeywill, a woman tied to Falder's fate, stands among them.

The acts move from the solicitors' office in July to the assizes in October. Act three enters a prison in December: the governor's office, a corridor, and a cell. Two years later the last act returns to the office in March. Galsworthy's design is plain: one small crime, then the slow machinery of law and prison working on a man.
keith-ancient-types-of-man-1911:
Arthur Keith, a Scots doctor and sage of man's rise, wrote this plain survey of fossil man in 1911. It was made for the lay reader, with clear plates and a brisk pace. Keith was then one of the best known names in the field in Britain.

He walks from the Neanderthal and Piltdown finds to the frames of Gibraltar and Java. His famed rebuild of the Gibraltar skull shows his hand at the craft of the time. The book taught a whole age the tale of fossil man as its chief men then told it.
king-john-pg1511:
This edition of Shakespeare's King John prints the full cast and scene plan. King John heads the English list, with Queen Elinor and Prince Henry. Young Arthur, Duke of Bretagne, stands as the rival claimant. Philip Faulconbridge, the Bastard, and Hubert de Burgh hold key parts.

France fields King Philip the Second, his son Lewis, and the Austrian duke. The contents move from Northampton to the French camp before Angiers. St. Edmundsbury, a battlefield, and Swinstead Abbey's orchard close the plan. Peter of Pomfret, a prophet, appears in the cast, true to the chronicles. The edition's apparatus shows the play's shape plainly: two kings, one boy's claim, and a bastard who holds England together.
lagrange-mecanique-analytique-1811:
Joseph-Louis Lagrange builds mechanics without a single diagram in Mecanique analytique, Volume One, in the 1811 edition. The whole of dynamics flows from one deep principle in his hands. Lagrange boasts in his preface that no figures will be found in the work, only algebra of the purest and most general kind.

Statics and dynamics gain a unity no earlier writer had reached. His methods still anchor how physicists treat motion and force today. The prose in French is calm, spare, and quietly proud throughout. Many call it the most elegant physics book ever written, a cathedral of reason raised on the work of Newton and his heirs.
lai-graelent-mason-1911:
Graelent is an anonymous Breton lai about a knight and his fairy mistress. Tales like it were told at medieval courts across France and Britain. Eugene Mason translated this one into English in 1911, alongside other lais of the same kind.

The fairy lady gives Graelent love and wealth, but she sets one hard rule. He must never speak of her to anyone. At court he breaks his word, and she vanishes. To win her back he must chase her through fountain and forest, past a white stag, in a pursuit that tests whether love can survive a broken promise.
lai-lespine-mason-1911:
L'Espine is an anonymous Breton lai, a short medieval tale of knights and fairy folk. No author is known for it. Eugene Mason translated the French text into English in 1911, when he gathered several of these old tales into one volume.

A young knight rides out to a thorn tree at night, drawn by a challenge and a strange summons. There he crosses into the land of the fairy king. Mortal rules stop working in that place, and wonder turns quickly to danger. The tale is brief and eerie, told in the spare way of the old Breton storytellers.
lawrence-white-peacock-1911:
D. H. Lawrence was a young schoolteacher in the Midlands when he wrote The White Peacock. His first novel, it was published in 1911 after years of drafting. Lawrence set it in the countryside around his home town of Eastwood in Nottinghamshire.

Two sisters, Lettie and Meg, move through courtships that go wrong in different ways. Around them, the gamekeeper Annable preaches a rough gospel of the body against polite society. Farming life, poaching, and the pit villages fill the background with rich detail. The novel is uneven and lush, but Lawrence's eye for nature and class tension is already fully alive.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-11:
Part Eleven opens with Chapter 51, called Reminiscences. Twain leaves for St. Louis aboard the City of Baton Rouge. He regrets talking with only two dozen steamboatmen, not a hundred. Social life in town had pleasantly swallowed his research time.

From the pilot-house bench he watches the boat straighten up. A cub takes the wheel as Captain Bixby steps in. The cub allows too much water between boat and ships. Twain feels nervous, remembering his own cub days exactly. Black smoke piled from the chimneys in the old-fashioned way. The cub presently closed up on the rank of steamships ahead.
london-south-sea-tales-1911:
Jack London cruised the South Pacific on his yacht Snark in 1907 and 1908, gathering material until illness forced him home. South Sea Tales, published in 1911, holds the fiction that came out of the Solomon Islands and Hawaii. It is his Pacific work at its most brutal and most humane.

The stories confront white traders, missionaries, and planters exploiting island peoples, and islanders answering in kind. One tale visits Molokai's leper colony, where London finds courage and dignity among the outcast sick. Another follows a pearl diver and a hurricane. London neither romanticizes the islands nor excuses the whites. The sea, the heat, and sudden violence rule these pages, told in his hardest prose.
mansfield-german-pension-1911:
Katherine Mansfield published this first book in 1911, when she was twenty-two and newly arrived in London from New Zealand. The sketches grew from her stay at a Bavarian spa, taking the waters among German guests she observed with a cold eye.

She skewers the pension's residents: their appetites, vanities, sentimentality, and casual cruelties. The pieces are short, sharp, and funny, with dialogue that pricks like pins. Mansfield later thought the book crude and tried to suppress it. Even so, the voice is already unmistakable: the outsider girl watching, and missing nothing. Her great stories were five years away.
marie-de-france-bisclavret-mason-1911:
Bisclavret, the Were-Wolf, is Marie de France's great medieval werewolf tale in Mason's 1911 translation. A Breton nobleman vanishes three days each week without explanation. His wife presses him until he confesses his secret.

He turns wolf each week and must hide his clothes to return human. The wife betrays him to a lover, who steals the clothing. Trapped as a wolf, Bisclavret lives gently at the king's court. The king's hound and the wolf's own behavior reveal the truth at last. Treachery, loyalty, and the beast within drive the lai. Marie treats her werewolf with surprising sympathy throughout the tale.
marie-de-france-chaitivel-mason-1911:
Chaitivel, the Dolorous Knight, is Marie de France's lai of love's cost in Mason's translation. Four accomplished knights all love one lady in Brittany. She cannot choose among them and keeps all four hopeful.

A tournament turns festive rivalry into real disaster for the suitors. Three knights die, and the fourth is maimed for life. The survivor proposes the lai be named for his sorrow. The lady instead argues it should bear her own grief's name. Marie leaves readers to judge whose loss runs deeper here. The debate over the title becomes the poem's true subject. Mason's 1911 translation closes Marie's set with this thoughtful, melancholy piece.
marie-de-france-chevrefoil-mason-1911:
Marie de France wrote short verse tales called lais in the twelfth century, and Chevrefoil is her smallest one. Its subject is Tristan and Iseult, the famous doomed lovers of medieval romance. Eugene Mason turned the poem into English prose in 1911.

Banished from court, Tristan cuts a message for Iseult into a hazel branch left beside her road. The sign works like the honeysuckle wound round the hazel tree. Neither plant can live once the two are pulled apart. In just a few pages the tale says all it needs about love that cannot be parted, even by exile or death.
marie-de-france-deus-amanz-mason-1911:
Deus Amanz, the Two Lovers, is Marie de France's bleakest lai in Mason's 1911 translation. A king in Normandy sets a brutal condition for his daughter's marriage. Any suitor must carry her up a steep mountain without resting.

A young lover accepts the test and obtains a strength potion beforehand. Pride makes him refuse the drink when the climb grows hard. He reaches the top carrying her, then dies of the effort. The lady dies of grief beside him on the summit. Love's cruel arithmetic governs the short, sad tale. Mason's translation preserves Marie's restraint, which makes the ending hurt more.
marie-de-france-eliduc-mason-1911:
Eliduc is one of the lais of Marie de France, the twelfth-century poet who wrote short verse tales of love and magic. Eugene Mason translated it into English in 1911. Its knight hero is torn between his wife at home and a new love across the sea.

Eliduc's second love falls into a deathlike sleep, and grief seems certain to win. Then a weasel wakes its dead mate by laying a red flower on it. Eliduc uses the same flower, and the shock of grace that follows changes every life in the tale. All three end by taking holy orders.
marie-de-france-equitan-mason-1911:
Marie de France's Equitan, translated by Eugene Mason in 1911, is a lai of adultery punished. King Equitan of the Bretons falls in love with his seneschal's wife. The seneschal is his loyal right-hand man and closest companion.

The lovers plot to kill the husband in a boiling bath. Equitan himself is forced into the scalding water instead and dies. The wife follows him into the same bath in the tale's grim justice. Marie draws the moral that evil planned for others falls on the planner. Mason's translation keeps the sting of her irony. The short lai shows Marie at her most crisp and unforgiving.
marie-de-france-fresne-mason-1911:
Fresne, the Ash Tree, is among Marie de France's tenderest lais in Mason's 1911 translation. A lady slanders a neighbor for bearing twins, then bears twins herself. Fearing the same charge, she abandons one baby at an ash tree.

A porter finds the child, and nuns raise her behind convent walls. The girl, called Fresne for the ash, grows into a lord's beloved. Her twin sister's wedding finally reveals the truth of her birth. A brocade cloth and a ring serve as the recognition tokens. Hidden birth and love recognized close Marie's delicate tale. Mason's English keeps its gentle, forgiving tone throughout.
marie-de-france-guigemar-mason-1911:
Eugene Mason translated Marie de France's Guigemar into English in 1911. Marie wrote her lais, short Breton tales in verse, in the twelfth century. Guigemar stands first among the twelve lais she composed.

A hunting accident wounds the knight Guigemar in the thigh. A magical ship with no crew carries him to a foreign shore. There a lady, locked away by her jealous husband, heals and loves him. A knotted shirt and a belt serve as tokens of their fidelity. Separation and recognition close the tale in Marie's delicate manner. Mason's translation introduces the twelfth century's great woman poet to English readers gently.
marie-de-france-lanval-mason-1911:
Lanval is Marie de France's most Arthurian lai, in Eugene Mason's 1911 translation. Sir Lanval, a poor foreign knight, receives little favor at Arthur's court. A fairy mistress chooses him in secret and enriches him.

She forbids him ever to speak of her love to anyone. Queen Guinevere then propositions Lanval and, when refused, accuses him falsely. Forced to defend himself, he breaks his vow and names his mistress. The fairy lady rides into court and vindicates him before all. Love on trial frames the tale's bright, strange climax. Mason's version keeps Marie's sparkle in this favorite among her lais.
marie-de-france-laustic-mason-1911:
Laustic, the Nightingale, shows Marie de France in miniature in Mason's 1911 translation. Two knights live as neighbors, and one loves the other's wife. The lovers can only talk through adjoining windows at night.

They claim their meetings are for listening to the nightingale sing. The jealous husband traps and kills the bird in revenge. He hurls its small body at his wife, staining her dress with blood. She sends the dead nightingale to her lover as a final message. He keeps it cased in a jeweled vessel forever afterward. Love, spite, and a dead bird fill Marie's shortest perfect tale.
marie-de-france-milun-mason-1911:
Milun is Marie de France's lai of patience rewarded, in Mason's 1911 translation. The famous knight Milun loves a lady he cannot marry openly. Their son is sent away to be raised by his aunt.

For twenty years a swan carries secret letters between the lovers. The swan flies the messages hidden under its feathers, year after year. The grown son becomes a champion and unknowingly faces his father in combat. Recognition comes through Milun's ring before either man is harmed. Father, mother, and son finally unite after the long separation. The swan post never fails in Marie's most patient love story.
marie-de-france-yonec-mason-1911:
Yonec is a lai by Marie de France, the twelfth-century writer of short verse tales about love and the strange. Eugene Mason made this English version in 1911. Its heroine is a young wife locked in a tower by an old, jealous husband.

A knight reaches her window in the shape of a hawk, and the two become lovers in secret. The husband sets a trap, and the hawk-knight dies of his wounds. Their son, Yonec, grows up hearing the hidden story. When he learns the truth, he takes up his father's sword and settles the debt in blood.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-11: Bourrienne's eleventh volume bears etext number 3561 at Gutenberg. Its head note joins the title to the year 1812. December 2002 is listed as the release date for the file. Inside the sample, though, a reader finds the license text and nothing else. The secretary's own words do not begin within the portion held here. So this note names the volume and its file facts, and claims no more than that.
my-novel-volume-11:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's eleventh book weighs hate as a force in civil life. Kind men call all wickedness a kind of madness, he notes. Yet clever rogues share much with the insane, he argues. Randal Leslie is his case: cunning, restless, and suspicious.

Randal thinks the whole world plots against his rise. His schemes grow wire-drawn to hide their own ugliness. Pride in his own wit blinds him to his shame. Lytton defends the portrait as true to refining minds gone wrong. The volume digs into ambition's dark engine, as the long tale moves toward its reckoning of hearts.
nansen-northern-mists-vol1-1911:
In Northern Mists, from 1911, Nansen turned historian of the Arctic quest itself. Volume One runs from the Greek sailor Pytheas to the Norse voyages. The great polar explorer traces how the North was slowly found, imagined, and mapped.

Nansen sifts sagas, maps, and travelers' tales, testing each claim of early discovery. Vinland, the Irish monks, and the Greenland settlements all get his keen, skeptical eye. He writes as a sailor who knows ice and fog from his own decks. The volume remains a classic survey of early northern exploration, learned and readable at once. Old maps are reprinted so readers can test his claims for themselves.
nansen-northern-mists-vol2-1911:
Volume Two of Nansen's In Northern Mists, also 1911, carries the history of Arctic discovery from the late Middle Ages toward Cabot. Nansen the explorer reads the old records like a man checking a chart. Myths slowly give way to coasts that can be sailed.

He treats Marco Polo's northern hints, the fabled islands on portolan maps, and the search for a sea road to Asia. The volume weighs what the Norse truly found against what later ages claimed for them. Nansen's verdicts are careful and sometimes sharp. The two volumes together survey a thousand years of northern dreaming and discovery.
nasa-tm-19680021153-research-achievement:
Instrumentation research for ground testing fills volume 11 of Marshall's Research Achievements Review, a 1968 memorandum, TM X-53743. Ground tests of rocket hardware are only as good as the instruments that measure them. Albert E. Schuler introduces the volume, which gathers new measurement tools built at the center in Huntsville, Alabama.

Alvin M. Payne describes gear for measuring the density of hydrogen slush, a partly frozen fuel, using radiation based densitometers. Harlan S. Harman then presents pressure sensors built for environmental extremes. His designs include a high temperature transducer with fast response. Together the pieces show how Marshall sharpened the measurements behind its test stands.
nasa-tm-19720010301-low-gravity-venting-:
Thomas L Labus, John C Aydelott, and Raymond F Lacovic of the Lewis Research Center reported these venting tests in February 1972, as NASA TM X-2479. They vented saturated Refrigerant 11 from a small cylindrical tank in low gravity. The Lewis five second zero gravity facility gave brief weightless runs. In orbit, liquid does not settle, so venting a tank can expel liquid instead of gas. Their tank was fifteen centimeters across.

The team studied three gravity levels, from full weightlessness to stronger pulls. The liquid clung to the tank walls with a near zero contact angle. Observers watched the liquid and vapor behavior during each venting run. The results guide the design of spacecraft tank vents. Refrigerant stood in for harder to handle propellants.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-11:
Volume eleven of Schaff's Nicene Fathers, first series, holds Chrysostom's homilies on the Acts of the Apostles and on the Epistle to the Romans. The volume dates from 1886. Chrysostom preached the Acts series near the end of his time in Constantinople.

The Acts homilies follow the apostles from Jerusalem outward, with Chrysostom marveling at their boldness and shaming his own softer age. The Romans homilies then work through Paul's hardest letter, untangling faith, law, and grace for lay hearers. His praise of Paul runs through both series like a refrain. The volume pairs the church's first story with its first theology, preached by its greatest preacher.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-11:
Volume eleven of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890, joins Sulpitius Severus, Vincent of Lerins, and John Cassian. The three are the voices of early western monasticism. Schaff and Wace edited the series.

Sulpitius wrote the life of Martin of Tours, the soldier-saint whose cloak, shared with a beggar, became legend. Vincent's Commonitory gives the famous rule for telling old faith from new error: what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all. Cassian's conferences then carry the wisdom of Egypt's desert monks to the West, on prayer, purity, and grace. The volume shaped how western monks lived and prayed for centuries.
nietzsche-twilight-idols-ludovici-1911:
Friedrich Nietzsche published Twilight of the Idols in 1889, a short summary of his mature thought. The English text here is Anthony M. Ludovici's translation of 1911. Nietzsche said he wrote it as a rest between larger works. Its subtitle calls it how to philosophize with a hammer.

Short sections strike at Socrates, German culture, morality, and metaphysics in turn. Famous maxims open the book, including what does not kill me makes me stronger. Nietzsche tests old idols by tapping them for hollow sounds. The style is fast, funny, and cutting. It is one of the best short entries into his thought.
onions-widdershins-1911:
Oliver Onions filled Widdershins, his set of tales from 1911, with ghosts that gnaw at the mind. Its most famed tale lures a painter to a flat where a fair voice calls. The flat holds him. Art, love, and dread blur till he can't break free.

Onions writes with care and a slow, sure hand. Fear grows from mood and small signs, not shocks. The set is a high mark of ghost tales from its age. Its lead tale is oft called the best house tale. Onions had a deft hand for folk who drift and dream. His ghosts prey on that drift, which makes the scares feel close and sad.
openalex-w1747388711:
Daniel Furtado Ferreira described this statistics software in 2011. His review appeared in a Brazilian agricultural science journal. Sisvar is a computer system for statistical analysis. It was first released in 1996, he reports. Work on it began in 1994 in Pascal language.

Three goals drove the project from the start. It served a statistics course at Lavras university first. It aimed to be a truly Brazilian free software tool. It also aimed to give researchers fast, trusted analysis. All initial goals were achieved, Ferreira reports. Users praise its accuracy, simplicity, and interactive design.
openalex-w1975654711:
Tom Wingfield, Carlton Evans, and co-authors ran this cohort study. It appeared in PLoS Medicine in the year 2014. Tuberculosis care is free in Peru, they note. Hidden costs still hit patients and their households hard. Such extreme costs are called catastrophic, yet poorly defined.

The team studied TB-affected households in Peru prospectively. They defined catastrophic costs and measured their weight. They compared that weight with drug-resistant disease. Both can drive adverse treatment outcomes for patients. Clear cost definitions help design support for poor households. The work links TB control to poverty protection.
openalex-w2059292511:
Avi Raveh, Phillip Delekta, Craig Dobry and colleagues searched sea microbes for antiviral compounds. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. Microbe products have yielded many medicines. Few had been tested against viruses. Marine bacteria offered a fresh place to look.

The team screened extracts from marine actinobacteria. A cell-based test flagged active extracts. Step-by-step separation isolated the active compound. It came from a new Streptomyces species off Papua New Guinea. The compound blocked many RNA viruses in cell tests. It worked by stalling a key energy pathway in cells. That stall starves viruses of building blocks. Related compounds showed similar antiviral effects. The work opens a route to broad antiviral drugs.
openalex-w2094457711:
Daniela Silva Canella, Renata Bertazzi Levy, Ana Paula Martins and colleagues linked ultra-processed foods with obesity in Brazil. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. Factory-made food and drink sales have risen worldwide. Obesity and chronic disease rose in parallel. The team tested the link with household data.

They used a national household budget survey. It covered nearly fifty-six thousand Brazilian homes. Homes were grouped into similar strata. Ultra-processed goods supplied very different energy shares across groups. Higher availability tracked with higher average body mass. It also tracked with more overweight and obesity. Plain processed foods showed no such link. The pattern held after adjusting for other factors.
openalex-w2127901511:
Jane Bryan, Phil Shearman, Gregory Asner, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2013. They compared forest damage in the three parts of Borneo: the Malaysian states of Sabah and Sarawak, and the small nation of Brunei. Timber cutting and oil palm planting had changed these forests faster than field surveys could track.

Using satellite images since 1990, the team mapped forest cover and logging roads across the region. They found hundreds of thousands of kilometres of roads cut through the forest. By 2009, nearly four-fifths of Sabah and Sarawak had felt high-impact logging or clearing. Brunei looked very different, with over half its land still under unlogged forest.
openalex-w2159061711:
Oliver Brady, Michael Johansson, Carlos Guerra, and colleagues published this study in Parasites and Vectors in 2013. They modeled how temperature shapes the survival of adult Aedes mosquitoes, the biters that spread dengue. A female must live long enough for the virus to mature inside her, so survival sets transmission risk.

The team fitted models to hundreds of published lab survival experiments for both major species. Field survival data then adjusted the lab curves to real-world conditions. One species survived better in both settings, while the other tolerated a wider temperature range. Full tables split survival by age and temperature. The authors stress that local, site-specific survival estimates matter for judging outbreak risk.
openalex-w2624462411:
Julien Emile-Geay, Nicholas P. McKay, and Darrell S. Kaufman lead the PAGES2k Consortium behind this 2017 database paper in Scientific Data. It gathers temperature-sensitive records from natural archives across the globe. Trees, ice, sediments, corals, and cave deposits all record past climate in their growth. Together they let scientists rebuild temperatures across the Common Era, the last two thousand years.

The database holds six hundred ninety-two records from six hundred forty-eight locations. It covers every continent and the major ocean basins. Record lengths run from fifty to two thousand years, with a median near five hundred fifty years. Nearly half the series track modern surface temperatures closely enough to help validate them. Reconstructions built on this shared, quality-checked foundation can be reproduced by others. That helps place today's warming firmly against natural climate variability.
openalex-w2788363011:
The ATLAS Collaboration evaluated missing transverse momentum reconstruction in this 2018 paper in the European Physical Journal C. The study uses the full 2015 dataset at thirteen TeV.

Rebuilding it combines calibrated electrons, muons, photons, taus, and jets. Soft activity from leftover tracks joins the sum, with careful steps to avoid counting any signal twice. The authors test scale, resolution, and sensitivity to running conditions with several metrics. They also lay out how errors on the measurement are derived. Good performance here underpins the credibility of ATLAS's new-physics searches. This paper is the reference for how the 2015 measurement behaved.
openalex-w2900756811:
Clotilde Théry, Kenneth Whitaker Witwer, and Elena Aïkawa lead the International Society for Extracellular Vesicles' 2018 position statement, MISEV2018. MISEV2018 tells researchers what studies of these vesicles must report. Hundreds of experts backed the consensus. Basic standards cover how vesicles are isolated, characterized, and described. Following them makes results repeatable across labs. The statement also updates terms and best practices since 2014. Fields drowning in hype need such ground rules to separate signal from noise. This document is the reference editors and reviewers now apply to vesicle research.
openalex-w3020256411:
Nancy Chow, José Muñoz, Lalitha Gade, and colleagues posted this preprint on bioRxiv in January 2020, before peer review. It traces the history and global spread of Candida auris, a drug-resistant yeast that has emerged in hospitals worldwide. The yeast spreads within health care settings and resists many antifungal drugs.

An early study had split the yeast into four regional groups, or clades. The team compared the genomes of three hundred four isolates from nineteen countries on six continents. The same four clades still dominate, though most now mix across regions. One South American clade kept the strongest geographic pattern. Two clades with opposite mating types even turned up in a single Kenyan facility.
openalex-w3091700111:
Ana Pedrosa, Letícia Bitencourt, Ana Fróes, and colleagues wrote this review in Frontiers in Psychology in 2020. It surveys the emotional, behavioral, and psychological impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. The illness began as a cluster of pneumonia cases in Hubei, China, in December 2019.

Within nine months, confirmed cases worldwide had passed twenty-six million. The authors searched the fast-growing literature through early September 2020, favoring case series, guidelines, pooled analyses, and forward-looking cohort studies. They reviewed and selected the work with a critical eye. The review gathers what was known about fear, grief, isolation, and strained behavior during the crisis. It offers clinicians and policymakers a map of the pandemic's mental toll.

Ahmed Abdelfattah, Shiri Freilich, Rotem Bartuv, and colleagues published this global study in 2021. Apple is among the most eaten fruits on Earth and the largest fruit crop of temperate regions.

Theirs is the first worldwide study of its kind, sampling fruit across many countries. Both fungal and bacterial communities on and in the fruit differed strongly by place of harvest. Even tissue within the fruit mattered, with skin and core hosting unlike mixes. Fungal diversity shifted enough to suggest links with the rot diseases each country later sees. A small shared core of microbes appeared in fruit from everywhere.
openalex-w4410636511:
M. Abdul Karim, J. Aguilar, Steven Ahlen, and the DESI collaboration present results from the survey's second data release. Their paper appeared in Physical Review D in 2025. The universe's expansion is speeding up. Explaining that acceleration is a central problem in cosmology.

The team measures baryon acoustic oscillations in the new data. These are frozen sound-wave patterns from the early universe. Their spacing works as a standard ruler for cosmic distances. Tracking the ruler across time reconstructs the expansion history. The measurements then constrain models of dark energy and gravity. Sharper constraints can rule out whole families of explanations for cosmic acceleration.
openalex-w4411165211:
Shigenori Ueda and Ikutaro Hamada study the valence bands of 4f rare-earth elements. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2025. It is part four of a series combining spectroscopy with theory. Rare-earths matter for strong permanent magnets and other technologies.

The authors use polarisation-dependent photoemission that probes deep below the surface. They compare the spectra with density functional theory calculations. Rare-earth 4f electrons stay tightly localised and create complex multiplet patterns. Matching measured and calculated bands tests whether theory captures those patterns. Better electronic maps of rare-earths support both basic physics and the design of magnetic materials.
openalex-w4415393411:
Ricard Ferrer and Toshiaki Iba review the molecular mechanisms of heatstroke. Their review appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2025. Heatstroke strikes when core body temperature passes forty degrees. Confusion, seizures, or coma follow, with inflammation and organ failure.

The authors trace the damage inside cells. Extreme heat unfolds proteins and triggers oxidative stress. Inflammatory signals spread through the body. Several programmed cell-death pathways switch on. Together these processes injure the liver, kidneys, brain, and blood system. Mapping the molecular cascade shows where treatment might interrupt it. That knowledge grows more urgent as heatwaves intensify worldwide and heatstroke cases climb.

openalex-w7204221811: Losing a pregnancy to miscarriage brings grief that nurses must meet with care. openalex-w7204991111: Police forces face tangled rules and high pressure to perform. openalex-w7207615311: Forty-three nursing students tried something new: quiz games on the Kahoot platform mixed with artificial intelligence tools in their coursework. Small and hands-on, it reads like a field note from the classroom.

plos-pbio-0020211:
Juergen Tautz, Shaowu Zhang, Johannes Spaethe, and their team tested how honeybees judge distance in PLOS Biology in 2004. Bees tell nestmates how far food is through their waggle dance. To do that, a bee must measure the trip, a skill called odometry, based on how the world streams past its eyes.

The team flew bees over varied ground and watched how their estimates changed. Rough, rich scenery made trips feel longer than smooth ground did. That fits an eye-flow measure rather than energy spent. The study shows a tiny brain solving a navigation task with a simple, robust rule, a result that interests both biologists and robot designers.
plos-pone-0000011:
Matthew Falagas, Konstantinos Fragoulis, and Ioannis Karydis compared drug prices across medicine in a 2006 PLOS ONE study. New antibiotics draw special worry: bacteria keep evolving resistance, so fresh ones are badly needed, yet firms say developing them pays poorly. The authors asked whether new antibiotics actually cost more than new drugs in other fields.

They set the price of new antibiotics beside drugs from other therapeutic categories, from heart medicine to cancer care. Price gaps, where they exist, feed the debate over why so few antibiotics reach the market. The comparison gives policy makers a factual base for arguments about incentives, patents, and the true cost of staying ahead of resistant germs.
plos-pone-0000111:
Donatella Bulone, Laura Masino, David J. Thomas, and their team studied protein clumping in PLOS ONE in 2006. Stretches of repeated glutamine, called polyQ, appear in several brain disease proteins, like the one in Huntington's disease. The longer the stretch, the more readily the protein clumps into toxic fibers.

The authors show the protein around the stretch matters as much as the stretch itself. The right context can delay clumping by holding the protein in a store of early, loose clumps called protofibrils. That delay changes how the disease clock might run. It also suggests a therapy idea: stabilize the harmless store, and the toxic fibers may never form.
plos-pone-0000211:
José M. Pérez, Iván L. Calderón, Felipe A. Arenas, and colleagues published this microbiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Potassium tellurite is a compound long known to poison bacteria, used for over a century to select them in the lab. Yet why it kills was an old puzzle, an ancient enigma, as the title says. The authors work on how tellurite harms bacterial cells.

Tellurite still appears in microbiology labs and in some industrial settings. Pinning down its toxic mechanism explains both its killing power and how some bacteria resist it. The paper brings modern molecular tools to a question that dates back to the early days of bacteriology.
plos-pone-0000311:
Victor Frak, Isabelle Croteau, Daniel Bourbonnais, and colleagues published this motor control study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Prehension is the act of reaching and grasping. The authors report that merely simulating a grasp, imagining or preparing the action, modifies actual prehension. This is evidence that the brain represents an object's graspable features together with the action of grasping it.

Mind and hand share one representation, in this account. That joint coding explains why thinking about a grip changes the grip itself. The finding matters for rehabilitation and for understanding how the brain plans skilled movements.
plos-pone-0000411:
Patrick Peretti-Watel and colleagues examined how stigma against people with HIV may feed the epidemic in France, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Discrimination can push people to hide their status, avoid testing, or skip care. The team gathered evidence on how common such discrimination is and how it connects to the spread of HIV.

If fear of mistreatment keeps people from knowing or sharing their status, the virus gains room to spread unseen. Documenting that chain matters for policy: fighting stigma becomes part of fighting the epidemic itself, alongside medicine. The study grounds that argument in French survey and social evidence rather than assumption.
plos-pone-0000511:
Christopher B. Guest and colleagues studied how diabetes changes the way immune cells swallow fat, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. In artery walls, cells called macrophages gorge on stored cholesterol, known as cholesteryl ester. They swell into the foam cells of artery plaques. The team found this fat swallowing is turned up in macrophages from diabetic mice.

Two surface sensors, CD36 and SR-A, do most of the swallowing. Diabetes sharply raises heart disease risk, and fat-stuffed artery cells are a strong suspect link. Naming the sensors that do the work gives drug makers clear targets. The study ties a whole-body disease to a cell's appetite, tested one sensor at a time.
plos-pone-0000611:
Bernhard Voelkl and Ludwig Huber tested what monkey imitation really copies, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Marmoset monkeys watched a demonstrator perform a novel technique to get food. The team examined imitation as faithful copying of the novel technique: whether the observers reproduced the method itself, not just the result.

True imitation, copying actions rather than outcomes, is a milestone in the evolution of learning and culture. Marmosets are cooperative breeders with rich social lives, a promising place to look for it. Careful tests matter because animals often appear to imitate while actually using simpler tricks, and telling the difference defines what social learning means.
plos-pone-0000711:
John F. Bruno and Elizabeth R. Selig measured how coral cover has declined across the Indo-Pacific, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Many factors had recently caused mass coral deaths in all the world's tropical oceans. Yet little was known about the timing, rate, or spatial variability of the loss. The Indo-Pacific holds a major share of the world's reef-building corals.

The authors set the region's figure at 75 percent of the world's reef-building coral territory, making its trend the global story. Their analysis covers timing, extent, and comparisons between subregions. A firm baseline matters for conservation: without knowing how fast cover fell, no one can tell whether protection is working.
plos-pone-0000811:
Sanjay Chandriani and Don Ganem sorted the host's responses during aggressive infection by a cancer-linked herpesvirus, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Lytic infection by Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus brings an extensive shutoff of host gene expression. The shutoff runs chiefly through accelerated messenger RNA turnover, driven by the viral SOX protein, which destroys host messages. A small number of host mRNAs had previously been found to escape or rise.

By measuring host transcript accumulation during infection, the authors reveal several classes of host responses. Some genes resist the shutoff, others are actively induced. Those classes point to defenses the cell mounts, and to host factors the virus cannot do without.
plos-pone-0000911:
Stephen Proulx, Sergey Nuzhdin and Daniel Promislow looked for direct selection on genetic robustness in yeast, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Theory says living things should evolve ways to keep a healthy form despite shocks from outside or from their own mutations. Several routes to that steadiness were already known.

What was missing was proof that selection acts on robustness itself, not just on traits it protects. Reading the yeast transcriptome, the full set of active genes, the authors argue the signature is there. The claim matters for how we think traits stay stable over generations. It also bears on why some mutations stay hidden until stress reveals them.
plos-pone-0001011:
Joachim Goedhart, Joop Vermeer, Merel Adjobo-Hermans and colleagues built new glowing protein pairs to detect a doubled immune factor, in PLOS ONE in 2007. FRET is a technique where one glowing protein passes energy to another when they sit very close. The classic pair uses blue and yellow green fluorescent proteins.

Newer red shifted proteins could work better, with less background. The team built FRET couples from them and used the pairs to detect homodimers of p65, two copies of an immune control protein joined together. Better probes mean cleaner live cell images of proteins meeting. That feeds many fields at once.
plos-pone-0001111:
Matthew Witt and Brendan Godley used ship tracking data to map fishing at sea scale, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Saving marine ecosystems needs a full picture of fisheries alongside maps of biodiversity. The UK government's vessel monitoring system tracks large UK registered fishing vessels by satellite.

Witt and Godley investigate patterns of fishing activity in that data. Knowing where effort concentrates, season by season, is the base layer for seascape scale conservation, protecting whole seascapes rather than single spots. Fishing maps also expose where protected areas would bite and where they would merely displace boats. The paper shows a surveillance system doubling as a science tool.
plos-pone-0001211:
Growing tissues in three dimensions, rather than as flat layers, is a goal of tissue engineering. Takuya Matsumoto and colleagues demonstrated a patterning method in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their system uses a strained fibrin gel, a gel made from a blood-clotting protein, pulled so its fibers align.

The authors show three-dimensional cell and tissue patterning in the strained gel. Cells placed in such a scaffold can be guided into organized arrangements that mimic real tissue. Techniques like this are valuable both for studying how cells behave in tissues and for building cell and matrix composites for repair.
plos-pone-0001311:
In regions where malaria is seasonal, some people carry the parasite at very low levels. The levels are too low to see under a microscope. Those hidden infections can restart transmission. Badria El-Sayed and colleagues ran a randomized, open-label trial in eastern Sudan, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Treating these symptom-free carriers could be a useful way to control malaria.

The trial compared artesunate plus sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine with the same regimen plus primaquine. The goal was to clear sub-microscopic P. falciparum infections and gametocyte carriage. Gametocytes are the parasite stage mosquitoes pick up. Their comparison tests whether adding primaquine clears the reservoir better.
plos-pone-0001411:
Jairam Lingappa and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on couples where one partner has HIV and the other does not. Most HIV spread in Africa occurs in such couples, who often do not know their state. These couples face a high rate of new infection. The team mapped how common such couples are by region.

They also tracked how many joined a trial of ways to block spread. Rates of mixed state couples varied a lot from place to place. That spread shapes where trials and care will do the most good. The data help aim scarce funds at the couples and regions at highest risk.
plos-pone-0001511:
Guido Michels and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the heart's pacemaker current. A set of channels drives the steady beat of the heart. Those channels were thought to have helper proteins that tune them, but few helpers were known. The team tested one such helper, called KCR1, in heart cells.

They show KCR1 curbs the pacemaker current and so slows heart rhythm. A brake on the beat is as vital as the drive itself. Faults in such brakes could underlie rhythm ills that now lack a cause. The work names a fresh target for rhythm drug research.
plos-pone-0001611:
Laura Wilding Crawford and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on pancreas shape faults in mice. A decade of work had named many factors that build the pancreas. Yet how its islets, the insulin hubs, take their right shape was still not known. The team read gene use in a mouse model where islet shape goes wrong.

Their gene lists flag paths that steer islet form as it grows. Faults in shape can blunt insulin release even when cells are present. That makes shape a real part of diabetes, not a side note. The lists give labs set leads for the next round of mouse tests.
plos-pone-0001711:
Ben Lopman and Simon Gregson reconstructed the history of HIV in Harare, Zimbabwe, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. HIV prevalence there had recently begun to fall, driven by high AIDS mortality and fewer new infections. To understand that turn, officials need to know when new infections, or incidence, peaked, and that date cannot be observed directly.

The authors used back-calculation, working backward from mortality statistics to infer past incidence. The full text gives the death data, the model, and their estimate of the peak year. Dating the peak helps judge which prevention efforts and behavior changes actually bent the epidemic's curve in one of the countries hit hardest by HIV.
plos-pone-0001811:
Laura D. Mydlarz, Sally F. Holthouse, Esther C. Peters, and their co-authors studied immune cells in sea fan corals in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Climate warming is making marine and land organisms, and even humans, more susceptible to emerging diseases. Coral reefs are among the ecosystems most impacted by climate stress, and coral immunity is ancient, inherited from the earliest multicellular animals.

The team examined granular amoebocytes, coral immune cells, and how they react to pathogen and climate stressors. The full text gives the cell responses under each stress. Knowing how coral defenders behave under heat and infection may help predict reef die-offs and protect the species that respond best.
plos-pone-0001911:
Ningli Cheng and co-authors tested how three genes interact in blood cancer in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. One gene, Bcl-2, can slow cell death, which can help cancer grow, yet in some settings it slows cancer instead. A second gene, p27, acts as a brake on cell division, and a third, Bax, pushes cells to die.

The team bred mice lacking the p27 brake, with or without changes in the other two genes, and watched for T-cell lymphoma. As the title states, loss of p27 teamed with Bcl-2 to drive the cancer, but not with Bax. Gene pairs, not single genes, set the risk here.
plos-pone-0002011:
Christian Voigt and co-authors asked why Amazon bats visit mineral licks, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Many tropical animals in Africa, Asia, and South America trek to salt or mineral licks to eat clay or drink clay-rich water. Two ideas compete: the clay adds scarce nutrients to the diet, or it soaks up plant toxins the animals eat.

The team studied bats of the Amazon rainforest that visit such licks. Food or detox: each idea makes unlike predictions about which bats come and when. Settling the question explains a striking habit and what it says about nutrient limits in rainforest food webs.
plos-pone-0002111:
Dennis Hansen, Christopher Kaiser, and Christine Muller applied a classic ecology model to endangered island plants, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The Janzen-Connell model states that plant-specific enemies, such as seed-eating pests, hit offspring hardest close to the mother tree. Most past tests asked how the model explains diversity in rich forests.

The trio turn it to a practical aim: seed dispersal and establishment of endangered plants on oceanic islands. They also discuss ecological analogues, stand-in species that can take the role of extinct seed carriers. Old theory, put to work for conservation on islands that have lost their dispersers.
plos-pone-0002211:
Wook Kim and co-authors checked whether common mitochondrial lineages raise prostate cancer risk in Korean men, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mitochondrial DNA is inherited from the mother and does not shuffle between generations, so its lineages, called haplogroups, are clean markers of ancestry. Some studies had hinted that mitochondrial variation might link to cancers, including prostate cancer.

The team compared haplogroups between patients and healthy men in the Korean population. They found no association between the common lineages and prostate cancer. A solid negative answer still helps, since it tells future studies to look elsewhere for the genetic roots of this cancer.
plos-pone-0002311:
Chris Paffen, Marnix Naber, and Frans Verstraten asked where in the brain a visual flip begins, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In binocular rivalry, the two eyes receive different images at the same spot. Perception alternates: only one image is seen at a time, then it switches. The phenomenon is a clean tool for studying how conscious perception is selected.

The team traced the spatial origin of a perceptual transition, the moment one image gives way to the other. Finding where the switch starts helps decide whether rivalry is settled in early visual areas or by higher decision centers. The answer bears on how the brain resolves any conflicting input.
plos-pone-0002411:
Ross-Ibarra and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Jeffrey Ross-Ibarra, Stephen I. Wright, John Paul Foxe, among others. Its subject is patterns of Polymorphism and Demographic History in Natural Populations of Arabidopsis lyrata. Many of the processes affecting genetic diversity act on local populations.

However, studies of plant nucleotide diversity have largely ignored local sampling. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002511:
Hadjantonakis joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Anna-Katerina Hadjantonakis, Elinor Pisano, Virginia E. Papaioannou, among others. Its subject is tbx6 Regulates Left/Right Patterning in Mouse Embryos through Effects on Nodal Cilia and Perinodal Signaling. The determination of left/right body axis during early embryogenesis sets up a developmental cascade that coordinates the development of the viscera.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002611:
Kitamura led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Masahiro Kitamura, Keisuke Nakashima, Yusuke Kowashi, among others. Its subject is periodontal Tissue Regeneration Using Fibroblast Growth Factor -2: Randomized Controlled Phase II Clinical Trial. The options for medical use of signaling molecules as stimulators of tissue regeneration are currently limited.

Preclinical evidence suggests that fibroblast growth factor (FGF)-2 can promote periodontal regeneration. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002711:
Ellen Kreijveld and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was immunological monitoring of renal transplant recipients to predict acute allograft rejection following the discontinuation of tacrolimus. Authorship is credited in the record to Ellen Kreijveld and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Transplant patients would benefit from reduction of immunosuppression providing that graft rejection is prevented. It goes on to note a further point. We have evaluated a number of immunological markers in blood of patients in whom tacrolimus was withdrawn after renal transplantation. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002811:
Laurent Gillet and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on the murid herpesvirus-4 gL regulates an Entry-Associated conformation change in gH. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Laurent Gillet, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The glycoprotein H (gH)/gL heterodimer is crucial for herpesvirus membrane fusion. It goes on to note a further point. Yet how it functions is not well understood. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002911:
Rufin VanRullen, Alvaro Pascual-Leone and Lorella Battelli studied a motion illusion with brain stimulation in 2008. A steady turning pattern can at times look as if it spins the wrong way. Such reversals have been taken as proof that motion vision works in discrete snapshots, though other accounts exist.

Their tool was repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, brief magnetic pulses to the scalp, aimed at the right parietal lobe. The PLOS ONE paper ties the illusion to the 'when' pathway, the brain route that times events. Vision scientists get a causal test, not just observation, of that link.
plos-pone-0003011:
Debbie Lawlor, Roger Harbord, Nic Timpson and co-authors pooled five studies on C-reactive protein and heart disease in 2008. Whether CRP itself causes coronary heart disease, rather than merely marking it, was unclear. Genetic variants that set CRP levels can act as a natural test of causality.

The combined data covered 4,610 cases among 18,637 participants. Using CRP genotype alongside measured protein tests both the marker and its genes against disease. Published in PLOS ONE, the scale gives the causal question a firmer answer than any single study could. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003111:
Martín Gómez Ravetti and Pablo Moscato built a five-protein signature for predicting Alzheimer's disease in 2008. Alzheimer's is a progressive brain disease with a huge cost in human lives. Its impact is a growing concern for governments of developing countries too, as elderly populations at risk grow larger.

A biomarker signature of five proteins aims to predict the disease from measurable levels, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, a small panel is more practical for clinics than a long list. Any such signature needs outside validation before guiding diagnosis, a caveat the field applies to all early markers.
plos-pone-0003211:
Joanne S. Allard, Leonie K. Heilbronn, Carolina Smith and colleagues test calorie restriction signals in cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Calorie restriction produces several health benefits and increases lifespan in many species. Studies suggest alternate-day fasting and exercise can also provide these benefits. Whether restriction extends lifespan in humans was not known, and a direct investigation takes decades.

The team treat cells in vitro with serum collected from humans on calorie restricted diets and measure indicators of longevity. Readers get a shortcut test of whether diet changes the blood in ways cells can sense. Cell responses can hint at mechanisms long before lifespan data exist.
plos-pone-0003311: Juan C. Motamayor and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on the Amazonian chocolate tree, Theobroma cacao, the source of cocoa. The title states its subject: how cacao populations differ by place and by genetics across their home region. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so this record states no specific findings.
plos-pone-0003411:
Atsushi Honma, Koh-ichi Takakura, and Takayoshi Nishida modeled a trick of nature in this 2008 paper. In Batesian mimicry, a harmless species copies the warning look of a harmful one. Predators that learn the warning leave both species alone. The authors asked when smart hunting by predators helps this trick persist.

Their model used predators that forage in the most rewarding way. Such predators can favor the mimic sharing the model's protection. The mimic gains safety without paying the cost of being harmful. The work clarifies when copying a warning signal pays off in nature.
plos-pone-0003511:
William J. Tyler and co-authors stimulated brain circuits with sound in this 2008 study. Most brain stimulation uses implanted electrodes or light devices. Both routes are somewhat invasive for patients and animals. Ultrasound can pass through tissue without surgery.

Low-intensity, low-frequency ultrasound was used to excite neuronal circuits remotely. The sound reached its targets from outside the body. Such control yields large experimental and therapeutic power. The work opened a noninvasive path for brain research and care. Sound-based control would also spare patients the risks of brain surgery. It needs no implants and no drugs to work.
plos-pone-0003611:
ZhongQiang Chen, Omar S. Harb, and David S. Roos hunted parasite invasion proteins by computer in this 2008 paper. Apicomplexan parasites include Toxoplasma gondii and the malaria parasite. They invade host cells using specialized secretory organelles. Those small organs, like micronemes and rhoptries, release key invasion molecules.

The team's in silico screen predicted proteins for those organelles. They then validated hits in living Toxoplasma gondii. Computer prediction plus cell tests pulls hidden machinery into view. Secreted proteins are prime targets for drugs and vaccines. These parasites infect billions of people and farm animals across the world. The drugs against them are few, old, and often harsh on the patients who need them most of all.
plos-pone-0003711:
Lina S. V. Roth, Anna Balkenius, and Almut Kelber published this animal vision study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Horses are active by day and night, and they have some of the largest eyes of any land animal. The authors asked whether those eyes are sensitive enough to see colors in dim light.

They measured the absolute threshold of color vision in horses through behavioral trials. The tests find the faintest light at which colors can still be told apart. The result maps what the night world looks like to one of humanity's oldest working partners.
plos-pone-0003811:
Christina Nilsson, Anna Skoglund, Anthony P. Moran, and colleagues published this bacteria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Helicobacter pylori settles in the stomach lining of half the world's people and stays for life. It is one of the most genetically diverse bacteria known, with new variants arising inside each host.

The team characterized single colonies to watch lipopolysaccharide diversity emerge within communities. Genetic changes in fucosyltransferase enzymes, which add sugars to the surface coat, drove the variety. The shifting surface sugars help this persistent colonizer stay ahead of the immune system.
plos-pone-0003911:
Carlos Prieto, Alberto Risueño, Celia Fontanillo, and co-authors built a map of human genes that switch on together in 2008. Microarray studies often hunt for such coexpression patterns across the genome. Most large studies, though, had not centered on human tissue samples. The team set out to build a network from human data.

Their PLOS ONE article draws on gene activity profiles from many human tissues. From them, they derived a network they judged trustworthy. Genes that rise and fall together often share jobs in the body. A solid human map helps researchers guess what unstudied genes do.
plos-pone-0004011:
Marco Canepari and Kaspar E. Vogt studied calcium signals in cerebellar neurons in 2008. Parallel fibers contact Purkinje neurons across long stretches of the cerebellum. Those contacts can trigger local calcium spikes in the branches. Whether such spikes cause lasting synaptic change was the question.

Their PLOS ONE article links dendritic spikes to a form of long-term potentiation. They report spikes saturate the cell's own calcium buffer. Freed calcium then helps set the lasting change. The work decodes how spatial patterns in fibers become stored signals. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004111:
Alexandra P. Rose presented an automated way to watch tree swallow nests in 2009. Studying how parents provision chicks has been limited by observation costs. Human watchers cannot cover whole days or long nestling periods. Attendance data therefore stayed patchy for many species.

Her PLOS ONE article describes automated monitoring of nest attendance. The method records visits across full days without a watcher present. With it, she measured time and individual variation in provisioning. Better data sharpen studies of how parents divide feeding work. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004211:
Jun Hayakawa and colleagues published this gene therapy study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The team had earlier reported on transplantation in two HIV-positive recipients, one of whom received retrovirus-modified blood stem cells meant to confer resistance to HIV. A key safety question for such therapy is where the retrovirus lands in the genome.

Here they report a long-term analysis of those retroviral integration sites in the treated patient. Tracking integration sites over years shows whether inserted genes stay quiet or disturb their neighbours. The follow-up is the kind of patient safety evidence gene therapy must produce.
plos-pone-0004311:
Juan Fargallo and colleagues published this ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most ideas about how predators limit small mammal numbers come from northern, boreal ecosystems. There, many predators specialise on voles, and predator-prey systems are simpler than in the south.

The team studied kestrels and their prey in a Mediterranean region instead. They weighed the effects of generalist predation and climatic factors on the dynamics between the falcons and their food. Their work tests whether northern rules about predators and prey hold under a Mediterranean sun. The Mediterranean setting is the point: warmer, drier, and more varied.
plos-pone-0004411:
Two proteins that crosslink actin may work better together. Osigwe Esue, Yiider Tseng, and Denis Wirtz test that idea in this 2009 PLOS ONE article. The close proximity of different crosslinking proteins inside cells suggests they cooperate to organize actin structures.

Actin networks drive cell adhesion, motility, and division. The authors hypothesize that alpha-actinin and filamin cooperatively enhance the stiffness of actin filament networks. Their title confirms that cooperative effect. Stiffer networks help explain how cells hold shape and generate force during movement. Cell adhesion and division rely on such networks, so cooperative stiffness has broad reach.
plos-pone-0004511:
A bacterial enzyme that attacks coral and its inner partners is described by Meir Sussman, Jos Mieog, Jason Doyle, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Coral diseases are a growing threat to reefs worldwide. Of the coral diseases whose culprits are known, most are caused by members of the Vibrio family of bacteria.

The enzyme is a zinc-metalloprotease made by a Vibrio. The team shows it causes photoinactivation of the coral's endosymbionts, the algae that live inside coral tissue and feed it. It also causes lesions in the coral tissue itself. Losing its algae starves and bleaches a coral. Naming the weapon helps explain how these bacteria wound reefs, and what might be blocked to protect them.
plos-pone-0004611:
Family trees of species only look like other branching patterns, and the likeness can mislead, warns Cristian Altaba in PLOS ONE in 2009. The superficial resemblance of phylogenetic trees to river networks, lightning, or family pedigrees invites searches for macroevolutionary patterns. Recent meta-analyses had reported finding regularities in the branching of trees, as if universal scaling laws governed them.

Altaba argues such trees are just statistical inferences of particular historical events. The artifacts, he contends, are universal, but they affect the branching of the trees themselves: the patterns come from how trees are built, not from a law of nature. The paper is a methodological caution for evolutionary biology, separating real history from mathematical mirage.
plos-pone-0004711:
Yann Tremblay, Patrick Robinson, and Daniel Costa offered a simpler way to clean animal tracking data, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Tracking wild animals is a fast growing field in ecology. Simple speed filters alone do not fix poor location points, yet past fixes were often complex and slow to run.

The team sought a lean method that still improves location estimates. Their approach aims to be easy to use on large tracking sets. Cleaner tracks mean truer maps of where animals feed, breed, and travel. That helps protect species and the places they need most. Future studies can use these results to refine both methods and theory.
plos-pone-0004811:
Rupesh Kotecha and colleagues modeled developmental patterns of auditory evoked magnetic fields in children, in PLOS ONE in 2009. As magnetoencephalography is of increasing utility in assessment of deficits and delays in pediatric brain disorders, fully knowledge working brain growth in children becomes imperative. The study was designed to characterize how auditory responses mature across childhood using noninvasive recordings.

Models describe the timing and strength changes with age. Normative trajectories help clinicians spot abnormal growth. Hearing and language disorders may be detected earlier. The work supports pediatric brain mapping. Such evidence helps the field move from broad claims toward tested detail. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004911:
Kushagra Bansal and colleagues showed PIM2 induced COX-2 and MMP-9 output in macrophages requires PI3K and Notch1, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Activation of inflammatory responses during granuloma formation upon mycobacterial infection is linked with tissue remodeling and extracellular matrix breakdown. Cyclooxygenase and metalloproteinase induction in macrophages was traced to kinase PIM2 acting through PI3K and Notch signaling pathways during tuberculosis related swelling.

A defined cascade drives tissue damaging enzymes. Interrupting nodes could limit lung destruction. Granulomas protect but also harm hosts. Signaling maps suggest combination interventions. Follow up work can check whether the same pattern appears in other settings. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0005011:
CDKN1C is a brake gene. Its protein, p57, stops cells from dividing out of control. Cancers often silence this gene. Xiaojing Yang and colleagues studied how in breast cancer cells. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They found the protein EZH2 directly targets CDKN1C.

EZH2 represses the gene mainly through its own action. Several silencing mechanisms back it up at once. DNA methylation is one of them. The finding names a key lock on a tumor suppressor. Picking that lock could restore the brake. The study also shows how layered cancer's silencing can be. One gene may need several locks released before it speaks again.
plos-pone-0005111:
Common lizards wear orange and yellow colors. The pigments are carotenoids, also used in immune defense. Patrick Fitze and colleagues linked those colors to stress. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. Under chronic stress, carotenoid colors often fade. The mechanisms behind the fading were largely unknown.

The lizards' colors reflected their stress response. Color change tracked the body's inner state. A lizard's paint job advertises its condition. Rivals and mates can read that advertisement. The study connects color to physiology in a wild reptile. It helps explain why honest signals stay honest. Faking bright colors requires the pigments stress consumes. The work joins a wider story about animal signals.
plos-pone-0005211:
Shigella bacteria cause severe gut disease by forcing their way into human cells. They do this by engaging receptors and signaling proteins on the cell surface. Vepachedu and colleagues found in PLOS ONE in 2009 that a host protein called Unc119 works against that invasion.

Unc119 is an adaptor that interacts with receptors and with tyrosine kinases inside the cell. The study showed it protects against Shigella infection by holding back the Abl family of kinases. Blocking those kinases keeps the entry route shut, revealing a natural guard that drugs might learn to copy.
plos-pone-0005311:
Epithelial ovarian cancer is deadly in part because it is found late. MicroRNAs, small regulatory RNAs, have shown promise as blood markers for early cancer detection. Wyman and colleagues cataloged those RNAs in ovarian tumors in PLOS ONE in 2009 using next-generation sequencing.

Sequencing small RNA libraries from tumors gives a full repertoire of which microRNAs are present and how much. That catalog is a hunting ground for marker candidates. A blood test built on such markers could catch this cancer while treatment still has its best chance. A blood test for this cancer would be a prize, since the disease is most often found late. When cure is rare, and a small RNA mark could be read from a simple blood draw.
plos-pone-0005411:
The human arm can reach the same target in many postures, since it has more joints than the task strictly needs. How the motor system uses that redundancy is a fundamental question. Trumbower and colleagues tested posture choice and stiffness in PLOS ONE in 2009.

People used self-selected postures to regulate stiffness across multiple joints during unconstrained tasks. Choosing a posture, in other words, is also choosing how rigid the arm will be. That insight helps design rehabilitation and prosthetics that work with the body's own strategy. How stiff we hold an arm is a choice the brain makes in a flash,. This work shows that the pose we pick is part of how that choice is made and held through a task.
plos-pone-0005511:
Ofer Ben-Tzvi and colleagues studied how young reef fish choose a home in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Young damselfish must pick a coral spot that gives food and safety from hunters. Adult fish of their own kind can attract settlers, but adults can also attack them.

The team tested how adult aggression changes where settlers choose to live. Young fish weighed the pull of adult company against the risk of being chased. Their choices show that settling is not just about the coral itself, but about the neighbours already there. Choices made in these first days often decide whether a young fish lives long enough to breed.
plos-pone-0005611:
Pierre Massion and co-authors tested early gene changes as a lung cancer warning in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Lung cancer grows through stages, and the tissue around a tumour often carries field changes that precede it. Extra copies of certain genes are among those early changes.

The team asked whether gains at six set DNA sites in preinvasive lesions mark people at high risk. A marker found before cancer forms could focus screening on those who need it most. Early warning is vital in a cancer usually caught late. Preinvasive lesions are sometimes found during scans for other problems, which makes a risk marker for them practical to use.
plos-pone-0005711:
Alexander Lange and co-authors explored in 2009 how a gene called Sox17 can restart young, flexible behavior in lung lining cells. Sox17 is needed to form the gut, blood vessels, and early blood stem cells. Switching it on in mature airway cells changes their fate.

The team found Sox17 pushes these cells to divide and turns down a growth-limiting signal path, TGF-beta through Smad3. Together those effects make adult cells act more like starter cells. The trick could one day help repair damaged airways. It also warns that the same switch, left on, might feed tumors.
plos-pone-0005811:
Xue-Qin Chen and co-authors reported in 2009 that a class of compounds can open a potassium channel linked to nerve protection. The compounds, arylbenzazepines, include one known to protect neurons in lab and animal tests. Part of that protection was credited to dopamine receptor action.

The team showed these compounds also strongly modulate the delayed rectifier potassium channel. Opening that channel can calm overexcited neurons and limit damage. This second mechanism may explain much of the protection seen. It points drug design toward the channel for stroke and degeneration research.
plos-pone-0005911:
Enrique Espinosa and co-authors tested in 2009 whether commercial gene-profile tests still work on the preserved samples hospitals actually keep. Gene profiling can sharpen prognosis in early breast cancer, but the technology is not widely available. The tests they checked were built for fresh tissue.

Using quantitative PCR on paraffin-embedded samples from past patients, they compared three known profiles, including the seventy-gene signature and the recurrence score. Performance on stored tissue decides whether the tests can be offered widely. Retrospective checks like this are how lab advances become clinic routine.
plos-pone-0006011:
Early Alzheimer's disease may begin at the synapse, the tiny gap where brain cells talk. Francesco Roselli, Peter Hutzler, Yvonne Wegerich and colleagues studied that site in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper looks at Shank and Homer, scaffold proteins that hold the receiving side of a synapse together. It also looks at soluble beta-amyloid, the protein that piles up in Alzheimer's.

The amyloid pulls those scaffold clusters apart, the title reports, through two separate paths that both run via NMDA receptors. A scaffold in pieces means a synapse that cannot hold its signal. The finding maps one early step of the disease and marks the pathways involved as possible places for a drug to step in.
plos-pone-0006111:
A chick walks within hours of hatching, a skill it must somehow prepare in advance. Young Ryu and Nina Bradley found the practice sessions in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies chick embryos in the final week inside the egg, which make distinct repetitive limb movements, and maps the leg muscle patterns those movements build for stepping.

Locomotor behavior begins in the egg, the title declares: the embryo is not idle, but rehearsing. Muscle patterns laid down before hatching explain the newborn's ready skill. The work shows development at its most economical, where a behavior is assembled and tuned before it is ever used in the world.
plos-pone-0006211:
Short sleep and obesity travel together in people, and two ideas try to explain why. Susan Harbison and Amita Sehgal tested one idea in fruit flies in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Perhaps genes that shorten sleep also change how the body stores energy, making the two traits fellow travellers.

Flies kept on long-term partial sleep loss showed no change in their energy stores, as the title states. Fat and sugar reserves stayed level despite the lost rest. The result weakens one simple account of the sleep-weight link in this model. It pushes the search toward feeding behaviour and other pathways instead.
plos-pone-0006311:
Brain steroids can act fast by tuning ion channels directly, not just by switching genes. Toru Kobayashi, Kazuo Washiyama, and Kazutaka Ikeda studied pregnenolone sulfate in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Neurosteroids are known to modulate several receptors and channels involved in brain signalling.

Pregnenolone sulfate potentiates Kir2.3, a potassium channel that lets potassium flow inward most easily, the team reports. Strengthening that channel steadies electrical activity in cells that carry it. The detail adds to the map of non-hormonal steroid actions. Such actions are targets for drugs affecting mood and excitability.
plos-pone-0006411:
Chronic heart failure involves a storm of inflammatory signals as well as a weak pump. Stephan von Haehling and colleagues studied leukocyte redistribution in heart failure patients in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Changes in cellular immunity had not been widely studied, and the impact of standard medication was uncertain.

The team investigated whether white blood cell redistribution occurs and whether beta blockers affect it. Beta blockers are standard heart failure drugs with possible immune side effects. Tracking immune cells may refine how treatment response is judged. The work widens heart failure care beyond the heart itself.
plos-pone-0006511:
Ivan Gorlov, Gary Gallick, Olga Gorlova, and colleagues compared two big gene-hunting methods in PLOS ONE in 2009.
