Genome-wide association studies and gene-expression profiling are two major technological breakthroughs. Both allow hypothesis-free identification of genes tied to disease. The authors ask whether the two methods give consistent results.

If association hits and expression changes point to the same genes, confidence in both rises. Where they disagree, each method's blind spots show. The comparison helps researchers decide how to combine the tools. It is a check on the machinery of modern genetics, using the field's own data.
plos-pone-0006611:
Hyeog Kang, Jae-Won Jung, Myung Kim, and colleagues studied regulation of a longevity-linked enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2009. SIRT1 is an NAD-dependent deacetylase that protects cells from stress-induced apoptosis. Its orthologues delay aging in lower eukaryotes. The team examined the kinase CK2 as a regulator of SIRT1.

Their title reports CK2 is the regulator of SIRT1 substrate-binding affinity, deacetylase activity, and cellular response to DNA damage. One kinase tunes several properties of the enzyme. That tuning could decide how cells survive genotoxic stress. SIRT1 regulation is a busy area for aging and cancer research.
plos-pone-0006711:
Elisha D. O. Roberson and Jonathan Pevsner created a way to picture shared DNA regions in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genotyping reads single-letter differences called SNPs across the genome. A basic goal is to see which stretches two people share. Shared stretches reveal relatedness, including relationships nobody expected. They also record where chromosomes crossed over during meiosis.

The authors built visualization tools for high-density SNP data. Their displays make long shared regions easy to spot. Meiotic recombination events become visible as switches between shared patterns. Clear pictures help geneticists check family links and mapping results. They also help catch sample mix-ups before they corrupt a study.
plos-pone-0006811:
Katharina Dickhaut and her team raised tumor-linked immune replies in live mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. Class II MHC tags show bits of protein to CD4 T cells. A bit must sit on the tag to start a strong reply. Most tags on a cell are already full. Full tags leave no room for new tumor bits.

Their tool is an MHC loading enhancer, shortened to MLE. It helps tumor bits load onto the tags. With more tumor bits on show, T cells struck back harder. A fix for this loading jam could make cancer vaccines work far better. The jam has capped vaccine design for years.
plos-pone-0006911:
Young Min Oh and colleagues predicted and then verified new target genes of a cancer transcription factor in PLOS ONE in 2009. The factor is STAT3, often overactive in human cancers. Identifying its true binding sites is a key step in mapping regulatory networks. Their approach, called STAT-Finder, is motif-based and comparative. It searches DNA sequences for functional binding patterns.

Predicted targets were validated experimentally in cancer cells. Novel STAT3 target genes emerged confirmed. Each target extends the map of what STAT3 controls. That map matters because STAT3 blockers are under development. Knowing downstream genes helps judge what those blockers will do.
plos-pone-0007011:
Catherine Worth, Gunnar Kleinau, and Gerd Krause compared receptor structures in PLOS ONE in 2009. G-protein-coupled receptors are major drug targets in the human body. For years, the only high-resolution structure was bovine rhodopsin. Then several new receptor structures arrived in quick succession, including squid rhodopsin.

The team aligned these structures by sequence and by shape. They asked what the growing set means for computer models of other receptors. Each new structure anchors models that drug designers rely on. Better models should sharpen the search for medicines that act on this huge receptor family.
plos-pone-0007111:
Gabrielle Lui, Olivier Manches, Juliette Angel, and colleagues studied a rare immune cell type in PLOS ONE in 2009. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells release huge amounts of type I interferon when they meet viruses. That alarm role is their fame. How well they present antigens to other immune cells was less clear.

The team showed these cells capture viral antigens from influenza-exposed cells. They then cross-present those antigens to killer T cells. Cross-presentation from a neighbor's debris expands their role. It means these interferon specialists also help launch targeted attacks, a point vaccine designers can use.
plos-pone-0007211:
Geneviève Boily-Larouche, Anne-Laure Iscache, Lynn S. Zijenah, and colleagues examined HIV transmission from mother to child in 2009. Such transmission is the main cause of HIV-1 infection in children worldwide. The authors focus on a receptor called DC-SIGNR, also known as CD209L.

DC-SIGNR is a C-type lectin receptor found in liver and lymph node tissue. Genetic variants can change how it works. The authors report that functional variants in DC-SIGNR are associated with mother-to-child transmission of HIV-1. Their findings may help explain why some exposed infants become infected and others do not.
plos-pone-0007311:
James C. Sullivan, Francis S. Wolenski, Adam M. Reitzel, and colleagues studied an ancient immune regulator in a sea anemone in 2009. NF-kappaB controls genes for innate immunity, development, and stress responses. It is evolutionarily conserved, with a highly conserved DNA-binding region across animals separated by hundreds of millions of years.

The anemone Nematostella vectensis carries two alleles, or versions, of this gene. The authors find both versions widely dispersed in nature. They report the two versions encode proteins with distinct activities. Their work shows functional variety in immunity genes long before vertebrates evolved.
plos-pone-0007411:
Maximiliano J. Jimenez-Dalmaroni, Nengming Xiao, Adam L. Corper, and colleagues studied a fat-sensing protein's role in immunity in 2009. CD36 is a membrane glycoprotein involved in platelet biology, blood vessel growth, and atherosclerosis. Toll-like receptors are among the most important receptors of innate immunity, detecting microbial products to start defensive responses quickly.

The authors study the soluble ectodomain of CD36, its outer part. They report it binds negatively charged diacylglycerol ligands. It also acts as a co-receptor for TLR2. Their PLOS ONE finding links fat transport machinery directly to microbial sensing in immune defense.
plos-pone-0007511:
Galit Tzur and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how the human liver develops. The liver performs hundreds of jobs, from processing food to clearing toxins. Its construction during development is guided by genes switching on and off in sequence. Tiny regulators called microRNAs fine-tune that process. The team profiled both gene activity and microRNA activity across liver development, side by side.

The paired profiles show microRNAs actively steering the building of the liver. Specific small RNAs rise and fall in step with the genes they govern. Those patterns reveal which regulators guide the organ from embryo to full function. A map like this helps researchers grow liver tissue in the lab. It also aids the search for what goes wrong in liver diseases that start early.
plos-pone-0007611:
Bertrand Lell and colleagues published a randomized trial report in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the malaria vaccine candidate RTS,S in children in Gabon. RTS,S combines part of the malaria parasite's circumsporozoite protein with a hepatitis B surface protein. Its effect depends heavily on the adjuvant, the immune-boosting additive mixed with it. Two adjuvant systems, AS01 and AS02, were in development. The trial compared them head to head in children.

The trial assessed both safety and the immune responses each formulation produced. Head-to-head data like this decide which version advances. Children in malaria regions are the vaccine's true audience, so Gabonese children were the right test group. A formulation that is safe and strongly immunogenic there earns the next, larger trial. The study is one of the decision points in the long RTS,S story.
plos-pone-0007711:
Yenny Djuardi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks what shapes the immune signals made by pregnant women and their babies. Early exposure to the environment helps form a child's innate and adaptive immunity. The mother's immune state is part of that environment.

The team measured cytokine production, the chemical messages of immune cells, in mothers and infants. They looked for factors that explain why some pairs matched and others differed. Infection history and local exposures were among the influences studied. Results like these inform care for mothers and newborns in regions with high infection burdens.
plos-pone-0007811:
Daniel Frank and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It surveys the microbes living on urinary catheters in hospital patients. Catheter infections are a leading cause of disease acquired in hospitals. Bacteria form biofilms, slimy shared coats, on the tubes. Those coats protect them from treatment.

Standard culture tests miss many biofilm species. The team used culture-independent methods, reading microbial DNA directly. They mapped the diversity living on Foley catheters. Knowing the full cast of organisms is a first step. It points prevention efforts at the right targets.
plos-pone-0007911:
Shashwath Meda and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines brain network connections during a memory task in schizophrenia. Many scans show abnormal regional activity in patients doing working memory tasks. Few had looked at integration between brain networks.

The authors used independent component analysis to find connected networks. During the encoding phase of working memory, patients showed anomalous connectivity. The fault seems to lie in how networks talk, not just in single spots. That wider view may explain why working memory falters in schizophrenia. It also suggests new targets for treatment research.
plos-pone-0008011:
Juhyun Choi and colleagues traced a shield that guards resting T cells in mice, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Naive T cells wait for years, ready to answer a first infection. All that waiting exposes them to oxidative stress, the slow rust of cell life.

A signal path led by the enzyme Mst1 and the factor FoxO kept those waiting cells safe. When the path failed, stress harmed the cells and thinned the ranks. The work shows how the immune system keeps its reserve force alive, a point of value for vaccines and for aging immune systems.
plos-pone-0008111:
Ana Neves-Costa and colleagues caught a chromatin mover in the act of silencing genes in PLOS ONE in 2009. The mover, Fun30, belongs to a family of enzymes that slide DNA spools to open or close genes. Quiet genome regions, called heterochromatin, keep their genes off by staying tightly packed.

Fun30 helped hold that silence in place. When it was gone, genes in the quiet zones leaked into activity. The finding adds a worker to the crew that guards the genome's quiet wards, a guard duty whose failure can stir disease.
plos-pone-0008211:
Maria E. Teves and colleagues studied how human sperm find the egg in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Sperm can swim toward a chemical signal, a process called chemotaxis. Progesterone is the main steroid released by cells around the egg. Even a tiny gradient of it attracts human sperm. The team set out to explain the molecular mechanism behind that pull.

Knowing the steps inside the sperm could clarify how fertilization begins. It could also reveal why some sperm fail to reach the egg. The work connects a hormone signal to sperm movement. That has value for fertility research and diagnosis.
plos-pone-0008311:
William Lee and colleagues improved a mutation prediction tool in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. New sequencing technology reveals vast numbers of genetic variants. Most variants do nothing, while some change protein function. High-throughput tools must flag the ones most likely to matter. SIFT is one such tool for predicting mutation effects.

Their bi-directional version, Bi-Directional SIFT, predicts a subset of activating mutations. Activating mutations are harder to spot than damaging ones. Catching them matters for cancer and drug research. The improvement helps researchers prioritize variants for laboratory testing.
plos-pone-0008411:
Xuejun Chen and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about how frog embryos take shape. Two proteins in the frog Xenopus are switched on by a growth signal in the young embryo. Both curb how much cells stick to each other through a glue protein named C-cadherin. How cells stick, or fail to stick, helps set the form of the whole body as it grows. The team asked how the two proteins work, both in their jobs and in their touch with each other.

They found the two form a three-part team with the glue protein. That team steers how cells stick and how the form is built. When cells can tune their grip in fine steps, flesh can fold and move in the right way. The work spells out a base step in how an embryo is shaped.
plos-pone-0008511:
Salem Adra and co-authors build a computer model of human skin in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Their model covers the epidermis, the outer layer of skin. It works in three dimensions and at multiple scales at once. A factor called TGF-beta1 plays a crucial role in tissue repair. Lab and animal data on it seem to give a paradox. The model aims to reconcile those conflicting results.

By simulating cells, signals, and tissue structure together, the model shows emergent behavior. Effects at cell level can explain patterns at tissue level. Such models can predict healing outcomes before clinical tests. The work is a step toward virtual trials for skin therapies.
plos-pone-0008611:
Bob Liu and co-authors study a factor in breast tumor growth in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. MMTV-Wnt1 tumors in mice show drastic differences in tumor vasculature. Their blood vessels differ from those of MMTV-Her2 tumors. Those differences had not been formally described. No angiogenic factors had been implicated in the Wnt1 tumor program. The team examine stromal cell-derived factor-1, also called CXCL12. It is a chemokine that recruits immune and vessel cells.

They find CXCL12 contributes to MMTV-Wnt1 tumor growth. It acts in part by involving Gr1 and CD11b positive immune cells. Those recruited cells support the tumor's blood supply and growth. Blocking CXCL12 might slow this tumor type.
plos-pone-0008711:
Mark Genung, Jean-Philippe Lessard, Claire Brown, and colleagues tested whether plant genetic variety lifts whole meadows. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study belongs to community genetics, a young field. Genes inside one common plant can ripple out to insects and other plants. Simple variety effects add up in a plain, expected way. The team wondered if mixtures could do more than that.

They grew plots with one plant genotype or with several mixed. Mixed plots produced more flowers than the parts predicted. They also drew more flower visitors, like bees. Variety inside a species can thus boost pollination for a whole patch.
plos-pone-0008811:
Yong Zhou, John Hancock, and Lenard Lichtenberger studied how a common painkiller scrambles cell membranes. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Indomethacin is an anti-inflammatory drug with many side effects. Its wide range of actions has never fit one simple target. The drug is water-and-fat loving, so it sinks into lipid membranes. Membranes organize much of a cell's signaling geography.

Indomethacin made uniform membranes break into uneven patches. Such heterogeneity could disturb many membrane proteins at once. One membrane effect might thus explain many drug actions. The idea refranes how this old drug should be understood.
plos-pone-0008911:
Emma Perez-Costas, Johanna Gandy, Miguel Melendez-Ferro, and colleagues toured a plentiful brain kinase under two kinds of microscopes. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The kinase, GSK3beta, is abundant throughout the brain. Chemistry tests placed it in several cell compartments at once. Light microscopy alone cannot resolve those tiny compartments. Electron microscopy gives the needed fine view.

Combining both methods mapped the kinase across mouse brain regions. Its locations inside neurons varied by region and compartment. A precise address book helps interpret the kinase's many brain jobs. GSK3beta is implicated in mood disorders and Alzheimer disease, raising the stakes.
plos-pone-0009011:
Jaehoon Chung and co-authors asked why nerve cells need a growth signal that never lets up, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Nerve growth factor, or NGF, turns PC12 cells into neuron-like cells. Only continuous NGF treatment completes that change. Brief pulses of the factor do not finish the job.

The team varied the timing of NGF exposure and tracked the cells' responses. Different steps of the change needed the signal at different times. Some switches had to stay on; others only had to fire once. Timing, not just dose, proved to be part of the instruction the cells read.
plos-pone-0009111:
Sonia Nemolato and co-authors mapped a repair peptide along the gut, comparing babies before and after birth, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Thymosin beta 4 is a small peptide with many jobs in cells. The group's earlier work hinted it helps human salivary glands develop. They now charted it across the gastrointestinal tract.

Staining showed where the peptide appears in foetal gut tissue. Adult gut tissue showed a different pattern of the same peptide. The shift suggests its role changes from building to maintenance. Age maps like this guide hopes of using the peptide in healing.
plos-pone-0009211:
Donia Amrouni and co-authors published this infection study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It uses rats to model sleeping sickness, the disease caused by Trypanosoma brucei parasites. Nitric oxide, a small gas made by cells, can kill these parasites. In infected animals, that killing power fades in both the body and the brain.

The team tracked where and how nitric oxide production changes during infection. They looked at the brain and the rest of the body side by side. They also identified which brain cells switch on the enzyme that makes nitric oxide there. Mapping those changes helps explain how the parasite survives, and why the disease reaches the brain.
plos-pone-0009311:
Tulio de Oliveira, Deenan Pillay, and Robert Gifford published this HIV family tree study in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV-1 comes in distinct subtypes that dominate different regions. Subtype C rules southern and eastern Africa. Over two decades it also spread fast through parts of South America, far from its home ground.

The team used virus family trees to trace how subtype C reached South America. Their analysis links the South American epidemic to the United Kingdom. A travel and migration bridge, rather than a direct jump from Africa, explains the route. Such detective work shows how epidemics hitchhike along human connections between continents.
plos-pone-0009411:
Ramon Ferrer-i-Cancho and Brita Elvevåg published this language study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Zipf's law is a famous pattern in word use. The most common word in a text appears about twice as often as the second, three times the third, and so on. Some argued that even random typing produces the same pattern, making the law trivial.

The authors test that claim directly. They show random texts do not produce the real rank distribution that Zipf described. The law therefore says something true about language, not just about counting. That defense keeps Zipf's law useful for linguistics and for spotting structure in other ranked data.
plos-pone-0009511:
Giovanni Boniolo, Marcello D'Agostino, and Pier Paolo Di Fiore proposed a formal language for biology in PLOS ONE in 2010. Research results are normally written in plain prose. Prose is rich, but it is too loose for computers to use directly. Their language, called Zsyntax, turns biological claims into exact, machine readable statements. It rests on a non standard logic chosen for that task.

The authors show how facts about molecules and cells can be written in the system. Once written so, computers could mine texts and even make forecasts. The aim is to make the vast biology literature usable by machines. That would help researchers find links no reader could hold in mind.
plos-pone-0009611:
Collin Diedrich and co-authors studied two infections together in monkeys in PLOS ONE in 2010. People with HIV face a high risk that quiet tuberculosis will wake and cause disease. That risk is high even when their CD4 cell counts look sound. The team used monkeys infected with SIV, the monkey form of HIV, that also carried latent tuberculosis. They tracked what changed before the tuberculosis woke.

Early loss of T cells in the blood, not the amount of virus, went with reactivation. That shifts attention from viral load to a specific immune loss. Clinics might watch that loss as a warning sign. The work sharpens the search for what tips latent tuberculosis into active disease.
plos-pone-0009711:
With age, the lens of the eye yellows and clouds, a change known as cataract. Line Kessel and colleagues tested a laser method to clear that clouding without surgery. Their report appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The method uses femtosecond laser pulses, flashes of light lasting a tiny fraction of a second. The pulses break down yellowed proteins inside the lens, a process called photolysis. Clearing the lens this way could one day spare patients an operation. The study tests whether the approach works on human lenses. Cataract surgery is common, but it still carries risks.
plos-pone-0009911:
The cornea, the clear front window of the eye, faces constant stress from light and air. Akihiro Higuchi and colleagues studied a protein that guards it against oxidative stress. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The cornea has no blood supply of its own.

Oxidative stress is damage from reactive oxygen molecules. The guard is selenoprotein P, a protein that carries the element selenium. The team showed it controls oxidative stress in the cornea. Keeping that shield strong may protect sight as eyes age. The study stayed with the eye's front surface.
plos-pone-0010011:
Yoshihiro Nakajima, Tomomi Yamazaki, Shigeaki Nishii, and co-workers built a brighter light tool for biology in PLOS ONE in 2010. They engineered an enhanced form of beetle luciferase, the enzyme that makes living things glow. Their green-emitting version, called ELuc, was meant for imaging inside living cells and animals.

In mammalian cells, ELuc gave a signal more than ten times stronger than firefly luciferase, the standard tool. A stronger, sharper signal means clearer pictures at higher resolution with less strain on samples. The probe could help track tumors, infections, and gene activity in living tissue over time.
plos-pone-0010211:
The authors were Paul Macey, Mary Woo, Rajesh Kumar, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study enrolled people newly diagnosed with obstructive sleep apnea. In apnea, breathing stops briefly many times during sleep. It affects at least ten percent of people and raises illness and death rates, yet its links to mood symptoms were unclear.

Earlier studies mixed in many other health problems, muddying the picture. In these newly diagnosed patients, the team related apnea severity to sleep, depression, and anxiety symptoms. Cleaner links can guide which symptoms doctors should expect and treat first.
plos-pone-0010311:
The authors were Sandrine Reigadas, Guerric Anies, Bernard Masquelier, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tracked HIV drug resistance in three patients. Raltegravir blocks HIV integrase, the enzyme that inserts viral DNA into human DNA. Resistance arises through mutations in that enzyme, and one common mutation was being replaced by changes at position 143 in these patients.

The team cloned and analyzed the Y143C and Y143R variants. They showed these mutations form an alternative resistance pathway and change enzyme function. Knowing escape routes helps doctors sequence HIV drugs after a first failure.
plos-pone-0010411:
Patrice Tchendjou and colleagues judged how well drug regimens stop mothers passing HIV to babies in Cameroon, for PLOS ONE in 2010. Since 2004, Cameroon had offered stronger multi-drug plans in routine public clinics. Options ranged from full therapy to short dual-drug courses. The team checked how well these worked in real services, not trial settings. Babies were assessed in early weeks and again later.

Real-world checks matter because clinics face stock gaps and missed visits. A regimen that works in trials may slip in routine care. Their results help officials choose which plans to expand. Preventing infection at birth spares a child lifelong treatment. This study measures how close routine practice comes to that goal.
plos-pone-0010511:
John Rowland and co-workers hunted for parts that help a small water microbe adjust to heat, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The microbe makes food from sunlight, like a plant does. One part of that sun-catching gear is the most heat-sensitive piece of all. How well the gear adapts to warmth may decide if such microbes thrive as the world warms. The team read gene activity as the cells got used to heat.

They looked for genes and proteins tied to that adjustment. Finding the parts involved explains how some microbes shrug off heat that kills others. Those same parts might one day be bred into crops or fuel-making strains. Nearly all life runs on food made from sunlight, so its heat limits matter widely. The study gives later work a list of parts to test one by one.
plos-pone-0010611:
Jane Yuxia Qin and colleagues compared gene switches used in labs every day, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Promoters are DNA stretches that turn a gene on. Some stay on all the time, while others respond to a drug dose.

The team tested eight always-on promoters side by side in mammal and fly systems. They also measured a switch turned on by doxycycline. Strength and steadiness varied more than most users assume. Publishing the full comparison saves labs from picking a switch by habit. The right choice can make or break a gene experiment.
plos-pone-0010711:
Behzad Imanian, Jean-François Pombert, and Patrick Keeling sequenced chloroplast genomes from two odd algae, in PLOS ONE in 2010. These plankton, nicknamed dinotoms, carry a whole diatom cell inside them. That inner tenant still runs its own chloroplasts, so sunlight capture happens three hosts deep.

The full chloroplast sequences came from Durinskia baltica and Kryptoperidinium foliaceum. Comparing them showed how reduced and reshaped the tenant's genome has become. Each layer of this nesting doll tells the same story: partners kept only what the partnership needs. Few cases show symbiosis turning into true cell structure so clearly.
plos-pone-0010811:
Christel Steen and colleagues measured energy enzyme activity in the brains of multiple sclerosis patients, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Brain scans had shown raised energy stores in white matter that looks normal in MS. The raised stores made no sense without knowing the enzyme that uses them. Creatine kinase B is that enzyme, moving energy where neurons need it.

In normal-appearing white matter, the enzyme's activity was reduced. Low activity with high stores fits a system backing up, not speeding up. Energy failure may therefore be part of MS damage even where tissue looks intact. Treatments that protect energy handling could complement the immune drugs that dominate MS care.
plos-pone-0010911:
Sanyi Tang, Yanni Xiao, Youping Yang and co-authors published this pandemic modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2010. When the 2009 H1N1 flu emerged, mainland China responded with unusually strict community measures, including Fengxiao, the sealing and control of affected communities and schools. Whether those measures actually slowed the virus was an open question with big policy stakes.

Using early lab-confirmed cases from Shaanxi province, the authors ran statistical simulations to estimate how fast the virus reproduced under the interventions. They also looked ahead to the Spring Festival, when nationwide travel would surge and test any gains. Tang and colleagues provide a quantitative check on drastic community controls. Their estimates can guide officials weighing school closures and movement limits in a future outbreak, especially around mass travel seasons.
plos-pone-0011011:
Mathieu Dalvai and Kerstin Bystricky published this breast cancer cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Antiestrogen drugs such as tamoxifen treat hormone-driven breast tumors and also freeze cells in one stage of the division cycle. The authors turned the question around: does the cycle stage itself change how strongly estrogen-driven genes are expressed?

In estrogen-responsive MCF-7 cells, the receptor gene and its downstream targets varied as much as threefold across cycle phases. The hormone-free culture conditions normally used in such experiments also trap cells in the phase where several target genes peak, confounding measurements. Adding antiestrogens and cycle effects together produced stronger, combined control of growth and gene expression. Dalvai and Bystricky warn that hormone experiments ignoring the cell cycle can misread drug action.
plos-pone-0011111:
Gutte, Oxbol, Kristoffersen and colleagues used rats to study lung clots in PLOS ONE in 2010. A clot that blocks lung vessels strains the heart at once. The team measured three heart related genes in rat hearts during such an event.

Those genes code for signals the heart makes under stretch and stress. Tracking how their activity changes shows the heart's first response to a lung clot. Such signals could become quick blood markers in emergency care. Fast markers would help doctors judge strain and choose treatment sooner for a dangerous and sudden illness.
plos-pone-0011211:
Kennedy, Katsuta, Jung and colleagues transplanted human insulin cells into mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. Pancreatic beta cells, which make insulin, face great stress when moved to a new body. The team looked at a protective response cells use to handle misfolded proteins after such a move.

Human cells switched that protective response on after transplant, helping them cope with the stress. Supporting this response could improve the survival of transplanted cells. Better islet transplants would move a lasting treatment for diabetes closer. The study shows graft stress is not just damage; it triggers defenses worth boosting.
plos-pone-0011311:
Nowak, Arredouani, Tun-Kyi and colleagues rescued immune cells in prostate tumors for PLOS ONE in 2010. A class of immune sentinels, NKT cells, should attack tumors but were poorly activated by prostate tumor cells. The team tested a pairing of an immune signal and a fat based activator to fix that fault.

The pairing corrected the defective activation in their experiments. Recruiting NKT cells back into the fight is a goal of cancer immunotherapy. A defined rescue recipe can be tested for wider use. It shows tumor immune faults may be reversible, not fixed, which widens treatment options.
plos-pone-0011411:
Anna Nilsson and colleagues demonstrated in 2010 that imaging mass spectrometry can map unlabeled drugs inside tissue in fine detail. Drug makers need to know where a drug goes within an organ, which tiny compartments it reaches, and in what amounts. Standard readouts blur those details, leaving guesses about why a drug works or causes side effects in one spot.

Their method scans tissue slice by slice and builds a high-resolution map of the drug itself, with no chemical label attached to distort its travel. Labels can change how a drug moves, so reading the drug directly is a real gain. Developers can now check whether a compound reaches the exact compartment where disease sits. The technique should sharpen dosing choices and help explain failures where a good drug never reached its target.
plos-pone-0011511:
Sandhya Marathe, Seemun Ray, and Dipshikha Chakravortty brought unwelcome news in 2010 about turmeric's celebrated compound. Curcumin is widely sold as a health booster with anti-inflammatory claims. The team tested it in mice infected with Salmonella Typhimurium, the gut germ behind much food poisoning, expecting, if anything, protection.

Instead, curcumin increased the germ's pathogenicity in the mouse model, making the infection worse rather than better. A popular supplement harming the host during a common infection is a warning that natural does not mean safe. Dose and context decide what a compound does, and an inflamed, infected gut is a different context from a healthy one. The study does not damn turmeric as food, but it argues that concentrated supplements deserve the same safety testing as drugs, especially during illness.
plos-pone-0011611:
Ville-Pekka Eronen and co-authors built a new way to score how genes interact, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The effect of one gene often depends on which other genes are present, a pattern called epistasis. Large screens now measure fitness for thousands of gene pairs, but reading clear signals from such huge tables is difficult.

Their method breaks the large fitness tables into simpler parts to score helpful and harmful interactions. Applied across the genome, it turns raw screen data into a clearer map of genetic teamwork and conflict. Other researchers can use the approach to find gene pairs that matter for health and disease.
plos-pone-0011711:
Tim Huijts, Jessica Perkins and Subramanian studied politics and self-rated health across Europe, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Earlier work had linked personal political beliefs to health, and separately linked countries' overall politics to health. The two levels, individual ideology and national regime, had never been examined together in one analysis.

Using a multilevel approach, the authors weighed both levels at once in European data. Their analysis shows how personal views and the political system around a person each relate to how healthy people say they feel. The findings suggest governance reaches into everyday wellbeing.
plos-pone-0011811:
Camila Romano and co-authors studied the dengue virus behind Brazil's 2010 outbreak, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dengue types one, two and three had caused yearly outbreaks in Brazil. The study reports the return of type two on the coast of São Paulo State that year.

The team read part of the envelope gene from samples taken from dengue fever patients during the outbreak. Comparing those reads yields fresh insight into which virus line came back and how it links to past strains. Such portraits help health teams judge how a returning type may behave.
plos-pone-0011911:
John Gill and co-workers used mice in 2010 to separate what hormones do, and do not do, to a puberty signal in the brain. Kisspeptin is a strong trigger for the hormone chain that starts reproduction, and it is widely proposed as a central controller of puberty's timing. Two distinct kisspeptin cell groups exist in mice, arranged differently in males and females.

The team studied mice lacking GnRH, the hormone kisspeptin normally drives, to see which developmental changes in kisspeptin need reproductive hormones and which happen without them. Splitting the two contributions shows that part of the puberty program runs on its own schedule. That helps explain how puberty can go wrong in more than one way.
plos-pone-0012011:
Amanda Vang and co-workers showed in 2010 that an enzyme called PDE8 helps effector T cells stick and multiply at speed. Effector T cells must switch off a braking signal carried by cAMP before they can act, and enzymes of the PDE family clear that signal. PDE4 was known to matter; PDE8 is induced when T cells activate.

The team found PDE8 regulating the rapid adhesion and proliferation of these effector cells, acting independently of ICER, a repressor in the same signaling web. Two brakes working separately means blocking one may not be enough in immune therapy. The result refines the map of how T cells time their first fast moves in an immune response.
plos-pone-0012111:
Richard Bergholz, Thomas Staks, and Klaus Rüther ran a controlled trial of a brain drug's effect on vision, reported in PLOS ONE in 2010. The drug blocks a common type of signal receptor in the brain and had been studied as a way to protect brain tissue after stroke. During early human trials, people who took it said their sight seemed altered, which raised a safety question worth testing directly.

Healthy volunteers received the drug or a dummy treatment, and their vision was checked in detail. Careful trials like this separate real side effects from chance complaints. Knowing exactly how a stroke drug affects sight helps doctors judge whether its possible benefits are worth the risks it carries.
plos-pone-0012211:
Manu Vanaerschot, Ilse Maes, Meriem Ouakad, and co-authors compared strains of a deadly parasite in PLOS ONE in 2010. Leishmania donovani causes visceral leishmaniasis, a wasting disease spread by sandfly bites that kills if untreated. The parasite must survive inside both the fly and the human host, two hostile settings that demand different tricks, including a distinctive defense against chemical attack.

The team linked how clinical strains survive in lab tests with how they survive in hosts. Strains that handle stress in a dish may be the ones that thrive in people, which would let labs predict dangerous strains cheaply. It also narrows the hunt for the parasite's survival secrets.
plos-pone-0012311:
Johannes von Burstin, Maximilian Reichert, Melanie Wescott, and co-authors studied a master pancreas protein's control of a duct marker, in PLOS ONE in 2010. PDX-1 orchestrates the pancreas's development and adult work, keeping early progenitor cells alive and guiding their choices. Keratin 19 marks the duct cells of the pancreas, and how PDX-1 controls it was the team's question.

They show PDX-1 regulates the keratin gene both by binding DNA directly and by ordering the destruction of another regulator, MEIS1. Layered control like this makes cell identity stable once chosen. Since pancreatic duct cells are the origin of the commonest pancreatic cancer, every detail of their control program has a second audience in oncology.
plos-pone-0012411:
Carl Yeoman, Suleyman Yildirim, Susan Thomas and colleagues compared genomes of Gardnerella vaginalis strains in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. This bacterium is common in the vagina and is strongly tied to bacterial vaginosis, a widespread condition. Yet the species name covers strains that may behave very differently, some harmless and some harmful.

Genome comparisons revealed wide gaps between strains in what they can eat and in tools linked to harming the host. Treating all Gardnerella as one threat is therefore too simple. Strain-level knowledge could lead to tests that tell risky colonization from normal flora, sparing many women needless treatment.
plos-pone-0012511:
Carsten Kuenne, Sonja Voget, Jordan Pischimarov and colleagues sequenced plasmids across the Listeria genus, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Plasmids are small DNA circles that bacteria trade, often carrying genes for survival in harsh places or for resisting treatment. Listeria includes Listeria monocytogenes, a foodborne killer, so its plasmid pool is worth mapping.

The team sequenced four plasmids, including two new ones from a monocytogenes strain type, and compared them across species. The comparisons show which traits travel between strains. Tracking mobile DNA helps food safety officials predict how a harmless environmental strain could pick up dangerous traits.
plos-pone-0012611:
Sheng, Gheytanchi and Aziz-Zadeh scanned the brains of people with psychopathic traits at rest. At rest, a set of regions called the default network stays active, then quiets when a task begins. Parts of that network sit at the back and front of the midline of the brain.

Their 2010 study found that how strongly this network switched off tracked with psychopathy scores. Weak switching off may fit the shallow social and emotional response seen in the condition. Brain scans cannot diagnose a person alone, but such links help map the biology behind these traits.
plos-pone-0012711:
Comin-Anduix, Sazegar, Chodon and co-authors tracked cell signalling in melanoma patients given an immune therapy. The treatment blocks CTLA4, a brake on T cells, using an antibody called tremelimumab. Their 2010 study read signal networks in blood cells from patients with melanoma that had spread.

They charted how the networks shifted once the brake was lifted. Those shifts show which immune paths the drug truly wakes in people, as opposed to mice. Such maps help predict who benefits and which second drugs might pair well.  Patient samples keep the work close to real care.
plos-pone-0299411:
Designing care with patients and clinicians, rather than for them, is called co-design, and Bridget O' Sullivan and colleagues report a workshop method for doing it quickly. Their PLOS One paper describes rapid appraisal discussions used inside a European project on technology-supported integrated care for older people with several conditions.

The method blends fast field appraisal with focused group talks, repeated with different user groups so needs surface early and often. The paper lays out the core steps so other teams can copy or adapt them. The authors argue detailed reporting of such methods matters, because complex care tools often fail when local context is ignored.
plos-pone-0336011:
Isaiah Osei Duah Junior, Danielle Rodriguez, and Cassandra Germain set out this 2026 PLOS One protocol. It plans a systematic review of how music changes the adult brain. Music engages hearing, movement, thought, and emotion at once. That makes it a strong natural test of the brain's power to rewire itself. The review will search seven databases for trials and observational studies. The focus is adults over fifty.

As a protocol, the paper lays out the plan. The team will gather proof on structural brain changes. They will also gather proof on network activity and blood-flow responses to music training or therapy. Where possible, they will link those changes to attention, thinking skills, and language. Two reviewers will extract data on their own. They will judge study quality with standard bias tools. The authors aim to unify findings now scattered across neuroscience.
plos-pone-0336611:
Abbas Ashoori and a team of Iranian researchers mapped where jungle cats are most likely to be killed by traffic in the Hyrcanian forests of northern Iran. These small wild cats face habitat loss and land change, but road deaths stand out as a direct, preventable threat. The team collected collision records and modelled risk with two different statistical approaches, checking the forecasts against each other.

Both models flagged the same danger belt: western Golestan, eastern Mazandaran, and central Gilan provinces. Human footprint mattered in both models, alongside slope or vegetation cover. The authors recommend managing roadside vegetation and building wildlife crossings in the highest-risk stretches, giving conservation planners a concrete map of where fences and passages would save the most cats.
plos-pone-0337311:
Machoka and colleagues, in a 2026 field study, test farm manure and soils in three Kenyan counties for leftover antibiotics and for genes that make germs resist those drugs. Heavy, loosely controlled antibiotic use on farms can seed the wider environment with both. The counties studied farm livestock intensively.

Samples came from thirty farms and were pooled for testing with sensitive chemical and genetic tools. A tetracycline drug, especially one form used widely in animals, was the most common residue, with the highest levels in pig manure. Some expected drugs were not found at all. Resistance genes, by contrast, were spread widely across samples. Which animal produced the manure and whether a sample was manure or soil mattered less than expected for most drug levels. The findings show that resistance genes move through farm waste even where drug leftovers are patchy, a warning for soil and water safety near farms.
plos-pone-0344411:
Leivy Patricia González-Ramírez leads a team of eight mapping how symptoms and well being connect in people seeking online psychological help, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rather than treating each questionnaire score alone, they built a network from seventy-four items answered by over nine hundred Mexican participants in an online well being program. Network analysis shows which feelings sit at the center of the web and which hang at its edges.

Well being items linked negatively to depression, anxiety, negative stress, and rigid thinking patterns, as expected. The most central items concerned how people judge themselves and their emotional state, suggesting self evaluation is a hub where many influences meet. The team also compared men's and women's networks for structural differences. For online programs with limited therapist time, knowing which nodes carry the most connections helps decide what to target in brief support.
plos-pone-0346611:
Gert-Jan Nabuurs and colleagues harmonised tree level forest inventory data from eighteen European countries, covering over two hundred and fifty thousand plots, to map forest structure consistently. Plots were classed by whether one or many species dominate and whether trunk sizes cluster narrowly or spread widely, giving six structure types.

Single species dominance covered just over half the surveyed forest, and narrow size spread was the norm. Regular structure, narrow sizes with one or few species, covered about ninety four percent of forest area by their method. Small plot sizes and a trunk size floor inflate that tidy share, the authors note. Europes forests are far more uniform than natural forests would be.
plos-pone-0347111:
Florence Gyembuzie Wongnaah and co-workers examine what women in Ghana know and feel about a pill that prevents HIV infection. The preventive treatment works well, yet uptake depends on awareness and approval. Their 2026 study uses a large national health survey from twenty twenty-two, covering close to fourteen thousand women of childbearing age across the country.

Only about one woman in eight both knew of the treatment and viewed it well. Rates varied widely by region, with the Ahafo region highest and Savannah lowest. Older women and women who had heard of other sexual health topics scored higher. Women reporting several recent partners scored lower, a worrying gap. The results point to where outreach about HIV prevention is most needed.
plos-pone-0347411:
Yijun Zhang and colleagues screen tropical produce from Hainan, China, for pesticides that routine monitoring misses, in this 2026 PLOS ONE food safety study. Hainan grows much of China's tropical fruit and vegetables, yet many chemicals used there sit outside the official residue watch list, leaving blind spots.

The team tested two hundred sixteen samples from across the island for one hundred seventeen off-list pesticides using sensitive mass spectrometry. Traces turned up in about one sample in ten, and most positive samples carried chemicals missing from routine monitoring, some without any legal residue limit. The authors argue the watch list itself needs widening if regulators want a true picture of what reaches the table.
plos-pone-0347611:
Murat Genc and colleagues put four leading chatbots through a cardiac life support exam in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Advanced cardiac life support is the standardized protocol for treating cardiac arrest, and the team posed fifty questions covering textbook knowledge, image-based items, and patient cases, asking each question three separate times.

Four systems were scored: DeepSeek R1, Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0, and ChatGPT-4o. The scores covered accuracy, sameness of answers across repeats, and handling of visual material. Performance differed across the models and question types, showing that a chatbot strong on facts may falter on images or waver between attempts. For clinicians and trainees, the message is that these tools vary enough to need checking against the official protocol.
plos-pone-0347811:
Anibal Castillo and three colleagues explore a low-cost way to count the tiny animals living in leaf litter, in this 2026 study. Forest floor invertebrates drive decomposition and soil health, yet identifying them the traditional way is slow, expensive, and depends on scarce expert knowledge. The team collected litter where a temperate forest meets open field, dried and ground it, and extracted environmental DNA shed by its inhabitants.

They compared several extraction kits and found one clearly recovered the widest diversity of invertebrate DNA. The animal communities differed between forest and field litter, and temperature strongly shaped which species appeared. Because the method needs no taxonomic experts, the authors present it as a practical tool for monitoring forest health, and for spotting pests and invasive species early across many kinds of habitats.
plos-pone-0347911:
Yelena Tsay and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It examines deaths among newborn babies in Kazakhstan from 2010 to 2023. The authors compare boys and girls, and look separately at the early and late parts of the first month of life.

The analysis is population-based and draws on Global Burden of Disease estimates, a large international health dataset. Breaking mortality and disease burden down by sex and timing shows where newborn care faces its heaviest load. Health officials in Kazakhstan and researchers comparing countries can use these patterns to target care for the most fragile days after birth.
plos-pone-0348011:
Yiyao Deng and colleagues tested whether blocking neutrophils, a type of white blood cell, can protect the brain and kidneys in lupus. In lupus, neutrophils spill web-like traps of DNA that damage tissue. Using mice bred to develop lupus, the team compared two drugs, avacopan and naringenin, against untreated animals.

Both drugs were examined for effects on memory, learning, and mood in maze and field tests, and on kidney function and tissue damage. Avacopan improved the cognitive problems seen in the lupus mice. Staining of brain and kidney tissue tracked how far neutrophils invaded and how much trap material remained. The work supports neutrophil control as a treatment angle for lupus's hardest complications.
plos-pone-0348111:
Sohei Ito and co-workers ask which cells in the aorta wall help a hormone drive dangerous ballooning of that vessel. The hormone angiotensin can swell the chest aorta through one of its receptors, risking a tear. Their 2026 mouse study tracks a family of cells marked by a protein called S100A4 and removes that receptor from those cells alone.

The hormone raised levels of the marker protein in the aorta, and the marked cells spread through the wall. They included muscle cells and support cells of several kinds. Removing the receptor from just this cell family shrank the swelling somewhat, but did not stop it. The cells play a real but partial role, so other wall cells must share the blame.
plos-pone-0348311:
Emily Rickard and Joel Lexchin built a fifty-one question scorecard for how medical societies govern their conflicts of interest, then applied it to sixty-eight Canadian societies. These societies write guidelines and train doctors while often taking industry money, yet nobody had measured their house rules systematically. The team searched public websites for policies across nine areas, from sponsored education to journal dealings.

Fewer than half the societies posted any conflict policy at all. Those that did covered on average under two of the nine areas, and even covered areas were thin, addressing about a third of the relevant items. Declaring speakers' interests at educational events was the commonest rule; rules for research funding, annual meetings, and staff barely existed. The authors conclude that Canadian medical societies police this risk narrowly and unevenly.
plos-pone-0348511:
Liye Han and colleagues tested a gentler oxygen treatment for patients waking up after oesophageal cancer surgery. Lungs often partly collapse once the breathing tube comes out, causing complications. In their 2026 trial, one hundred patients in the recovery unit received either standard oxygen through a mask or high-flow warmed oxygen through the nose, and ultrasound scans tracked lung collapse.

The high-flow group's lung scores improved far more, their blood oxygen ran higher, and only ten percent developed lung complications within a week, against thirty-six percent with standard care. Fewer patients suffered low-oxygen episodes, and sedation and circulation stayed similar. The authors recommend the approach for this high-risk recovery period.
plos-pone-0348611:
Md Mehedi Hasan and colleagues describe CLIN-LLM, a diagnostic support system designed to be cautious where ordinary chatbots are reckless. Their 2026 framework reads a patient's symptoms and vital signs, names likely diseases with a stated confidence level, and drafts treatment suggestions grounded in real doctor-patient dialogues rather than free invention.

Cases the system finds uncertain, about one in five, are automatically routed to a human expert. Built-in checks screen antibiotics and dangerous drug combinations. In tests the system classified diseases from text with high accuracy and cut unsafe antibiotic suggestions sharply compared with a leading general chatbot, while clinicians rated its treatment drafts sound. The team targets clinics with few specialists, where guarded automation could help most.
plos-pone-0348811:
Jabia Mostofa Chowdhury builds a three-dimensional computer model of how an eye drug spreads and fades after injection into the gel of the human eye. The drug blocks abnormal vessel growth in wet macular disease, but human measurements inside the eye are scarce. The 2026 model tracks flow and diffusion under four body scenarios, varying gel state and exit routes for the drug.

Predicted drug lifetimes inside the eye ran from under three days to over four, matching the broad range reported in people. Levels near the macula, the drug's target, could be checked against the floor needed to suppress vessel growth. A tested model like this can explore dosing schedules on a screen instead of in patients' eyes.
plos-pone-0349011:
Roman Holík and colleagues ran a twelve-week jump training trial in thirty-seven young male footballers aged ten to eighteen, asking whether growing bodies at different maturity stages respond differently. Players were sorted by a standard maturity estimate into before and after their growth spurt, then assigned by chance to twice-weekly plyometric sessions or normal training. Speed, agility, jumps, and leg stiffness were tested before and after.

Jump training improved sprinting in both maturity groups, and it alone lifted broad jump and single-leg triple jump, while leg stiffness rose in trainees and sagged in the older control players. Agility improved everywhere regardless of group. Formally, maturity never changed the training effect. The authors endorse jump training across adolescence for speed and explosive power, without needing to time it around the growth spurt.
plos-pone-0349111:
John Owuoth and colleagues measured how often HIV spread among young adults at high risk in Kisumu County, western Kenya, where infection rates run far above the national average. They enrolled six hundred nineteen HIV-negative adults aged eighteen to thirty-five who reported multiple recent partners, many from fishing villages. Participants were tested every three months for up to two years.

Eleven new infections appeared during the follow-up, giving an incidence just under one per hundred person-years, with most infections in the first year. Comparing those who did and did not acquire HIV pointed to risk factors prevention programs can target. Local incidence numbers like these tell health teams whether their efforts are reaching the right people.
plos-pone-0349211:
Jonas Rusnak and colleagues tested whether the drug bulevirtide, which blocks a bile acid transporter in the liver, changes artery disease in mice. They used mice bred to develop atherosclerosis, fed a Western-style diet. Groups received bulevirtide, rifampicin, both drugs, or no drug for four weeks.

Both drugs raised bile acid levels in the blood, and the combination raised them most. Yet cholesterol, other blood fats, plaque size in the aorta, and immune cell content in plaques did not change. The result separates two ideas: raising bile acids in blood is not, by itself, enough to shrink artery plaques in this model.
plos-pone-0349311:
Gabriel Laporta and colleagues studied how deforestation changes infection in the palm-dwelling insects that carry Chagas disease in the southwestern Brazilian Amazon. These triatomine bugs live in palm crowns and harbor the Chagas parasite and a harmless relative. Field teams surveyed twenty landscape units in 2022 and 2024, collecting bugs from palms at measured distances from homes, with forest cover mapped by drones and satellites.

The two parasites answered the landscape differently. The Chagas parasite became more likely as forest cover fell and homes came closer, while its relative followed a contrasting pattern. The result connects land policy to disease risk in a direct way: clearing forest near houses appears to raise the odds that the insects near people carry the dangerous parasite.
plos-pone-0349411:
Shima Rezaei and co-authors followed tomato plants in fish-based growing systems over two years to learn why some plants wilt and die. In these aquaponic setups, fish waste feeds the plants, but sludge can build up around roots and starve them of oxygen. During the first year, coupled systems with poor drainage lost about a fifth of their yield to wilt.

Adding settling tanks and timed pumps fixed the flow, and coupled systems then outyielded the separated ones by a wide margin. Some wilting remained, and sick roots held far less oxygen plus more microbes linked to root disease, while healthy roots carried helpful bacteria. Keeping roots oxygen-rich emerges as the central lesson for long-running systems.
plos-pone-0349511:
Kukiat Tudpor and a team of researchers fed a powder made from partly defatted house crickets to rats bred to have high blood pressure, asking whether the food could protect their bones. Fourteen female rats took the powder daily for four weeks or received a plain substitute, after which their thigh bones were scanned and bent until they flexed to test strength.

Treated rats kept stronger bones than controls, withstanding more force before giving way, even though the inner structure of the bone looked unchanged. Their blood pressure also rose less over the month than that of untreated rats. Cricket powder is rich in protein and minerals, and the results hint it may support bone strength where high blood pressure and weak bones occur together.
plos-pone-0349611:
Toshiko Furukawa and Takuya Iimura built a mathematical model of one of nature's classic trades. Legume plants give carbon to Rhizobium bacteria in their roots, and the bacteria return nitrogen the plant cannot capture alone. Their model adds a strict energy budget, since every exchange costs ATP, the cell's energy currency, and any imbalance is settled by changing bacterial biomass.

Using measured energy costs and the carbon-to-nitrogen ratios of both partners, the model makes three predictions that match real observations. Among them, the plant supplies relatively little carbon while the bacteria supply generous nitrogen, and the shares shift predictably as each partner's body ratio changes. The model explains why this trade stays fair enough to persist.
plos-pone-0350011:
Tuodi Zhang, Songtao Shen, and Yingyi Xu optimized a hybrid system that cleans rural sewage while generating a trickle of electricity: a planted wetland wired as a microbial fuel cell. Winter cold makes rural treatment harder, and electrode settings decide performance. Their 2026 study tuned three electrode parameters statistically for a reed-planted vertical-flow system treating village wastewater.

The hybrid beat a plain wetland clearly. The plain system's outflow missed China's strictest rural discharge limit for organic pollution, while every hybrid configuration met it. At the best settings, the system removed about eighty-nine percent of the pollution load, matching the model's prediction closely. The authors present the tuning recipe as guidance for decentralized village sewage treatment in cold seasons.
plos-pone-0350111:
Nicholas O. Schulte and coauthors published a study in PLOS ONE on squeezing the most species from seawater DNA sampling without overspending. At an intertidal site off Point Conception, California, they compared two filter types, large capsules and small syringe discs, under one lab workflow. Gene markers stood in for vertebrates and for broader animal and plankton life. Each filter's DNA was copied ten times, to ask whether more copies or more samples find more species.

Discs found more vertebrate species than capsules at every comparison level, partly because the workflow processed a smaller effective share of each capsule's larger extract. For the broader marker, the filters performed about equally. Adding copies of one sample accumulated species about as well as adding fresh field samples along their uniform shoreline. Pooling copies worked too. Cheaper, simpler filtration, they conclude, can match or beat pricier setups when the workflow is held constant.
plos-pone-0350611:
O'Shea and colleagues set out a study plan in 2026 on heat, aging, and Alzheimer's disease in South Florida. Five hundred adults aged fifty and older will have their home addresses linked to satellite heat maps. The team will test recent and long-term heat exposure against thinking scores, blood markers, and brain scans.

Heat may also act through inactivity, isolation, and inflammation, which the study will measure. Tree cover near homes will be checked as a possible shield. If neighborhood heat truly tracks brain decline, planting and cooling plans become health policy, especially for older adults in fast-warming cities.
plos-pone-0350811:
Xuejin Ye and co-authors studied a simple blood index in intensive care patients with acute kidney injury in 2026. The index multiplies white cell count by blood sugar, joining two signs of stress and inflammation, and the team asked whether it predicts death.

They drew on two large hospital databases covering more than one hundred thousand admissions. Patients in the highest quarter of the index died more often at one and three months than those in the lowest. The link held after adjusting for other risks and across patient groups. A cheap index from routine tests could help flag kidney patients in danger early.
plos-pone-0351011:
Adanze Nge Cynthia and colleagues mapped what helps and what blocks health care for migrants from Sub-Saharan Africa living in Europe. Fourteen studies passed their checks after searches of five large databases. Most used interviews and close observation. Themes were drawn out by sorting findings across studies rather than counting visits alone.

Three big themes stood out. Gaps in insurance, shaky legal status, and heavy paperwork blocked care in study after study. Undocumented people, women, and people living with HIV faced layered risks. Language gaps and poor cultural fit added further strain. Only one study focused on ageing and long term care choices, a blind spot as these communities grow older in Europe.
plos-pone-0351111:
Mingqiang Wang simulates how railway fasteners muffle inspection sound waves in this 2026 study. Ultrasonic guided waves can scan long stretches of rail for hidden cracks. They travel the full cross-section as they go. Real rails, though, are clamped down by fastener systems. Those clamps bleed wave energy and shorten the inspection range. Wang built a three-dimensional model coupling the fastener's static grip with the wave's fleeting dynamics. A standard preload force squeezed the fasteners in the simulation.

Comparisons were stark. Fastened rail lost wave energy far faster than free rail. Stress maps showed where the clamping concentrated force. Two mathematical styles of modelling the contact were also tested against each other. For rail operators, the physics sets realistic expectations: inspection systems must be calibrated for fastened track, not laboratory rail. Understanding exactly how the clamps drink the signal helps engineers place sensors and interpret echoes on working lines.
plos-pone-0351211:
Quan Zhou and colleagues used a large 2018 survey of healthy ageing in China to study older adults who live apart from their children. More than five thousand such empty nest elders, aged sixty and older, were included. Questions covered arm function, exercise habits, and thinking ability. About fifteen percent showed impaired thinking.

Limited arm function linked with higher odds of poor thinking, even after other factors were counted. Exercise sat in the middle of that link, carrying part of the effect: weak arms may cut activity, and less activity may dull thinking. Because data came from one point in time, cause cannot be proved. Keeping arms strong and daily activity up may still support the ageing mind.
plos-pone-0351311:
Rural officials need current maps of buildings to catch illegal construction and plan disaster response. Jingling Zhong and colleagues built a deep learning system that finds rural buildings in drone and satellite images despite tangled backgrounds, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Three ideas drive the system. Attention modules read buildings at several sizes while muting vegetation and shadow noise. A feature pyramid reroutes information so large and small buildings are both caught. And a learning strategy squeezes value from the few hand-labeled images available by mining the hardest examples. Wide experiments showed gains over standard detectors, offering village governments faster, cheaper mapping.
plos-pone-0351411:
Lingna Huang and colleagues studied women who had induced abortions at a large maternity hospital in Fujian, China. They compare patients from before and after the country adopted its three-child policy. Their 2026 study asks whether the policy changed why pregnancies were unintended and which contraceptive methods women had been using.

Hospital records cover one year on each side of the policy change. They show that not using contraception stayed the leading cause of unintended pregnancy, though its share fell. Among women who did use contraception, condoms and withdrawal remained the most common choices despite their higher failure rates. The authors conclude that little shifted in method choice, so health services still need to tackle non-use and reliance on weak methods.
plos-pone-0351511:
Rahme Nese Safakli and coauthors published a study in PLOS ONE on whether malaria drugs strain the heart's energy system, a safety question for mass drug campaigns. The team worked with human heart muscle cells grown from stem cells, tuned to resemble atrial tissue. They exposed the cells briefly and for longer periods to single malaria drugs and combinations, then measured how well the cells' mitochondria breathed.

Mefloquine, alone and in combinations, reduced mitochondrial respiration, signaling weaker energy production. Long exposure to halofantrine cut the cells' maximum breathing rate and their spare capacity. Four other standard malaria drugs left mitochondrial function intact at both time scales Ivermectin, an anti-parasite drug used in malaria programs, looked harmless briefly but reduced coupling efficiency over longer exposure. The pattern is presented as early safety evidence for treatment programs, with a call for work on the reasons behind the harmful cases.
plos-pone-0351911:
Shomaila Mehmood, Pankaj Bhatia, and Samson Jamesdaniel test a rescue for hearing threatened by chemotherapy, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Cisplatin saves lives, especially in children, but it permanently damages hearing in many patients, and only one preventive drug is approved, for children only. The team gave mice cisplatin alongside MnTBAP, a compound that mimics the body's own antioxidant enzymes, and then measured hearing with electrical and acoustic tests and inspected the inner ear's cells.

Cisplatin alone scarred the system: a damage marker rose in hearing cells and their nerve partners, both cell types died back in the cochlea's middle and base, and hearing thresholds climbed. With the antioxidant aboard, those changes were prevented: hearing sensitivity held, and the cellular damage reversed. The mouse evidence strengthens the case that oxidative chemistry drives this side effect, and that a mopping up drug might one day protect adult patients too.
plos-pone-0352111:
Jingmei Zhou and colleagues improved an animal-inspired search algorithm to sharpen indoor positioning by ultra-wideband radio, the technology behind precision tags in warehouses and hospitals. Walls bend and block the signals, and the standard first-guess method wobbles badly off line of sight. Their upgrade chains that first guess to a grey wolf optimizer toughened with chaotic scrambling, a smoother convergence curve, and shifting weights between exploration and focus.

In complex test environments the improved algorithm settled on the true position faster and landed closer than five rivals, including the standard methods and the unimproved wolf pack. Indoor positioning sounds minor until a robot, a dementia patient, or a forklift depends on it. Better math on the same radios means upgrades without new hardware on the walls.
plos-pone-0352311:
Caiyun Liu and colleagues pooled clinical trials to ask whether adding antibiotics helps treat peri-implantitis, an infection that eats at the bone around dental implants. The usual first step is a deep mechanical cleaning of the implant surface. They searched major databases and combined twenty-two randomized trials comparing cleaning plus antibiotics with other care.

Across the trials, adding antibiotics improved several gum measures, including shallower pockets, better attachment, and less bleeding and plaque. The gains over cleaning with other add-ons were uneven, and the trials differed a lot from one another, which weakens certainty. Still, for dentists weighing whether the drugs are worth it, the pooled evidence leans toward a real, modest benefit on top of thorough cleaning.
plos-pone-0352511: Gu and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how power companies prepare for huge blackouts. Utilities keep a reserve fund and stock emergency gear, and the two choices trade off against each other. The team worked out a joint plan that sizes the fund and places resources together, for several kinds of large blackouts. Better joint planning could shorten the next big outage.
plos-pone-0352811:
Yukari Nakajima and three colleagues test whether two growth factors can speed wound healing. Their 2026 experiment used forty healthy laboratory mice. Each mouse received two circular full-thickness skin wounds. Injections near the wound delivered one growth factor, the other, or both together. A control group received plain saline. One factor targets blood vessel growth, the other lymphatic vessels. Healing was photographed and measured for fifteen days.

The honest headline is a null result. Wounds in every group healed almost identically. Neither factor, alone or combined, beat saline. Counts of new blood and lymphatic vessels inside the healing tissue also matched across groups. One detail did emerge. Larger collecting lymph vessels failed to regrow across wounds, while tiny capillary lymphatics did regenerate. Publishing clear negatives like this saves other laboratories from repeating an attractive but ineffective treatment idea.
plos-pone-0353111:
Llewellyn and colleagues set out a pilot trial plan in 2026 on home exercises for high blood pressure. The plan enrolls seventy treated adults in Newcastle, England, split between a home program and usual care. The home group will do wall squats, a still-hold exercise, three times weekly with remote supervision for twelve weeks, then continue with behavior support.

The pilot judges whether people join, stay, and find the program acceptable over twenty-four weeks. Blood pressure at the clinic and across the day will also be tracked. A workable home option could widen treatment choices for people who dislike gyms or drugs alone.
plos-pone-0353311:
Irvin and colleagues, in a 2026 study, work to improve polygenic risk scores for high blood pressure. Such scores add up many small genetic effects into one risk number, and they often perform unevenly across ancestry groups. The team compared two scoring methods and asked whether extra biological notes on each variant, and a fairer reference panel, could help.

Scores were tuned in a large stroke study with European American and African American participants, then tested in a second study of hypertension genetics. In European Americans, the improved approaches explained several times more risk than the standard setup. In African Americans, gains were real but smaller, so the gap between groups narrowed only partly. Adding notes on what each variant does, and using a reference panel drawn from multiple ancestries, both helped. The authors frame this as progress toward genetic risk tools that serve more than one population well.
plos-pone-0353511:
An editorial note from The PLOS One Editors in 2026 concerns a study comparing salmon availability for two killer whale groups in summer feeding areas. Readers should note this flag on the record. A reader had questioned how the findings were interpreted and how fully prey and feeding information was explained.

Editors followed up with the authors and sought advice from a board member skilled in population data. They concluded that the findings remain supported. The note adds context on earlier research, study limits, and why sites were chosen. It closes gaps in the published explanation rather than changing results, and it lets readers weigh the whale feeding claims with fuller information.
plos-pone-0353611:
Helen Sharp and four colleagues published this 2026 pilot trial for children whose behavior problems survived standard parent training. Their new therapy, RICAP, brings children into reflective work with parents. One hundred and five families first received the established Incredible Years program; children still above the clinical line were randomized to the new therapy or usual clinic care.

Eight months on, parents and teachers disagreed: teacher reports favored usual care on some measures. Sharp stresses the trial proves the two-stage design is feasible, and warns future trials to expect reporter differences.
plos-pone-0353911:
Wang and colleagues, in a 2026 experiment, measure how firefighters' fans clear smoke from a building with an awkward layout. Smoke destroys visibility fast and makes rooms unsurvivable, so crews use fans to push or pull air through openings. Their test space was a two-story structure with bent, non-linear halls joined by a stairwell.

Using harmless artificial smoke, the team compared blowing air in, sucking air out, and a combined push-pull setup, repeating each run several times. The combined mode cleared the space to near-full visibility fastest, cutting clearing time by about a quarter against blowing in and a third against sucking out. Even so, the combined gain fell short of what simply adding the two single effects would promise. The authors offer their numbers as a baseline for training and for clearing smoke after the flames are knocked down, not as a guide for raging fires.
plos-pone-0354311:
This entry is an Expression of Concern issued in 2026 by the editors of PLOS One, and it should be read as a warning label, not as research findings. It concerns an earlier article that claimed a small RNA called MiR-125b slows a pig virus by dampening an immune pathway. After publication, readers raised doubts about the methods and several figures.

The editors list the problems plainly. The test materials were designed from the wrong monkey species' sequences for the cells used. Panels in two figures appeared to overlap or repeat across different conditions, and one figure lacked a detectable background. Board members added that key checks were missing, including proof the treatment worked. The authors answered, supplied corrected versions of two figures and extra data files, and explained their image handling. The editors state they are issuing the notice because the core doubts about the experiments remain unresolved.
plos-pone-0354511:
Louis Tshimanga and co-authors present in 2026 a leaner design for outlining brain tumours in three dimensional scans. Transformer based models read global context well but demand heavy computing, which many labs lack. Their design keeps a standard convolutional encoder and pools a fixed small set of tokens from its feature maps, so token count no longer grows with image size.

On a major glioma challenge dataset the model matched a leading heavy rival on the standard overlap score while using far less memory, time, and parameters. Its attention maps also showed plainly where it looked. Easier training on modest hardware could widen who can develop such tools.
plos-pone-0354611:
Satwik Motaganahalli and co-authors present in 2026 a pilot trial plan on how long antibiotics should run for diabetic foot ulcers where a bedside probe touches bone. That finding suggests bone infection, but in low risk outpatients the test often overcalls it, and bone infection care is heavy. Patients without early X-ray signs will receive either a short or a standard longer course.

Main aims are feasibility and safety: recruitment, staying in the trial, sticking to the plan, harmful events, and hospital stays. Later X-rays and any need to restart treatment or operate add early clinical hints. Results will shape a larger trial on safer, shorter treatment.
plos-pone-0354711:
Yuxin Nong and seven colleagues follow nearly ten thousand people with diabetes in the UK Biobank to ask whether dirty air harms their smallest blood vessels, reporting in 2026. Microvascular complications, damage to eyes, kidneys, and nerves, are among diabetes' most disabling outcomes. The team linked long-term pollution exposure estimates to health records over a median follow-up of more than twelve years.

About one participant in five developed a microvascular complication, and those breathing the most polluted air faced clearly higher risk than those breathing the cleanest. The pattern held for both nitrogen dioxide and larger airborne particles and survived a battery of checks. Risk seemed to rise even at fairly low exposure and showed up early. The authors argue clean-air measures belong in diabetes prevention plans, not just lung health policy.
plos-pone-0354811:
Weixuan Wang, Junhui Wu, and Shaomei Shang published this 2026 analysis of chronic kidney disease in the world's oldest adults. Using the Global Burden of Disease 2021 database, they tracked cases, deaths, and lost healthy years for people aged seventy-five and over across more than two hundred countries, from 1990 to 2021.
