Burden patterns differed widely by region and level of development, so a single global response fits poorly. Wang urges health systems facing fast population aging to tailor kidney screening and care to their own older residents, using this country-level map to place resources.
plos-pone-0355111:
Yuhong Xue and co-authors upgrade in 2026 a popular detection model to find cracks in road surfaces more reliably. Cracks vary in shape, hide in busy backgrounds, and need fine detail, so standard models miss many. Their version fuses normal and heat images early, uses a windmill shaped filter to pull crack features, and adds a wider viewing layer for large cracks.

On a cross border road damage dataset the upgraded model scored higher on accuracy and related measures than the original and other leading models. The authors present it as a dependable tool for automatic road inspection in smart transport systems.
plos-pone-0355211:
Khorshed Alam and co-authors tested brain-inspired computing for spotting intrusions on networks of small connected devices. Such devices cannot run heavy security software, so detection must be light. Their 2026 study built detectors on reservoir computing, where a fixed recurrent pool does most of the work and training stays minimal.

The team tried two reservoir designs on a recent dataset of well over a million network flows, covering many attack types. Both designs performed close to the standard deep learning models used for comparison. They did so while using far fewer computing resources. Alam and colleagues argue reservoir models deserve more attention as a fast, lean option for guarding device networks in real time.
plos-pone-0355411:
Lihui Zhou, Xiansheng Liu, and Shuai Jin build a forecasting model for the temperature of key components inside high-speed train electrical cabinets, in this 2026 study from China. A component running hot can signal overload, poor contact, or failing insulation, and catching the rise early prevents breakdowns and fires. The team assembled time-series data on component temperatures alongside environmental and operating conditions, then pitted a memory-based deep learning network against three established forecasting methods.

The deep network won on both accuracy and stability across standard error measures, tracking long trends and short swings in temperature alike. The authors also tuned its architecture and the length of history it reads, since those choices shaped performance. They present the model as reliable technical support for condition monitoring and early fault warning in equipment whose failure would strand a train.
plos-pone-0355611:
Ke Yang and colleagues present in 2026 a light computer vision system for reading codes engraved on surgical tools. Clear reading matters so each tool can be traced, yet shine off metal, blur, and faint marks make the codes hard to find. Their design adapts a text spotting network with a smaller backbone and adds modules for edge alignment and for focusing on useful channels.

On their own tool dataset the system scored highly and beat its base design by several points, while running fast with few parameters. It also did well on a public scene text set. Hospitals could use such a reader to track tools with less manual work.
plos-pone-0355711:
Arifa Qazi and Attaullah Memon work on a core problem in control engineering in this 2026 paper. Their problem is making a nonlinear system follow a desired reference and shrug off changing disturbances, without measuring everything inside it. Their design pairs a high-gain observer, which estimates the system's hidden states from its outputs, with a controller built on inverse optimal principles and a compensator that keeps steady-state error at zero.

The scheme is meant to keep the optimality and toughness of state-feedback control while working from realistic, partial measurements. The authors tested it in simulation on a nonlinear DC motor, a standard stand-in for real actuators. Against baseline controllers, their design showed stronger robustness and better transient behavior. They present it as a practical route to high-performance control in machines whose behavior refuses to stay simple and linear.
plos-pone-0356611:
Xuguang An, Jin Zhang, Xiaofei Hou, and Chenghao Yang describe a planned clinical trial of brain stimulation for depression that has resisted standard treatment, published as a study protocol in 2026. The trial will enroll seventy patients whose blood tests show raised inflammation, and will test a strong form of alternating current stimulation applied through the scalp.

Half the patients will receive real stimulation for four weeks and half a sham version, with neither patients nor raters knowing which. The team will track depression scores, response and remission rates, brain wave changes, and safety signals such as abnormal heart or brain activity. If stimulation helps this inflamed subgroup, it would support matching depression treatments to biology rather than trial and error.
plos-pone-0356811:
Ana Lúcia Nunes Diniz and colleagues traced childhood tuberculosis in Rio de Janeiro State from 2010 to 2023. They used national notification records. They also used a statistical method that finds the years where trends bend. Their 2026 analysis focused on cases in children and teenagers. It set the pattern against social indicators for the same years.

After earlier declines, reported incidence turned upward from 2020 through 2023. The sharpest rise came in children under five. This is the group most vulnerable to severe disease. The same years saw the state's development index slip. Inequality and infant deaths climbed. The authors cannot prove the social slide caused the tuberculosis rise. But they argue child-focused surveillance and outreach should strengthen when living conditions worsen.
plos-pone-0357011:
Arne Stolp and colleagues published a 2026 paper in PLOS ONE introducing a new way to measure how political views slant people's judgment of evidence. Biased evaluation is often confused with simply holding a political position. Drawing on signal detection theory, a method from psychology, they built a scale that separates a person's accuracy at telling strong evidence from weak evidence from the pull of their ideology.

Two studies with German samples, covering climate and energy policy plus domestic security and migration, gave early support for the scale. Biased judgment turned out to be distinct from education and political knowledge, so it cannot be explained away as ignorance. It also showed some consistency across the two issue areas, suggesting a general habit rather than topic-specific reactions. In the German setting, the bias seemed tied more to social identity and values than to party loyalty alone.
plos-pone-0357311:
Negawo Lelissa and Tewodros Mulugeta published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on fake and watered-down farm chemicals in Ethiopia's Wolmera district, near Addis Ababa. As farming expands, demand for pesticides and fertilizers grows, and with it the market for adulterated products. The authors interviewed several hundred farmers, field agents, and cooperative workers about how common the problem is, what forms it takes, and what damage it does.

Respondents confirmed that adulterated products circulate in local markets, with herbicides, fungicides, and insecticides the most commonly faked. Dilution and under-filled packages were the tricks most often reported. Farmers described damaged crops, lost yields, and wasted money, and said the experience eroded their trust in farm chemicals generally. The authors call for a working regulation system, technology that can spot counterfeits, and real accountability for fraud along the supply chain.
plos-pone-0357411:
Kristina M Kokorelias leads a team of eight publishing the plan for a review of how compassion is defined in dementia caregiving research, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Compassion is praised constantly in care settings, yet researchers use the word loosely, blending it with empathy and emotional labor until it means almost anything. The planned scoping review will map empirical studies of unpaid family caregivers, asking how it, including self compassion, is framed, defined, and turned into measurable practice.

The protocol follows established scoping methods and reporting guidance, searching four major health and psychology databases. Qualitative, quantitative, and mixed studies all qualify, while purely theoretical pieces do not. The payoff the authors promise is a foundation: clear meanings on which future programs for exhausted family caregivers, and honest tools to measure whether those programs work, can finally be built. In a field running on goodwill, definitions are infrastructure.
plos-pone-0357611:
Siyi Song and colleagues test how fitness-themed social media posts affect young women in China, in a 2026 online experiment. Posts of this kind promise drive and discipline but often praise one narrow body shape. Earlier work focused mostly on Western users, so the team asked whether the same harms appear in a Chinese setting with different beauty norms.

More than four hundred women aged from the late teens to mid twenties viewed exercise posts, thin-focused posts, or calm nature scenes. Both image sets lowered how much viewers valued their own bodies and what those bodies can do, with the thin-focused set doing the most harm. Song and co-authors urge readers and platforms to treat workout content as a possible risk, not pure motivation.
plos-pone-0357811:
Ali Shakhshir and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on appendicitis severity in Palestine, asking what can be learned from the removed appendix itself. Clinicians know the usual signs of complicated appendicitis, gangrenous or perforated, but the organ's gross measurements are rarely studied, and Palestinian data were missing. At a Jerusalem charitable hospital, the team reviewed a decade of appendectomies, keeping just over a thousand confirmed cases in four severity grades.

Many features differed across grades, from vomiting and operation length to white cell counts and hospital stay. In the adjusted model, one finding was expected: a hard fecal stone in the appendix more than doubled the odds of complicated disease. Another was not: higher white cell counts oddly went with lower odds. Age, sex, and a common inflammation marker showed no independent link. Overall prediction stayed weak, cautioning against reading severity off any single measure.
plos-pone-0357911: Borráz-León and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study with an odd mix: wealth, health, cats, and a parasite. Toxoplasma gondii is a common parasite often carried by cats. The team compared country-level data from ninety-three nations with how well people said they felt. Such broad comparisons can hint at links worth testing closely, though they cannot prove cause on their own.
plos-pone-0359311: Shi and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how soil-like matter forms without life. They fed glycine, a simple amino acid, into reactions that build humic-like substances, the dark matter that enriches soil. Two clays, montmorillonite and kaolinite, were compared as helpers in the process. How clays steer this chemistry bears on soil health, carbon storage, and ideas about early Earth.
plos-pone-0359411: Erfanifar and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a review on self-injury among teens in Iran. The review will search past work for what raises the risk of self-injury without suicidal intent, and what protects teens from it. Such behavior is a warning sign that calls for care, not punishment. A planned map of risks and protections can guide counselors and families toward the factors they can change.
plos-pone-0359511: Wang and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study asking whether sports facilities can stand in for exercise itself. The question sounds odd: can having gyms and courts nearby give some of the wellbeing that exercise brings? The evidence came from four waves of a large Chinese family panel survey. The answer matters for city planners weighing what public facilities do for health.
plos-pone-0360411:
Ge Song, Siti Hajar Halili, and Zamzami Zainuddin wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on university teaching. Their setting is EFL classrooms, where students learn English as a foreign language. The authors look at interactive response systems, tools that let students answer and react during class through devices.

Going beyond engagement, the study also examines student attitudes and technology acceptance, meaning whether learners find the tools welcome and worth using. A system students resist will fail no matter how active it makes a lesson look. Language teachers and course designers can use these findings when deciding whether response technology belongs in their classrooms.
plos-pone-0360511:
Junji Shimauchi and colleagues built and tested prediction models in 2026 for patients seen by a hospital Medical Emergency Team. These teams are called to wards when a patient suddenly worsens, and within minutes they must judge who needs intensive care and who may not survive. The authors asked whether information available at that moment could predict two outcomes: the need for ICU level intervention, and death within fourteen days.

Their retrospective cohort study developed the models from past cases and checked them by internal validation. A reliable early warning would help teams act sooner for the patients at greatest risk, and plan honestly with families. Prediction at the moment of crisis, rather than on admission, is the gap this work addresses.
pmc-10767911:
Milacic, Beavers, Conley, and co-authors describe the 2024 edition of the Reactome Pathway Knowledgebase. Reactome is a free, expert-checked store of how molecules act together inside cells. It covers normal body processes and also processes that go wrong in disease, all checked by hand.

Each process is stored as an ordered chain of molecular events, from a signal arriving to a cell response. That structure lets researchers place their own data on known pathways and spot what changed. As a core shared resource, Reactome helps labs compare results and build on the same trusted map.
pmc-12972711:
Jerrard and colleagues publish a protocol in this 2026 paper for a scoping review about the words intensive care teams use. Critically ill patients need tightly coordinated multidisciplinary care, yet the concepts underpinning that care, what teams mean by familiar terms, are defined inconsistently, which corrodes communication. Concept analysis studies exist to pin such terms down, but nobody has mapped which ones have been analyzed.

The planned review will search four major databases plus dissertation archives, from inception onward, for concept analysis studies concerning the management of critically ill adults at any stage of the care pathway. Duplicate independent screening and extraction are specified, with results charted in tables and mapped visually across the pathway from admission to recovery. The authors, who registered the protocol openly, aim to show which concepts are settled, which are contested, and where definitional gaps invite future analysis.
pmc-13217211:
Alshehhi and colleagues update what is known about food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome, a severe food allergy in children. Unlike classic allergy, it does not run through IgE antibodies, and its causes stay unclear. It usually starts in the first year of life, often after rice, oats, or cow's milk, foods many babies meet early.

An acute episode begins one to four hours after eating, with repeated vomiting, diarrhoea, and limpness. Bad cases drain fluids until blood pressure falls. Because the picture looks like sepsis or stomach flu, babies are often misdiagnosed at first. The review gathers current thinking on causes, testing, and day-to-day management for families.
pmc-13237811:
Yu and colleagues ask whether allergic diseases and tooth decay truly travel together. Asthma, allergic rhinitis, and eczema share trends and risk factors with dental caries, and both sets of conditions wear down quality of life and raise care costs. Coincidence of timing, though, is not proof of any real link.

The team combined two approaches: a systematic review with meta-analysis of past studies, and Mendelian randomisation, which uses genes as natural experiments to test cause. Together they weigh both association and possible causation between each allergy and decay. The chapbooks, too, keep coming, tales and wonders from the cheap stalls. Band eleven shows Scheible's stock unthinned near the close: the rescue of old print still ran at full pace.

Olive Schreiner published Woman and Labour in 1911 in London. Schreiner, the South African novelist of The Story of an African Farm, had worked on the book for years and lost a longer draft. The published part became her feminist classic.

Schreiner argued that modern industry had taken women's old work out of the home, leaving leisured women as parasites on men's labor. She demanded that women win back a share in all fields of work, not as a favor but as a right. Her image of the leisured woman, ornamental and dependent, stung readers across the English-speaking world. The book shaped suffrage-era thought on women and work.

He draws on Hebrew tradition, Greek practice, and the occult teaching of his own circle. The book served the revival's students as their handbook for the hidden arithmetic of words.

Sepharial's Second Sight, published in 1911, studies clairvoyance, the claimed power of seeing what the senses cannot reach. He divides his subject into natural second sight and induced clairvoyance, trained by practice. The book surveys both with an occultist's sympathy and a reporter's care.

Scottish Highland seers, crystal gazers, and modern psychics all pass through his chapters with their cases and claims. Sepharial weighs the evidence for a faculty beyond the five senses and finds much of it, in his judgment, hard to dismiss. The study preserves the period's best case for second sight as its believers made it.
simmel-philosophische-kultur-1911:
Simmel gathered his essays as Philosophical Culture in German in 1911. The volume is his most readable book, the one where his gift for finding deep meaning in surface things shines brightest. Simmel wrote essays the way other philosophers wrote systems, one bright subject at a time.

The pieces treat Rodin the sculptor, Goethe the poet, the handle of a vessel, fashion, and the inner life of the modern city. Money, which his great Philosophy of Money had analyzed, returns here in essay form. Each piece begins with something small and opens onto the whole structure of modern culture. The book shows why Simmel's lectures drew crowds in Berlin: he made sociology an art form. Readers new to Simmel are still advised to start with these essays.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau: The eleventh volume of the Confessions nears the journey's end. Rousseau's troubled memories grow dreamlike and strangely tender. The old wounds ache a little less sharply now. Twilight of a tormented and brilliant soul, softly fading.
the-phrenological-journal-and-science-of: The Phrenological Journal and Science of Health, 1911. The health journal. This book preserves that periodical. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
the-stokesley-secret-pg3411: Charlotte Yonge’s Stokesley Secret delights young readers. The Victorian moralist tells a wholesome tale. Children learn kindness through adventure. A true girls’ favorite for all time, Yonge, a children's tale, Charlotte Yonge, young readers.
the-tragical-history-of-doctor-faustus-f: Marlowe's Faustus in its longer 1616 printing, the version that added comic scenes and expanded the devil's pageantry. Scholars still debate which quarto is closer to what Marlowe wrote, making this text essential for comparison. Either way, the story of the scholar who traded his soul for knowledge remains English drama's supreme temptation tale.
the-wandering-jew-volume-11: Eugène Sue's Wandering Jew, volume eleven: the grand finale. The serial's magnificent close. Melodrama's last word. The bestseller's end, sue's magnificent finale, the serial ends, melodrama's last word, the finale, the grand finale, Sue.
tob-0011:
One hundred fourteen sayings, and nothing else, make up the Gospel of Thomas. A complete copy in Coptic came to light at Nag Hammadi in Egypt in 1945. No birth story, no miracles, no cross: only the voice of Jesus, teaching in short, sharp lines.

Some sayings match the known Gospels; others sound strange and new. The most quoted promises that the kingdom is inside the hearer and all around, yet people do not see it. Scholars argue over the book's date and sources to this day. The evidence notes no public-domain translation is attached yet. The sayings alone explain the fame.
tob-0039-d11:
Roll 16 is a later reel of the Doctors' Trial microfilm, the verbatim record of the Nuremberg case of 1946 to 1947. By this point the proceedings against the Nazi physicians were far advanced. The transcript keeps the trial day by day, without summary.

Further testimony and exhibits enter the record here as prosecution and defense press their cases toward judgment. The defendants included doctors who had run camp experiments and officials who oversaw them. Kept entire and unedited, the rolls let any reader check later histories against the source. This reel continues the archive that documents how the trial built toward its verdicts and its medical code.
tob-0111:
A. E. Waite, the English occult scholar, restored the Hermetic Museum to print with his own English versions of classic alchemical tracts. The set first appeared in Latin in 1678, gathering works like the Golden Tripod and Sendivogius's New Light of Alchemy. Waite's edition carries his commentary throughout.

He treats alchemy as a spiritual discipline as much as a laboratory art, a view that shaped his whole career. The Victorian revival of alchemy speaks with his voice in this volume. Verified from a pre-1930 edition, the Museum remains a standard shelf of the old tracts, with Waite as a learned, opinionated guide.
tob-10111:
Cyprian, bishop of Carthage in North Africa, wrote On the Unity of the Church in the third century, after fierce persecution had split his church. Some Christians who had lapsed under torture wanted back in, and rival bishops claimed power.

Cyprian argues that the church is one body and that no one can hold faith apart from its bishops and its shared life. His famous claim, that outside the church there is no salvation, shaped Catholic teaching on the church for centuries. The short treatise still anchors debates about unity, authority, and schism.
tob-12911:
Edward FitzGerald's 1859 free translation made the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam among the most quoted verses in English. Khayyam was a Persian astronomer and mathematician; tradition credits him with quatrains, four-line poems, spoken in a skeptical, wine-toasting voice. FitzGerald reshaped selected quatrains into a loose sequence that English readers adopted as one poem.

Wine, roses, and the fleeting hour are urged against the certainty of death and the silence beyond it. Scholars argue over how much is Khayyam and how much FitzGerald, and the argument itself is part of the book's history. As seize-the-day wisdom from medieval Persia in Victorian dress, it remains irresistible.
tob-4011:
Giambattista della Porta of Naples filled twenty books with the wonders of Natural Magick, first in 1558 and enlarged for decades. The English version here rests on a verified 1919 public-domain edition. Porta ran an academy of secrets and tested marvels with boyish delight.

Optics, magnetism, distillation, invisible writing, and strange gardening all get hands-on treatment. Some recipes work, some amuse, and a few alarm. For two centuries the book was a household favorite across Europe, reprinted again and again. It shows the age when science and magic had not yet parted, and when experiment itself still felt like a marvel.
tob-4111:
Ralph T. H. Griffith turned the Rigveda into flowing English verse, and volume one holds the first half of his translation. Griffith, a scholar in India, aimed to make the oldest hymns of India sing for Victorian readers. Agni, Indra, and the gods of storm and dawn lead the collection.

Famous creation hymns ask who really knows how the world began, a note of honest doubt amid the praise. Sacrifice, battle, and prayer shape the rest. Griffith's meter carries lines that prose versions flatten. Verified from the 1919 edition, volume one shows why his Rigveda outsang every rival of its century.
tob-4311:
Valmiki is the name linked to the Yoga-Vasishtha, a huge Sanskrit work of wisdom teaching. Volume one of four, in Vihari-Lala Mitra's translation, opens a long talk between the sage Vasishtha and Prince Rama. Rama is young, troubled by the world, and full of questions about life and death.

Vasishtha answers through stories, arguments, and vivid images. He teaches that the world is shaped by mind, that desire binds people to illusion, and that clear knowledge brings freedom. The teaching unfolds slowly, with tales inside tales. It stands among the longest and deepest works of Hindu thought.
un-ga-res-11:
What should the first Secretary-General of the United Nations be paid? Resolution 11, passed on 24 January 1946, fixes the terms of the post. The pay must be high enough to draw a person of rank and skill. It must also let him keep the standing of the job, in view of the heavy load the Charter lays on the role.

The wage is set to yield a net 20,000 U.S. dollars. A grant of 20,000 more covers the costs of the role, and a furnished house is kept up by the UN. The first term runs five years. At its end, a second term of five years stands open.
un-ga-res-3411:
South Africa's apartheid regime drew a pledge of support for its foes in Resolution 3411, adopted by the General Assembly on 28 November 1975. The vote came as the UN marked its thirtieth year. The text recalls the long chain of Assembly votes condemning apartheid. It rests on the pledges of the Charter and of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

The Assembly proclaims a special duty. The UN and the world at large owe that duty to the oppressed people of South Africa and to their liberation movements. The same duty runs to those jailed for the fight. The brave struggle of the people, and the heavy price they paid, are praised in plain terms.
un-ga-res-a-69-11: Joint work with the Shanghai Cooperation Organization fills Resolution A/69/11, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The bloc, which links China, Russia, and Central Asian states, has held observer status at the Assembly since 2004. Past votes of 2009, 2010, and 2012 framed the tie, and the two bodies' staffs signed a joint pledge in April 2010. The bloc is called a key regional player on safety in its part of the world.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 11, adopted on 24 January 1946, set the terms of appointment of the Secretary-General. The Assembly held that the post, with its heavy duties under the Charter, had to offer terms good enough for a person of high standing to take it and keep it.

The first Secretary-General was to serve five years, with a chance of one more five-year term. Pay was set as a net sum of 20,000 United States dollars plus a like sum as a representation allowance, with a furnished home. The resolution also approved guidance on how future terms could change, and on nomination by the Security Council and appointment by the Assembly, in private and by secret ballot.

General Assembly Resolution 3411 C (XXX), adopted on 28 November 1975, proclaimed a special duty toward South Africa's oppressed people. The Assembly met in the thirtieth anniversary year of the United Nations. It praised the brave fight of that people under their liberation movements. It noted the heavy price they had paid for self-rule.

The text states that the United Nations and the world community bear a special responsibility. The responsibility is toward the oppressed people of South Africa and their movements. It is also toward those jailed, held down, or driven out for fighting apartheid. It promises growing focus and all needed means to end apartheid fast. It promises to work closely with the Organization of African Unity.

General Assembly resolution 69/11 (2014) deals with cooperation between the United Nations and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, an observer since 2004. The Assembly notes the organization's role in regional security. That includes counter-terrorism work through its Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure. It includes cooperation with the United Nations drug office. It proposes regular talks between the two secretariats. The Secretary-General is asked to report to the seventy-first session. United Nations agencies are urged to run joint programs with the organization.
un-sc-res-111:
Resolution 111 deals with an attack by Israeli regular forces on Syrian forces inside Syria on 11 December 1955. The text was adopted on 19 January 1956, though the catalog record gives 1955. The vote was eight to two, with Iran abstaining. UN truce reports said the attack broke the Israel-Syria armistice deal and crossed the demilitarized zone.

The Council also notes Syrian interference with Israeli activity on Lake Tiberias, which broke the armistice terms as well. It holds that this interference in no way justified the Israeli attack. The resolution is one of a run of Council rulings from these years that tried to keep the 1949 armistice lines from sliding into open war.
un-sc-res-1311:
UNOMIG's mandate was renewed on 28 July 2000. The tenth session of the coordinating council had met in Sukhumi on 11 July. The two sides signed a protocol on steadying the security zone. They also agreed to speed work on a protocol for refugee return to Gali and on a draft peace agreement. The Secretary-General's report of 21 July guided the Council.

The Council extended UNOMIG's mandate for six months. It strongly backed the Secretary-General's and his special representative's sustained efforts toward a full settlement. The parties bore the duty to engage in the talks, the Council underlined. Their pledge not to use force to settle the conflict was welcomed. Earlier deals on the ceasefire and on steps inside the zone had to be applied. The population changes forced by the war were restated as unacceptable. Every refugee's right to return home in safety was affirmed once more.
un-sc-res-1411: In the sequence of Security Council decisions, Resolution 1411 is the entry catalogued for 2002 in this library. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations.
un-sc-res-1511:
Resolution 1511, adopted in October 2003, gave legal cover to the foreign forces then occupying Iraq. The United States led a multinational force, but its authority needed the Council's backing. The members authorized the force to take all needed steps to keep security.

The text also urges countries to send troops and money, backs an Iraqi Governing Council timetable toward elections, and expands the UN's own role where safety allowed. Coming months after Resolution 1483, it completed the legal frame for postwar Iraq. Readers see occupation policy being rebuilt as shared international business.
un-sc-res-1611:
On July 7, 2005, bombs tore through London's trains and a bus, killing 52 people. The Security Council answered the same day with Resolution 1611. In it, the members condemn the attacks without reserve and send sympathy to the victims' families.

The text urges every country to help Britain bring the bombers, their planners, and their backers to justice. It repeats the Council's view that terrorism is a threat to peace everywhere, whatever its claimed cause. Brief and direct, the resolution is the world's formal voice speaking in the first hours after an attack.
un-sc-res-1711:
United Nations Security Council Resolution 1711 deals with the Democratic Republic of the Congo at election time. The Council adopted it on 29 September 2006. The Congo was holding its first free elections in decades, with a presidential run-off still ahead. Extra troops borrowed from the Burundi mission were helping guard the process.

The text extends the United Nations mission, called MONUC, until 15 February 2007. The added military and police strength stays for the same period, but only as a stopgap. Both presidential candidates are urged to renew their pledge to fair play. The Council backs the plan to make Kinshasa a weapons-free city province, with fighters kept in camps.
un-sc-res-1811: Resolution 1811 is a formal act of the Security Council, preserved here in the wording of the UN's official record via Wikisource. The document speaks once, as a body, after negotiation among fifteen delegations. That single voice, with its findings and its numbered decisions, is the content of the entry, kept complete for reference and citation.
un-sc-res-1911:
Côte d'Ivoire's mission was extended amid voter list disputes on 28 January 2010. The Ouagadougou Agreement of 2007 and its four supplements set the peace frame. A presidential election, due within ten months of the deal, was years late. Progress toward a final voters list had been made. The Council recalled its December 2009 statement backing a credible vote.

The Council extended UNOCI's mandate until 31 May 2010. It restated its resolve to back a credible electoral process in full. Ivorian leaders were urged to publish the final voters list without delay and to keep the process open to civil society. The special representative's certification role was restated: his word would frame the Council's judgment of the process. Election dates set by the Ivorian parties, once certified, would guide the mission's planning. The Council stressed that a free and fair vote remained the path out of the long crisis.
un-sc-res-2011: Resolution 2011 is a formal act of the fifteen-member Security Council, preserved here in official-record wording through Wikisource. Its paragraphs were drafted to be implemented by people who were not in the room, which is why they spell out duties so plainly. The entry preserves that plain spelling entire, from first finding to last instruction.
un-sc-res-211:
India and Pakistan got a dated cease-fire order on 20 September 1965. The Secretary-General had consulted both governments under resolutions 209 and 210. Their replies to his appeal differed, and no cease-fire had yet taken hold. The Council judged an early halt to the fighting the first step toward settling Kashmir and the other disputes.

The Council demanded that a cease-fire take effect on Wednesday, 22 September 1965, at 0700 hours GMT. Both governments had to issue the orders at that moment. All armed personnel would then pull back to the positions held before 5 August 1965. The Secretary-General was asked to provide help in watching the cease-fire and the withdrawal. All states were called to avoid any act that might inflame the region. Once the order held, the Council would weigh steps toward a settlement of the political problem beneath the war.
un-sc-res-311:
South Africa's apartheid drew the Council's condemnation at Addis Ababa on 4 February 1972. The meeting heard invited speakers on the question, along with the special committee on apartheid. South Africa's repression was growing, and its military build-up continued. The government had refused every Council call for a peaceful settlement under the Charter.

The Council condemned South Africa for pursuing apartheid in breach of its Charter duties. It restated its total opposition to the policy. The struggle of South Africa's oppressed people for their human and political rights was recognized as legitimate. Pretoria was urgently called to free all persons jailed, interned, or restricted under apartheid. All states were called to observe the arms embargo strictly. Governments and private givers were urged to fund United Nations programs for the humanitarian and training needs of apartheid's victims. Groups teaching and training South Africans won the Council's praise.
un-sc-res-411:
Rhodesia's attacks on Mozambique were condemned with a call for aid on 30 June 1977. Mozambique's president had cabled the Secretary-General on 18 June. A FRELIMO minister described the recent acts of aggression in detail. The African ministers at Libreville had taken up the crisis.

The Council strongly condemned the illegal racist minority regime for its aggression against Mozambique. It declared that such acts, with the attacks on Zambia and Botswana, were grave breaches of those states' sovereignty. South Africa was condemned for backing the Rhodesian regime against the sanctions decisions. The regime's survival was named a source of insecurity for the whole region. Mozambique won praise for keeping the sanctions faithfully. The Council demanded full respect for Mozambique's borders. It asked the Secretary-General to arrange prompt aid for Mozambique's losses and called on all states and United Nations bodies to give it.
un-sc-res-611:
The killing of a senior Palestinian leader in Tunis was condemned on 25 April 1988. Tunisia's complaint letter of 19 April told of an attack at Sidi Bou Said on 16 April 1988. The raid took human life, above all in the assassination of Khalil El Wazir, the Palestine Liberation Organization's second in command. The Council recalled resolution 573 (1985), passed after Israel's bombing of Tunis that year.

The Council condemned vigorously the aggression against Tunisia's sovereignty and territorial integrity. It was a flagrant breach of the Charter and of international law, the text said. Member states were urged to take measures to stop such acts against the sovereignty of any state. The Council voiced its determination to take fitting steps to see the text carried out. The Secretary-General was asked to report urgently on any new facts in the case.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Switzerland wanted the world court's law without the UN itself. Its famed neutrality kept it out of the new body. But court rules let non-members join the court's statute on set terms. The Assembly would fix those terms, with the Council's advice. Resolution 11, from 1946, gave that advice.

Berne would join the statute once it filed a signed pledge. The pledge had three parts. The Swiss would accept the court's statute in full. They would take on the duties of UN members under the Charter's court clause. And they would pay a fair share of the court's costs. The Assembly would set that sum after talks with Berne. The text shows how the postwar order bent, just a bit, to fit a proud neutral.

Security Council resolution 111 was adopted on 19 January 1956, by 8 votes to 2, with 1 abstention. It condemns an Israeli attack on Syrian forces of 11 December 1955 near Lake Tiberias. According to the Chief of Staff of the Truce Supervision Organization, Israeli regular forces had crossed the demilitarized zone and entered Syria. They acted in deliberate violation of the Israel-Syria General Armistice Agreement.

The Council holds that Syrian interference with Israeli activities on Lake Tiberias in no way justified the attack. It condemns it as a flagrant violation of the cease-fire and the Charter. It expresses grave concern at Israel's failure to meet its obligations. It warns that it will have to consider further measures if Israel does not comply in future. It calls on both parties to respect the demarcation line and demilitarized zone. It asks for an immediate exchange of all military prisoners.

Resolution 1311, adopted on 28 July 2000, extends the UN Observer Mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, amid the Abkhazia conflict. The Georgian and Abkhaz sides had just met in Sukhumi and signed a protocol to steady the security zone. They also agreed to speed work on drafts covering refugee return to the Gali region and a pledge against renewed fighting. The zone was fairly calm but still unstable.

The Council extends UNOMIG until 31 January 2001. It backs work on sharing powers between Tbilisi and Sukhumi as the core of a full settlement inside Georgia. It repeats that population shifts caused by the conflict are unacceptable and that all refugees and displaced people may return home in safety and dignity. It demands strict respect for the 1994 Moscow ceasefire deal and calls on both sides to fight crime in the conflict zone together.

Judges who hold two nationalities raise a legal puzzle, and this text of 17 May 2002 solves it. The war crimes tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and for Rwanda both bar two judges of the same nationality from sitting together. At least one elected judge already held more than one nationality, so the rule needed clarifying.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council amended both tribunal statutes. A judge with two or more nationalities now counts as a national only of the state where they normally exercise civil and political rights. The replacement articles are set out in annexes. The change kept the balance rules workable without forcing dual-national judges off the bench.

Iraq's path back to self-rule under occupation is addressed on 16 October 2003. The Governing Council had formed a committee to prepare a constitutional conference. The day Iraqis govern themselves, the Council repeats, must come quickly, while stability still has to be restored first.

A multinational force under unified command is authorized to contribute to security in Iraq, building on the framework set earlier that year. The occupying Authority is called on to hand governing powers back to Iraqis as soon as practicable and to report on progress with the Governing Council. States are urged to give the force troops and resources, and a United Nations role is backed as conditions allow.

Bombs struck London's transport system during the morning rush on 7 July 2005, and the Council condemned the attacks that same day. It acted within hours, in line with its statements after earlier attacks in Bali, Istanbul, and elsewhere.

The attacks are condemned without reservation and treated, like any act of terrorism, as a threat to peace and security. Deepest sympathy goes to the victims and their families and to the people and government of the United Kingdom. All states are urged to cooperate actively, under resolution 1373, to find and bring to justice those who carried out, organized, and sponsored the attacks.

Congo's first democratic elections in decades drive Resolution 1711, adopted on 29 September 2006. Voters had turned out in great numbers on 30 July for the first round, and the presidential run-off and provincial polls were set for 29 October. Fighting between forces loyal to the two remaining candidates had shaken Kinshasa in August. Militias still threatened the east.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MONUC until 15 February 2007, keeping the extra military and police strength approved earlier. It extends to 31 December 2006 the temporary transfer of a battalion, a hospital, and 50 observers from the Burundi mission, ONUB. It calls on all Congolese parties to keep the elections free, fair, and peaceful, keep security forces impartial, and avoid incitement. The Secretary-General must recommend by the end of January 2007 how MONUC's mandate should adjust after the elections.

Somalia's arms embargo Monitoring Group is extended again on 29 April 2008. The text recites the embargo's exemptions with care. Arms and training meant solely for the African Union mission, AMISOM, do not breach the ban. The same holds for help building Somalia's own security institutions, under the conditions set. All other flows of weapons into Somalia remain banned.

The group's mandate is extended so it can keep documenting violations and naming supply routes, reporting through the sanctions committee. The committee itself is asked to act on the group's findings and to visit the region. The renewal came as AMISOM struggled with too few troops and Somalia's transitional government faced a growing insurgency, making the embargo both harder to enforce and more central to policy.

Côte d'Ivoire's delayed presidential election drives Resolution 1911, adopted on 28 January 2010. The Ouagadougou Political Agreement of 2007 had set a path to reunite the divided country and hold a vote within ten months. The first round had slipped again, to late February or early March 2010, though a provisional voters list had been published and certified.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the UN Operation in Côte d'Ivoire, UNOCI, until 31 May 2010, and extends the backing given to the French forces that support it. It urges Ivorian leaders to publish the final voters list and set the election date. It says the UN envoy's certification of each stage is vital for a credible vote. It also signals it may raise troop levels from 7,450 to at most 7,950 once the final list appears.

Afghanistan is the subject of Resolution 2011, adopted on 12 October 2011. The International Security Assistance Force, called ISAF, was helping the Afghan government fight the Taliban. It was also building up Afghanistan's own security forces. A transition plan was meant to hand responsibility to Afghan authorities over time.

The Council extended ISAF's authorization for twelve months, until 13 October 2012. The states serving in the force could take all necessary measures to carry out its mandate. The text backed Afghan-led reforms under the Kabul Process. It pressed for progress on government, corruption, and drug trafficking. Security gains were tied to development and the rule of law. The message was that military work alone would not settle Afghanistan.

Resolution 211, adopted on 20 September 1965 by ten votes to none with Jordan abstaining, sets a hard deadline for the India-Pakistan war. The Secretary-General had shuttled between the two capitals under earlier September resolutions, with uneven replies to his ceasefire appeal. The Council judged that an early end to hostilities was the essential first step toward settling Kashmir and the other disputes.

It demanded that a ceasefire begin on Wednesday, 22 September 1965, at seven in the morning, Greenwich time. Both governments were to order their forces to stop and then pull all armed personnel back to the positions held before 5 August. The Secretary-General was to provide the help needed to supervise both steps.

Apartheid is condemned outright in Resolution 311, adopted on 4 February 1972 by fourteen votes to none with France abstaining, during the Council's special meetings in Addis Ababa. South Africa kept intensifying repression at home and building up its military, the Council charged, while refusing every UN call for a peaceful solution under the Charter. Invited South Africans and the Assembly's apartheid committee addressed the session.

The Council condemned the South African government for continuing apartheid in violation of its Charter obligations. It repeated its total opposition to the policy. And it recognized the legitimacy of the struggle of South Africa's oppressed people to win their human and political rights, language with real weight in 1972.

Mozambique under fire is the charge in Resolution 411. It passed by a full vote on 30 June 1977. Samora Machel, the state's chief, had wired the UN with the news. A top FRELIMO man told the hall of raid after raid by Rhodesia's white-led rebel regime. The African bloc's council, in session at Libreville, had taken up the raids too. They killed Mozambicans and wrecked homes, roads, and goods.

The Council voiced hot wrath at the steady raids. It condemned the attacks and the worse turn the Rhodesia crisis had taken. It called for world aid to flow to Mozambique. It restated the right of Zimbabwe's people to rule their own land in freedom. The raids, aimed at camps of Zimbabwe's fighters, dragged Rhodesia's war past its own borders.

Resolution 611, adopted on 25 April 1988, condemns an Israeli assassination raid in Tunisia. Tunisia's complaint letter of 19 April described the attack six days earlier at Sidi Bou Said, in which several people were killed, most prominently Khalil al-Wazir, a senior Palestinian commander. The Council noted that it had condemned a similar Israeli raid on Tunisia in 1985 and demanded Israel not repeat such acts.

The Council vigorously condemned the new aggression against Tunisia's sovereignty and territorial integrity as a flagrant violation of the Charter. It called the raid a serious and renewed threat to peace and stability in the Mediterranean. Israel was again told to refrain from such attacks.

Lithuania had restored its independence in March 1990, defying Moscow. Soviet troops killed civilians in Vilnius in January 1991. By late summer the coup in Moscow had failed. Recognition poured in. Resolution 711, adopted without a vote on 12 September 1991, took up Lithuania's application for UN membership.

The Council recommended Lithuania's admission to the General Assembly. The Assembly seated it five days later, beside Estonia and Latvia. For Lithuanians, the UN seat sealed their break with the Soviet Union. It restored a state erased from the map in 1940. The Baltic admissions were among the most symbolic of the Cold War's end.
underhill-mysticism-1911:
Underhill's Mysticism, published in 1911, is the epochal study of the nature and growth of man's spiritual consciousness. She wrote it after years of reading the mystics of many lands in their own words. The book defined the modern study of mysticism for the English-speaking world.

Underhill maps the mystic way in stages: awakening, purgation, illumination, the dark night, and the unitive life. She illustrates each stage from Teresa, John of the Cross, Julian, and dozens of lesser-known witnesses. Her mix of scholarship, sympathy, and clear order turned a scattered library into one readable story.
vaisesika-sutras-sinha-1911:
Nandalal Sinha translated the Vaisesika Sutras of Kanada into English in 1911. Kanada founded the Vaisesika school of Indian philosophy in ancient times. His sutras argue that everything reduces to eternal atoms combining under unseen law.

Earth, water, fire, air, minds, and souls all get sorted into categories. The system lists qualities, actions, and relations with rigorous care. Atomism was therefore born in India as well as in Greece. Sinha's edition includes commentary helping readers through the compressed aphorisms. The Vaisesika later merged closely with the Nyaya school of logic. Sinha's translation made this rigorous ancient physics available in English.
vinogradoff-growth-of-the-manor-1911:
Vinogradoff published The Growth of the Manor in 1911, his second great study of medieval England. The manor, a lord's estate worked by dependent tenants, was the seedbed of English rural society for centuries. Vinogradoff asked where it came from, and his answer reached back to Rome.

He follows the manor from possible Roman roots in the villa, through the free village communities of the early English, to its feudal prime under the Normans. The lord's hall becoming the manor court is the story's turning point, as custom hardened into jurisdiction. His evidence is charters, surveys, and court rolls, handled with famous precision. The book dug to the roots of English society and settled questions scholars had argued for a generation. It stands beside his Villainage as a foundation of manorial studies.
waite-pictorial-key-to-the-tarot-1911:
Arthur Edward Waite gave the modern tarot its fixed face and book in 1911. The Pictorial Key to the Tarot explains the deck he devised with the artist Pamela Colman Smith. That deck, the Rider-Waite, is the one most readers still learn on.

Waite tells the lore of the cards, then walks through each trump and suit card in turn. He gives the meanings he held true and scorns mere fortune-telling tricks. His readings stress sign and soul over luck and dread. For a century, tarot study has run in the channel this book cut.
ward-realm-ends-1911:
Gifford Lectures again gave James Ward his platform in The Realm of Ends, published in 1911. The subtitle joins its two themes: pluralism and theism. Ward pictured the world as a realm of many free agents, each with its own ends. That picture stood against any single force ruling all.

Across the lectures he asks how many centers of life can form one moral world. God, in his account, works with free beings rather than moving them like tools. He draws on science and on daily moral experience alike. The book states his mature system in full. It rewards readers patient with big questions.
wattles-science-being-great-1911:
Greatness completes Wattles's trilogy in The Science of Being Great, published in 1911 after his death. Getting Rich and Being Well came first; this last book asks what a person should become. Wattles answers that greatness means expressing the advancing mind within, the soul growing into its full size.

He writes for ordinary readers who suspect they were made for more than their present station. Perception, faith, and steady purpose form his path, stated in short, firm chapters. The trilogy's close shows the reach of New Thought ambition: money, health, and character all under one law of thought.
wells-country-of-blind-and-other-stories:
H. G. Wells put out The Country of the Blind, and Other Stories in 1911. The book holds a long run of his short tales from the years past. Its title tale is one of his most famed works. A lost range in the Andes hides a vale where all are blind.

A climber falls into the vale and thinks he can rule the blind folk. Their touch and ear prove sharp past his sight, and his plans fail. The Empire of the Ants tells of ants that learn war and sweep up a river land. The set is a strong late store of Wells's short art.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol11:
After a gap in printing, Volume XI of the Journal of Discourses appeared at Liverpool in 1867. Brigham Young and his fellow leaders fill its pages with sermons taken down as spoken. The church they led had weathered war years and kept building, and the pulpit voice here sounds settled and sure.

Doctrine, history, and counsel blend in the talks, aimed at Saints old and new. The Journal's long run lets readers trace how teachings were repeated and reshaped over time. Volume XI resumes that record after the pause, a key link between the early and later sets.
zimmern-greek-commonwealth-1911:
Alfred Zimmern published The Greek Commonwealth in 1911, a portrait of Athens in the 400s BC. Zimmern treats politics, economy, and thought as parts of one whole. The polis, or city-state, is his central subject. Pericles' Athens stands at the height of its power and art.

He explains farms, trade, slaves, festivals, and assemblies in plain terms. Thucydides serves as his chief guide and hero. Zimmern wrote for students and general readers, not only specialists. The book became the classic English portrait of fifth-century Athens. Its warm liberal faith in the city-state reflects its age. Later scholarship revised details, yet the whole still charms and instructs.
zohar-de-pauly-french-vol-6-1911:
Jean de Pauly finished his French Zohar in 1911 with this sixth tome. The Zohar, the Book of Splendor, is the supreme work of the Kabbalah, an Aramaic commentary on the Torah ascribed to the school of Moses de Leon. De Pauly's six tomes form the only complete translation of it in the public domain.

The closing tome brings the long commentary to its end, with the last portions of the Torah read as maps of the divine life. Rabbi Shimon and his companions have by now taught a whole cosmos: God in ten lights, Israel in exile, and the world awaiting repair. De Pauly's achievement gave the West its first full Zohar. The set stands complete in this volume.
